The Architecture of Association: How Classical Conditioning Builds Learned Responses
column8: Pavlov (1927): "Any external stimulus which is to become the signal in a conditioned reflex must overlap in point of time with the action of an unconditioned stimulus." In delay conditioning, the CS onset precedes US onset with temporal overlap, and this arrangement is the most effective for establishing classical conditioning.
column9: Delay conditioning is a type of forward conditioning in which presentation of the conditioned stimulus precedes and overlaps presentation of the unconditioned stimulus, and it is the most effective method for establishing a conditioned response.
column13: Delay conditioning, in which the CS onset precedes and temporally overlaps the US onset, is the most effective arrangement for establishing a classically conditioned response.

Domain Code: The Architecture of Association: How Classical Conditioning Builds Learned Responses
column8: Pavlov, I.P. (1927). Conditioned reflexes: An investigation of the physiological activity of the cerebral cortex. Oxford University Press: "Any external stimulus which is to become the signal in a conditioned reflex must overlap in point of time with the action of an unconditioned stimulus." In delay conditioning, the CS onset precedes and temporally overlaps the US onset, and this arrangement is the most effective method for establishing a conditioned response.
column9: Delay conditioning, where the conditioned stimulus precedes and overlaps presentation of the unconditioned stimulus, is the most effective method for establishing a conditioned response through classical conditioning.
column13: Delay conditioning, in which the CS precedes and temporally overlaps the US, is the most effective method for establishing a classically conditioned response.

Domain Code: The Architecture of Association: How Classical Conditioning Builds Learned Responses
column8: Rescorla, R.A. (1988). Pavlovian conditioning: It's not what you think it is. American Psychologist, 43(3), 151-160: "The previously neutral conditioned stimulus comes to elicit the response" after pairing with the unconditioned stimulus. "One, initially neutral in that it elicits no response, is called the conditioned stimulus (CS); the other, which is one that consistently elicits a response, is called the unconditioned stimulus (US)."
column9: In classical conditioning research, the white rat was the conditioned stimulus, because it produced a startle response after being repeatedly paired with the unconditioned stimulus, an unexpected loud noise, which naturally elicited a startle response.
column13: In classical conditioning, a neutral conditioned stimulus (CS) acquires the ability to elicit a conditioned response after repeated pairing with an unconditioned stimulus (US) that naturally elicits a response.

Domain Code: The Architecture of Association: How Classical Conditioning Builds Learned Responses
column8: Watson, J.B. & Rayner, R. (1920). Conditioned emotional reactions. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 3(1), 1-14: "The instant the rat was shown, the bar was struck immediately behind his head." The CS (white rat) was presented and overlapped in time with the US (loud noise), consistent with delay conditioning -- the CS precedes and temporally overlaps the US. Watson used this forward/delay conditioning procedure to establish Little Albert's conditioned fear response to the white rat.
column9: John Watson used delay conditioning to establish Little Albert's fear response to white rats.
column13: Watson used delay conditioning with Little Albert, presenting the CS (white rat) before and overlapping with the US (loud noise) to establish a conditioned fear response.

Domain Code: The Architecture of Association: How Classical Conditioning Builds Learned Responses
column8: Rescorla, R.A. (1988). Pavlovian conditioning: It's not what you think it is. American Psychologist, 43(3), 151-160: The CR is typically similar to but may differ from the UR, and is generally less intense. Rescorla notes "an important, but poorly appreciated, fact about conditioning that makes nonsense of any claim that a signal simply acquires the ability to evoke the response to the US."
column9: The conditioned response elicited by a neutral stimulus in classical conditioning is usually less in intensity than the unconditioned response.
column13: The conditioned response in classical conditioning is typically similar to but less intense than the unconditioned response.

Domain Code: The Architecture of Association: How Classical Conditioning Builds Learned Responses
column8: Pavlov (1927): "If a tone of 1000 d.v. is established as a conditioned stimulus, many other tones spontaneously acquire similar properties, such properties diminishing proportionally to the intervals of these tones from the one of 1000 d.v." Stimuli resembling the original CS elicit the CR despite never being directly paired with the US.
column9: Stimulus generalization occurs when stimuli similar to the original conditioned stimulus elicit the conditioned response without ever being presented with the unconditioned stimulus.
column13: Stimulus generalization occurs when stimuli similar to the original CS elicit the conditioned response despite never being directly paired with the unconditioned stimulus.

Domain Code: The Architecture of Association: How Classical Conditioning Builds Learned Responses
column8: Watson, J.B. & Rayner, R. (1920). Conditioned emotional reactions. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 3(1), 1-14: After conditioning Little Albert to fear the white rat, "the response to the rabbit, the dog, and the fur coat were [also] evoked." Albert's fear response to other white, furry stimuli -- though never directly paired with the loud noise -- demonstrates stimulus generalization: stimuli resembling the original CS elicit the CR without separate conditioning.
column9: Little Albert's response to other white furry stimuli was due to stimulus generalization.
column13: Little Albert's fear response to other white, furry stimuli never paired with the loud noise demonstrated stimulus generalization, as shown by Watson and Rayner (1920).

Domain Code: The Architecture of Association: How Classical Conditioning Builds Learned Responses
column8: Pavlov (1927): "The hitherto quiet dog began to squeal in its stand, kept wriggling about, tore off with its teeth the apparatus for mechanical stimulation of the skin." "The clashing of excitation with inhibition led to a profound disturbance of the usual balance between these two processes." Experimental neurosis arises when an organism must discriminate between highly similar stimuli.
column9: Pavlov's canine subjects exhibited "experimental neurosis" due to the requirement to make difficult discriminations between similar stimuli, which provoked agitation and aggression.
column13: Pavlov's experimental neurosis arose in dogs required to make difficult discriminations between highly similar stimuli, producing agitation and disrupted behavior.

Domain Code: The Architecture of Association: How Classical Conditioning Builds Learned Responses
column8: Pavlov (1927): "Repeated application of a conditioned stimulus which is not followed up by reinforcement leads to a weakening of the conditioned reflex." "Left to themselves extinguished conditioned reflexes spontaneously recover their full strength after a longer or shorter interval of time." "It cannot be regarded as an irreparable destruction of the conditioned reflex... evidenced by the fact that the extinguished reflexes spontaneously regenerate in course of time." Extinction suppresses rather than eliminates learned associations.
column9: Spontaneous recovery refers to the return of an extinguished conditioned response without the conditioned stimulus being presented again with the unconditioned stimulus, confirming that a conditioned response is suppressed rather than eliminated by extinction trials.
column13: Spontaneous recovery — the return of an extinguished CR after a rest interval without reconditioning — demonstrates that extinction suppresses rather than permanently eliminates the learned association.

Domain Code: The Architecture of Association: How Classical Conditioning Builds Learned Responses
column8: Pavlov, I.P. (1927). Conditioned reflexes: An investigation of the physiological activity of the cerebral cortex. Oxford University Press: "Left to themselves extinguished conditioned reflexes spontaneously recover their full strength after a longer or shorter interval of time." "It cannot be regarded as an irreparable destruction of the conditioned reflex." Spontaneous recovery after extinction trials demonstrates that extinction is due to internal inhibition (active suppression) rather than the erasure of the learned association.
column9: Pavlov's observation of spontaneous recovery of a conditioned response after extinction trials provides evidence that extinction is due to internal inhibition.
column13: Pavlov's observation of spontaneous recovery after extinction provides evidence that extinction results from internal inhibition (active suppression) rather than erasure of the learned association.

Domain Code: Beyond the Basics: Higher-Order Conditioning, Blocking, and Overshadowing
column8: Rizley, R.C. & Rescorla, R.A. (1972). Associations in second-order conditioning and sensory preconditioning. Journal of Comparative and Physiological Psychology, 81(1), 1-11: "A typical second-order conditioning situation in which S1 is first paired with a US and then S2 is regularly followed by S1. As a consequence of the first stage, presentation of S1 elicits a CR, while during the second-order conditioning stage S2 also comes to elicit that CR." CS2 elicits a CR even though it was never directly paired with the original US.
column9: Pavlov's higher-order conditioning experiment involved pairing a tone with food so that the dog salivated when the tone was presented alone, and then pairing a light with the tone so that the dog also salivated when the light was presented alone.
column13: In second-order conditioning, CS2 acquires the ability to elicit a conditioned response after being paired with CS1, even though CS2 was never directly paired with the original unconditioned stimulus.

Domain Code: Beyond the Basics: Higher-Order Conditioning, Blocking, and Overshadowing
column8: Pavlov (1927): Higher-order (second-order) conditioning involves first establishing a conditioned stimulus (CS1) by pairing it with an unconditioned stimulus, then pairing a new neutral stimulus (CS2) with the already-established CS1. "A well-established conditioned stimulus is used in the place of the unconditioned stimulus" so that CS2 also acquires the ability to elicit a conditioned response when presented alone, without ever having been directly paired with the unconditioned stimulus.
column9: Higher-order conditioning involves treating the initial conditioned stimulus as an unconditioned stimulus and pairing it with a neutral stimulus so that the neutral stimulus also becomes a conditioned stimulus and elicits a conditioned response when presented alone.
column13: In higher-order (second-order) conditioning, a new neutral stimulus (CS2) paired with an already-established CS1 acquires the ability to elicit a conditioned response without ever being directly paired with the unconditioned stimulus.

Domain Code: Beyond the Basics: Higher-Order Conditioning, Blocking, and Overshadowing
column8: Kamin, L.J. (1969). Predictability, surprise, attention, and conditioning. In B.A. Campbell & R.M. Church (Eds.), Punishment and aversive behavior (pp. 279-296): Prior conditioning to stimulus A "blocks" conditioning to stimulus B when both are presented as a compound AB paired with the US. The US must be "surprising" for new learning to occur. When the US is already fully predicted by the pre-trained CS, no additional associative strength accrues to the new stimulus presented simultaneously.
column9: In classical conditioning, blocking occurs when a new neutral stimulus is simultaneously presented with a previously conditioned stimulus before presenting the unconditioned stimulus, preventing the new neutral stimulus from becoming a conditioned stimulus.
column13: Kamin's blocking effect occurs when prior conditioning to stimulus A prevents new conditioning to stimulus B when AB is compounded with the US, because the US is no longer surprising.

Domain Code: Beyond the Basics: Higher-Order Conditioning, Blocking, and Overshadowing
column8: Kamin (1969): Prior conditioning to stimulus A prevents conditioning to stimulus B when both are presented as a compound AB paired with the US. The US must be surprising for learning to occur. If the US is fully predicted by Stimulus A, no new learning about Stimulus B occurs.
column9: Blocking occurs when a new neutral stimulus is presented with a conditioned stimulus, preventing the new stimulus from becoming a conditioned stimulus.
column13: Kamin's blocking effect demonstrates that prior conditioning to stimulus A prevents new learning about stimulus B in an AB compound because the US must be surprising for conditioning to occur.

Domain Code: Beyond the Basics: Higher-Order Conditioning, Blocking, and Overshadowing
column8: Mackintosh, N.J. (1976). Overshadowing and stimulus intensity. Animal Learning & Behavior, 4(2), 186-192: "Pavlov (1927) used the term 'overshadowing' to describe the observation that conditioning to a relatively weak stimulus might be severely attenuated if it was always presented in conjunction with a more intense stimulus." "When one component was markedly more salient than the other, the more salient overshadowed the less salient."
column9: Testing the effects of overshadowing involves presenting two neutral stimuli together before the unconditioned stimulus, which leads to the less salient conditioned stimulus being overshadowed by the more salient one.
column13: Overshadowing occurs when a more salient stimulus presented in compound with a less salient stimulus attenuates conditioning to the less salient stimulus.

Domain Code: Consequences That Shape Behavior: Reinforcement, Punishment, and the Operant Framework
column8: Thorndike (1911): Thorndike's research with cats in a puzzle box led to his development of the law of effect: "Of several responses made to the same situation, those which are accompanied or closely followed by satisfaction to the animal will, other things being equal, be more firmly connected with the situation... those which are accompanied or closely followed by discomfort to the animal will, other things being equal, have their connections with that situation weakened."
column9: Thorndike's research with cats in a puzzle box led to his development of the law of effect.
column13: Thorndike's law of effect states that responses followed by satisfying outcomes are strengthened while those followed by discomfort are weakened, derived from his puzzle-box research with cats.

Domain Code: Consequences That Shape Behavior: Reinforcement, Punishment, and the Operant Framework
column8: Skinner (1953): "We define the negative reinforcer (an aversive stimulus) as any stimulus the withdrawal of which strengthens the behavior." Behavior that terminates an aversive stimulus is strengthened by removal of that stimulus.
column9: Negative reinforcement occurs when a behavior continues or increases because performing the behavior results in the termination or withdrawal of a stimulus, as exemplified by a woman who eats chocolate because it reduces her anxiety.
column13: Negative reinforcement strengthens behavior by removing an aversive stimulus contingent upon that behavior.

Domain Code: Consequences That Shape Behavior: Reinforcement, Punishment, and the Operant Framework
column8: Dinsmoor, J.A. (1977). Escape, avoidance, punishment. Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior, 28(1), 83-95: "The only requirement is that these responses produce earlier termination of the shock when the animal is holding the bar down at the moment of onset than when it is somewhere else, off the bar." The behavior that results in removal of the aversive stimulus is the one being negatively reinforced. Always identify whose behavior is being strengthened by the removal of the aversive stimulus -- that individual is under negative reinforcement control.
column9: Mrs. Smith's reprimands for her son Sam hitting the family dog are being controlled by negative reinforcement.
column13: In negative reinforcement, the behavior that produces removal of an aversive stimulus is strengthened; always identify whose behavior is increased by the aversive stimulus's removal.

Domain Code: Consequences That Shape Behavior: Reinforcement, Punishment, and the Operant Framework
column8: Lerman, D.C. & Vorndran, C.M. (2002). On the status of knowledge for using punishment. Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis, 35(4), 431-464: Negative punishment involves "the removal of stimuli, often called negative punishment (i.e., response cost, time-out from positive reinforcement)." The removal of a desirable stimulus following a behavior decreases the likelihood of that behavior occurring in the future.
column9: Negative punishment occurs when a behavior decreases or stops because a stimulus is removed following the behavior, as in the situation where a 12-year-old boy stops teasing his younger sister because his parents subtract 50 cents from his weekly allowance whenever he does so.
column13: Negative punishment decreases the future probability of a behavior by removing a desirable stimulus contingent upon that behavior.

Domain Code: Consequences That Shape Behavior: Reinforcement, Punishment, and the Operant Framework
column8: Moher, C.A. et al. (2008). Non-generalized and generalized conditioned reinforcers. Behavioral Interventions, 23(1), 13-38: Generalized conditioned reinforcers "may be less sensitive to the effects of satiation" because their effectiveness "does not depend on a single kind of deprivation." "Increasing the number of backup reinforcers with which the token was paired resulted in the effectiveness maintaining during satiation conditions."
column9: Generalized reinforcers (e.g., money, tokens) are less susceptible than primary and secondary reinforcers to satiation because they can be exchanged for a variety of back-up (primary) reinforcers.
column13: Generalized conditioned reinforcers (e.g., money, tokens) are less susceptible to satiation than primary reinforcers because their effectiveness depends on access to multiple backup reinforcers rather than a single deprivation state.

Domain Code: Consequences That Shape Behavior: Reinforcement, Punishment, and the Operant Framework
column8: Skinner, B.F. (1953). Science and human behavior. Macmillan: A positive discriminative stimulus (S^D) "sets the occasion" for a response by signaling that reinforcement is available. In its presence, the operant response is reinforced; in its absence, the response goes unreinforced. The S^D does not elicit the behavior but rather indicates that reinforcement is contingent upon the response.
column9: A positive discriminative stimulus signals that a behavior will be reinforced.
column13: A positive discriminative stimulus (S^D) signals that reinforcement is available for a response but does not elicit the behavior; it sets the occasion for the operant response.

Domain Code: Consequences That Shape Behavior: Reinforcement, Punishment, and the Operant Framework
column8: Baer, D.M., Wolf, M.M., & Risley, T.R. (1968). Some current dimensions of applied behavior analysis. Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis, 1(1), 91-97: The discriminative stimulus (SD) signals that reinforcement is available for a particular response; in its presence a response is reinforced, and in its absence it goes unreinforced.
column9: When using stimulus control to increase a behavior, the presence of a discriminative stimulus indicates that the behavior will be reinforced.
column13: A discriminative stimulus (SD) signals that a particular response will be reinforced, thereby increasing the probability of that response in its presence.

Domain Code: Consequences That Shape Behavior: Reinforcement, Punishment, and the Operant Framework
column8: Dinsmoor, J.A. (1977). Escape, avoidance, punishment. Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior, 28(1), 83-95: "More rapid termination of the shock selectively reinforced the behavior of holding the bar down." Escape conditioning is a form of negative reinforcement in which a behavior terminates an ongoing aversive stimulus.
column9: Continuing to say "I love you" to his mother whenever she yells at the boy is a result of escape conditioning, where the behavior is maintained because it allows the boy to "escape" his mother's yelling.
column13: Escape conditioning is a form of negative reinforcement in which a behavior is strengthened because it terminates an ongoing aversive stimulus.

Domain Code: Consequences That Shape Behavior: Reinforcement, Punishment, and the Operant Framework
column8: Mowrer, O.H. (1956). Two-factor learning theory reconsidered. Psychological Review, 63(2), 114-128: "Basically the two-factor, or two-process, hypothesis holds that habits are learned on the basis of the reinforcement provided by reward, or drive reduction, and that fears are learned (conditioned) on the basis of the contiguous occurrence of a signal and punishment." Avoidance conditioning combines (1) classical conditioning of fear to a neutral stimulus and (2) operant conditioning (negative reinforcement) in which the avoidance behavior is maintained because it reduces conditioned fear.
column9: Avoidance conditioning is an example of two-factor learning that combines classical conditioning and negative reinforcement.
column13: Mowrer's two-factor theory holds that avoidance conditioning combines classical conditioning of fear to a neutral cue and operant negative reinforcement in which the avoidance response is maintained by reducing conditioned fear.

Domain Code: Consequences That Shape Behavior: Reinforcement, Punishment, and the Operant Framework
column8: Mowrer, O.H. (1956). Two-factor learning theory reconsidered. Psychological Review, 63(2), 114-128: "Basically the two-factor, or two-process, hypothesis holds that habits are learned on the basis of the reinforcement provided by reward, or drive reduction, and that fears are learned (conditioned) on the basis of the contiguous occurrence of a signal and punishment." Avoidance involves (1) classical conditioning of fear to a neutral stimulus and (2) operant conditioning of avoidance behavior reinforced by fear reduction.
column9: Mowrer's (1960) two-factor theory of learning proposes that avoidance conditioning is an example of two-factor learning because it combines classical conditioning and negative reinforcement (operant conditioning).
column13: Mowrer's two-factor theory proposes that avoidance behavior involves classical conditioning of fear to a neutral stimulus and operant conditioning (negative reinforcement) in which avoidance is maintained by fear reduction.

Domain Code: Schedules, Shaping, and the Fine-Tuning of Behavior
column8: Lerman, D.C. et al. (1996). Responding maintained by intermittent reinforcement. Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis, 29(2), 153-171: "Switching from an INT to a CRF schedule prior to extinction may lower the baseline response rate." Continuous reinforcement carries a high risk of satiation, while transitioning to intermittent reinforcement reduces satiation risk and maintains behavior.
column9: Switching from a continuous schedule to an intermittent schedule of reinforcement reduces the risk for satiation when a parent is using positive reinforcement to establish a desirable behavior in their child.
column13: Switching from a continuous reinforcement schedule to an intermittent schedule reduces the risk of satiation while maintaining behavior.

Domain Code: Schedules, Shaping, and the Fine-Tuning of Behavior
column8: Nevin, J.A. & Grace, R.C. (2000). Behavioral momentum and the Law of Effect. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 23(1), 73-90: "Variable-ratio (VR) schedules usually maintain much higher response rates than VI schedules." The variable ratio schedule produces the highest and most consistent response rate among the four basic intermittent schedules. When using positive reinforcement to establish or increase a behavior, use of the variable ratio schedule maximizes resistance to extinction.
column9: When using positive reinforcement to establish or increase a behavior, use of the variable ratio schedule of reinforcement will maximize the behavior's resistance to extinction.
column13: The variable-ratio schedule produces the highest and most consistent response rates and maximizes resistance to extinction among the four basic intermittent reinforcement schedules.

Domain Code: Schedules, Shaping, and the Fine-Tuning of Behavior
column8: Nevin, J.A. & Grace, R.C. (2000). Behavioral momentum and the Law of Effect. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 23(1), 73-90: "Variable-ratio (VR) schedules usually maintain much higher response rates than VI schedules." Among the four basic intermittent schedules (FR, VR, FI, VI), the variable-ratio schedule produces the highest and most consistent response rates and the greatest resistance to extinction.
column9: The variable ratio schedule of reinforcement produces the highest and steadiest rate of responding and the greatest resistance to extinction.
column13: The variable-ratio schedule produces the highest, steadiest rate of responding and the greatest resistance to extinction among the four basic intermittent reinforcement schedules.

Domain Code: Schedules, Shaping, and the Fine-Tuning of Behavior
column8: Hagopian, L.P. et al. (2011). Reinforcement schedule thinning following functional communication training. Behavior Analysis in Practice, 4(1), 4-16: Schedule thinning involves "altering the reinforcement schedule, usually in a systematic and progressive manner across multiple sessions, until some terminal schedule, judged to be practical for care providers to implement, is reached." The systematic, gradual transition from dense to lean reinforcement schedules.
column9: Reducing the amount of positive reinforcement, referred to as thinning, involves going from a "thicker" reinforcement schedule to a "thinner" one.
column13: Schedule thinning is the systematic, gradual transition from a dense (thick) to a lean (thin) reinforcement schedule until a practical terminal schedule is reached.

Domain Code: Schedules, Shaping, and the Fine-Tuning of Behavior
column8: Hagopian, L.P. et al. (2011). Reinforcement schedule thinning following functional communication training. Behavior Analysis in Practice, 4(1), 4-16: Schedule thinning involves "altering the reinforcement schedule, usually in a systematic and progressive manner across multiple sessions, until some terminal schedule, judged to be practical for care providers to implement, is reached." Thinning is the gradual transition from a denser (thicker) to a leaner (thinner) reinforcement schedule.
column9: Reducing the amount of positive reinforcement is referred to as thinning.
column13: Thinning refers to the gradual, systematic reduction of reinforcement density, transitioning from a denser to a leaner reinforcement schedule.

Domain Code: Schedules, Shaping, and the Fine-Tuning of Behavior
column8: Herrnstein, R.J. (1961). Relative and absolute strength of response as a function of frequency of reinforcement. Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior, 4(3), 267-272: "The relative frequency of responding on a key equaled the relative frequency of reinforcement from it." The matching law states that the relative rate of responding on a particular alternative matches the relative rate of reinforcement obtained from that alternative. When two or more concurrent schedules operate simultaneously, the organism distributes its behavior proportionally to the reinforcement each schedule delivers.
column9: The matching law predicts the effects of two or more concurrent schedules of reinforcement on the behaviors that are being reinforced.
column13: Herrnstein's matching law states that an organism's relative rate of responding on concurrent schedules proportionally matches the relative rate of reinforcement obtained from each alternative.

Domain Code: Schedules, Shaping, and the Fine-Tuning of Behavior
column8: Reynolds, G.S. (1961). Behavioral contrast. Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior, 4(1), 57-71: Positive behavioral contrast occurs when reinforcement for one behavior in a multiple schedule is discontinued while reinforcement for the other behavior remains unchanged, resulting in the still-reinforced behavior increasing in rate above its original baseline level, while the no-longer-reinforced behavior decreases.
column9: Positive behavioral contrast occurs when two behaviors are being reinforced and the reinforcement for one behavior is stopped while reinforcement for the other behavior stays the same, resulting in the behavior that is no longer reinforced decreasing and the behavior that is still receiving the same amount of reinforcement increasing.
column13: Positive behavioral contrast occurs in multiple schedules when reinforcement for one behavior is discontinued, causing the rate of the still-reinforced behavior to increase above its original baseline.

Domain Code: Schedules, Shaping, and the Fine-Tuning of Behavior
column8: Reynolds, G.S. (1961). Behavioral contrast. Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior, 4(1), 57-71: "The increase in the rate of responding during one component of a multiple schedule when the conditions in another component are changed so as to decrease the rate of responding during that component" constitutes behavioral contrast. When reinforcement is discontinued for one behavior but maintained for another, the still-reinforced behavior increases in rate -- a phenomenon termed behavioral contrast.
column9: The boy's response to the change in reinforcement, where the point system is stopped for cleaning the cat box but not for taking out the garbage, is referred to as behavioral contrast.
column13: Behavioral contrast occurs when discontinuing reinforcement for one behavior in a multiple schedule causes the rate of the still-reinforced behavior to increase above its original baseline level.

Domain Code: Schedules, Shaping, and the Fine-Tuning of Behavior
column8: Terrace, H.S. (1963). Discrimination learning with and without "errors." Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior, 6(1), 1-27: "S--'s duration and brightness is progressively increased until S+ and S-- differ only with respect to wavelength." Fading is the systematic and gradual removal of prompts (supplementary cues such as brightness or size differences) so that behavior comes under the control of the natural discriminative stimulus alone.
column9: The gradual removal of visual or auditory hints or cues (prompts) is referred to as fading.
column13: Fading is the systematic, gradual removal of supplementary prompts so that behavior comes under control of the natural discriminative stimulus alone.

Domain Code: Schedules, Shaping, and the Fine-Tuning of Behavior
column8: Terrace, H.S. (1963). Discrimination learning with and without "errors." Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior, 6(1), 1-27: "S--'s duration and brightness is progressively increased until S+ and S-- differ only with respect to wavelength." By gradually changing stimuli, organisms can learn discriminations "without errors." Fading involves the gradual withdrawal of auxiliary stimulus differences (prompts) so that behavior comes under control of the natural discriminative stimulus alone.
column9: In the context of operant conditioning, fading refers to the systematic and gradual removal of prompts.
column13: Fading is the systematic and gradual removal of prompts so that behavior comes under control of the natural discriminative stimulus alone.

Domain Code: Applied Principles and the Bridge to Research Methods
column8: Skinner, B.F. (1948). "Superstition" in the pigeon. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 38(2), 168-172: Skinner referred to the unusual behaviors exhibited by pigeons -- such as bowing, turning, and hopping on one foot -- as "superstitious behavior." When pigeons were delivered food pellets every 15 seconds regardless of their behavior, they developed ritualistic responses as if those behaviors caused the food delivery. "The bird behaves as if there were a causal relation between its behavior and the presentation of food, although such a relation is lacking."
column9: B. F. Skinner (1948) referred to the unusual behaviors, such as bowing, turning, and hopping on one foot, exhibited by pigeons who were delivered food pellets every 15 seconds regardless of their behavior as superstitious behaviors.
column13: Skinner termed the ritualistic behaviors (bowing, turning, hopping) pigeons developed under noncontingent fixed-time food delivery superstitious behavior, as if the behavior caused food delivery.

Domain Code: Applied Principles and the Bridge to Research Methods
column8: Reynolds, G.S. (1961). Behavioral contrast. Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior, 4(1), 57-71: When reinforcement is stopped for one of two concurrently reinforced responses (e.g., pressing Bar B), positive behavioral contrast predicts that the still-reinforced response (pressing Bar A) will increase in frequency while the no-longer-reinforced response (pressing Bar B) decreases.
column9: If reinforcement is stopped for pressing Bar B, a rat will press Bar A with greater frequency and Bar B with less frequency.
column13: Positive behavioral contrast occurs when reinforcement is discontinued for one of two concurrently reinforced responses, causing the still-reinforced response to increase in frequency.

Domain Code: Applied Principles and the Bridge to Research Methods
column8: Steckler, A. & McLeroy, K.R. (2008). The importance of external validity. American Journal of Public Health, 98(1), 9-10: External validity concerns "whether causal relationships can be generalized to different measures, persons, settings, and times."
column9: External validity refers to the extent to which research results are generalizable to other people, settings, and times.
column13: External validity refers to the degree to which research findings can be generalized to different persons, settings, and times.

Domain Code: Applied Principles and the Bridge to Research Methods
column8: Denzin (1970/2017): Triangulation is "the combination of two or more theories, sources of data, research methods, in the study of a singular phenomenon." Between-methods triangulation specifically involves combining both qualitative and quantitative methods to collect data on the same research question, enhancing confidence in findings by leveraging the complementary strengths of different methodological approaches.
column9: Triangulation refers to the use of more than one approach to the investigation of a research question in order to enhance confidence in the ensuing findings, and between-methods triangulation involves including both qualitative and quantitative methods to collect data.
column13: Between-methods triangulation combines qualitative and quantitative data collection on the same research question to enhance confidence in findings by leveraging complementary methodological strengths.

Domain Code: Applied Principles and the Bridge to Research Methods
column8: Messick, S. (1995). Validity of psychological assessment. American Psychologist, 50(9), 741-749: Concurrent validity involves administering the test and criterion at approximately the same time and correlating the scores.
column9: Evaluating a newly developed 10-item screening test's concurrent validity involves administering the test to a sample of clinic patients along with an established (validated) 50-item measure of depression and correlating the two sets of scores.
column10: Test Validity - Content and Construct Validity
column13: Concurrent validity is established by administering a new test and an established criterion measure at approximately the same time and correlating the two sets of scores.

Domain Code: Applied Principles and the Bridge to Research Methods
column8: Mosier (1951): Cross-validation involves applying a prediction equation from one sample to a new, independent sample. The validity coefficient is typically smaller in the cross-validation sample because sample-specific chance factors that inflated the original coefficient are absent.
column9: When a test is cross-validated on another sample, the criterion-related validity coefficient usually is smaller than the initial coefficient obtained on the original sample.
column10: Test Validity - Content and Construct Validity
column13: Cross-validation typically yields a smaller validity coefficient than the original sample because sample-specific chance factors that inflated the initial coefficient are absent in the new sample.

Domain Code: Relationships in Data: Correlation and Bivariate Statistics
column8: Mukaka, M.M. (2012). A guide to appropriate use of correlation coefficient in medical research. Malawi Medical Journal, 24(3), 69-71: Pearson's product moment correlation coefficient "represents the strength of the putative linear association between the variables in question." "It is used when both variables being studied are normally distributed." Appropriate when both variables are continuous and measured on an interval or ratio scale.
column9: The Pearson r correlation coefficient would be used to determine the degree of association between age in years and reaction time in seconds, as both represent a ratio scale of measurement.
column13: Pearson's product moment correlation coefficient measures the strength of a linear association and is appropriate when both variables are continuous and normally distributed on interval or ratio scales.

Domain Code: Relationships in Data: Correlation and Bivariate Statistics

column13: Tertiary circular reactions in Piaget's substage 5 (12–18 months) involve infants deliberately varying their actions to observe different outcomes, reflecting intentional experimentation.

column9: According to Piaget, children begin to be able to observe another child perform a complex action and then imitate that action for the first time on the following day when they're between 18 and 24 months of age.
column13: Piaget placed deferred imitation at sensorimotor substage 6 (18–24 months), but Meltzoff demonstrated it can occur as early as 9–14 months, challenging Piaget's timeline.

Domain Code: How Minds Begin: Piaget's Sensorimotor Stage and the Construction of Infant Knowledge

These abilities reflect the child's capacity to create mental representations -- internal images of objects and events that can be recalled and acted upon in the absence of the original stimulus. The emergence of representational thought marks the transition from sensorimotor to preoperational intelligence.
column9: Piaget attributed children's ability to engage in deferred imitation and make-believe play to the ability to create mental representations, which emerges during the final substage of the sensorimotor period at about 18 months of age.
column13: Piaget attributed deferred imitation and make-believe play to the emergence of mental representation during substage 6 of the sensorimotor period at approximately 18 months, marking the transition to preoperational intelligence.

Domain Code: How Minds Begin: Piaget's Sensorimotor Stage and the Construction of Infant Knowledge
column8: Bauer (2007) / Berk (2018): "Childhood (infantile) amnesia is the inability to recall autobiographical events from before age 3–4, attributed to immature brain structures, lack of coherent self-concept, and limited language for encoding narrative memories."
column9: Sense of self and language skills are most useful for understanding childhood amnesia, the inability of adults to recall events they experienced before the age of 3 or 4.
column13: Childhood (infantile) amnesia—the inability to recall autobiographical events before age 3–4—is attributed to immature brain structures, lack of a coherent self-concept, and limited language for encoding narrative memories.

Domain Code: How Minds Begin: Piaget's Sensorimotor Stage and the Construction of Infant Knowledge
column8: Piaget (1964) / Berk (2018): "Accommodation involves modifying an existing schema or creating a new one to incorporate information that does not fit existing cognitive structures." When a child recognizes that a cat does not belong in the 'dog' schema and creates a new 'cat' schema, this is accommodation — adjusting mental structures to account for new experiences.
column9: A young child's realization that the neighbor's cat is not the same as the family dog and starting to call it "kitty" instead of "doggie" is an example of accommodation according to Piaget's theory.
column13: Accommodation, per Piaget, involves modifying an existing schema or creating a new one when new information cannot fit existing cognitive structures, as when a child creates a separate "cat" schema after recognizing a cat is not a dog.

Domain Code: How Minds Begin: Piaget's Sensorimotor Stage and the Construction of Infant Knowledge
column8: Piaget (1964) / Berk (2018): "Assimilation is the process of incorporating new information into an existing cognitive schema without modifying the schema." When a child interprets the moon's apparent movement as 'following' them, the child is assimilating this observation into the existing schema that things that move alongside you are following you.
column9: In this situation, the child is assimilating the apparent movement of the moon into what he already knows - i.e., things that move with you are following you.
column13: Assimilation, per Piaget, is incorporating new information into an existing schema without modifying it, as when a child interprets the moon as "following" them based on an existing schema about moving objects.

Domain Code: How Minds Begin: Piaget's Sensorimotor Stage and the Construction of Infant Knowledge
column8: Case (1985) / Shaffer & Kipp (2014): "Neo-Piagetian theories retain Piaget's constructivist stage framework but integrate concepts from information-processing theory — particularly working memory capacity, processing speed, and executive function — to explain stage transitions."
column9: Neo-Piagetian theories of cognitive development are best described as a combination of elements of Piaget's constructivist theory and information processing theories.
column13: Neo-Piagetian theories (Case, 1985) retain Piaget's constructivist stage framework while integrating information-processing concepts such as working memory capacity, processing speed, and executive function to explain stage transitions.

Domain Code: The First Words: How Infants Build a Language from Sound and Meaning
column8: Brown & Bellugi (1964): "In English the order of words in a sentence is an important grammatical signal. Order is used to distinguish among subject, direct object, and indirect object." Phonemes are the smallest units of sound that signal a difference in meaning.
column9: The smallest distinctive units of sound in a language are referred to as phonemes.
column13: Phonemes are the smallest units of sound in a language that signal a difference in meaning.

Domain Code: The First Words: How Infants Build a Language from Sound and Meaning
column8: Brown (1973) / Berk (2018): "A morpheme is the smallest unit of language that carries meaning. Free morphemes (e.g., 'do,' 'cat,' 'run') can stand alone as words. Bound morphemes (e.g., '-ed,' '-ing,' 'un-') must be attached to other morphemes to convey meaning."
column9: An example of a morpheme is "do".
column13: A morpheme is the smallest unit of language that carries meaning; free morphemes can stand alone while bound morphemes must attach to other morphemes to convey meaning.

Domain Code: The First Words: How Infants Build a Language from Sound and Meaning
column8: Brown & Bellugi (1964): Children's speech preserves the word order of adult models but omits functors — inflections, auxiliary verbs, articles, prepositions, and conjunctions. Free morphemes can stand alone as words (e.g., 'do'); bound morphemes cannot stand alone and must attach to another morpheme (e.g., 'pre-,' '-ism').
column9: Morphemes are the smallest meaningful units in a language, such as "inter," "er," "ism," "pre," and "post" in English.
column13: Free morphemes can stand alone as words, while bound morphemes must attach to another morpheme; children's telegraphic speech preserves adult word order but omits bound grammatical morphemes and functors.

Domain Code: The First Words: How Infants Build a Language from Sound and Meaning
column8: Brown (1973) / Berk (2018): "Morphemes are the smallest meaningful units of language. The word 'unsustainable' contains three morphemes: the bound morpheme 'un-' (prefix meaning 'not'), the free morpheme 'sustain' (can stand alone as a word), and the bound morpheme '-able' (suffix meaning 'capable of'). Thus it has two bound morphemes and one free morpheme."
column9: The word "unsustainable" has two bound morphemes and one free morpheme.
column13: The word "unsustainable" contains three morphemes: one free morpheme (sustain) and two bound morphemes (un- and -able).

Domain Code: The First Words: How Infants Build a Language from Sound and Meaning
column8: Wolff (1969) / Berk (2018): "Newborns produce three distinct cry patterns: the basic (hunger) cry, the angry cry (louder and more intense), and the pain cry (sudden onset, long initial cry followed by breath holding)."
column9: Newborns emit three different cries that indicate hunger, anger, or pain.
column13: Wolff identified three distinct newborn cry patterns: the basic/hunger cry, the angry cry (louder and more intense), and the pain cry (sudden onset with a long initial cry followed by breath holding).

Domain Code: The First Words: How Infants Build a Language from Sound and Meaning
column8: Oller (2000): "Babbling emerges between 3–6 months with repetition of vowel-consonant combinations, initially including sounds from multiple languages."
column9: Babbling emerges between 3 and 6 months of age and initially involves the repetition of single vowel-consonant combinations that include sounds from different languages.
column13: Babbling emerges between 3–6 months with repetition of vowel-consonant combinations and initially includes sounds from multiple languages before narrowing to the native language.

Domain Code: The First Words: How Infants Build a Language from Sound and Meaning
column8: Kuhl (2004): "Infant babbling narrows to primarily native-language phonemes by approximately 9–10 months, reflecting perceptual narrowing."
column9: Infant babbling initially includes sounds from all languages but begins to narrow to the sounds of the infant's native language by about 9 months of age.
column13: By approximately 9–10 months, infant babbling narrows to native-language phonemes through perceptual narrowing, having initially included sounds from all languages.

Domain Code: The First Words: How Infants Build a Language from Sound and Meaning
column8: Goldfield & Reznick (1990): "The vocabulary spurt typically begins around 18 months when children have acquired approximately 50 words, with word learning accelerating dramatically."
column9: The vocabulary spurt, when babies use about 50 words, usually begins around 18 months of age.
column13: The vocabulary spurt typically begins around 18 months when children have acquired approximately 50 words, after which word learning accelerates dramatically.

Domain Code: The First Words: How Infants Build a Language from Sound and Meaning
column8: Chomsky (1959): "The fact that all normal children acquire essentially comparable grammars of great complexity with remarkable rapidity suggests that human beings are somehow specially designed to do this." Humans possess an innate capacity for language allowing detection of native language structure from limited input.
column9: Noam Chomsky attributed language acquisition to an innate language acquisition device.
column13: Chomsky proposed that humans possess an innate language acquisition device that enables rapid acquisition of complex grammar from limited input.

Domain Code: Words in the World: How Language Meets Social Context
column8: Clark (1973) / Berk (2018): "Underextension occurs when a child restricts a word to only a specific instance of the category rather than applying it to all members."
column9: Underextension occurs when a child applies a word only to a specific person, object, or event rather than to all the people, objects, or events it applies to.
column13: Underextension occurs when a child restricts a word to only a specific instance of a category rather than applying it to all members of that category.

Domain Code: Words in the World: How Language Meets Social Context
column8: Clark (1973): "Overextension occurs when a child applies a word too broadly — using it for objects sharing some perceptual feature with the referent but not belonging to the correct category."
column9: When a child learns the word "dada," she initially applies it to all adult males, which is an example of overextension.
column13: Overextension occurs when a child applies a word too broadly to objects sharing a perceptual feature with the correct referent, as when "dada" is used for all adult males.

Domain Code: Words in the World: How Language Meets Social Context
column8: Brown & Bellugi (1964): "At about eighteen months children are likely to begin constructing two-word utterances; such a one, for instance, as Push car." Two-word combinations (telegraphic speech) emerge between 18-24 months, using high-content words in grammatically meaningful order while omitting functors.
column9: Children use two words to create a simple sentence, such as "juice gone," "get toy," and "big doggie," by about 18 to 24 months of age.
column13: Telegraphic speech, emerging between 18–24 months, consists of two-word utterances that preserve meaningful word order while omitting grammatical functors such as articles and prepositions.

Domain Code: Words in the World: How Language Meets Social Context
column8: Grice (1975) / Berk (2018): "Pragmatics is the social use of language in context, including understanding humor, sarcasm, implied meaning, conversational rules, and interpreting nonliteral language."
column9: People who struggle with pragmatic language often have difficulty understanding humor and sarcasm.
column13: Pragmatics is the social use of language in context, encompassing humor, sarcasm, implied meaning, conversational rules, and nonliteral language interpretation.

Domain Code: Words in the World: How Language Meets Social Context
column8: Gumperz (1982) / Berk (2018): "Code-switching is the practice of alternating between two or more languages or language varieties within a single conversation or utterance." Bilingual and multilingual speakers use code-switching strategically to signal group identity, establish solidarity, convey emphasis, or navigate social contexts.
column9: Code-switching is used by bilingual and multilingual speakers to establish solidarity with listeners belonging to their own minority group.
column13: Code-switching is the practice of alternating between languages or language varieties to signal group identity, establish solidarity, convey emphasis, or navigate social contexts.

Domain Code: Words in the World: How Language Meets Social Context
column8: Morales & Hanson (2005): "Language brokering can have both positive effects (cognitive benefits) and negative effects (role reversal stress)."
column9: Language brokering, the act of translating and interpreting within immigrant families by children and adolescents for their parents, can have both positive and negative effects on the child and the parent-child relationship.
column13: Language brokering — children and adolescents translating for immigrant parents — can have both positive effects (cognitive benefits) and negative effects (role reversal stress) on the child and parent-child relationship.

Domain Code: Words in the World: How Language Meets Social Context
column8: Wertsch (1984): "Vygotsky defined the zone of proximal development as 'the distance between the actual developmental level as determined by independent problem solving and the level of potential development as determined through problem solving under adult guidance or in collaboration with more capable peers.'" Higher mental functions first appear on the social plane before being internalized on the individual plane.
column9: According to Vygotsky's theory, the acquisition of knowledge depends primarily on social interactions.
column13: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development is the distance between a child's independent problem-solving level and the level achievable with adult guidance or collaboration with more capable peers.

Domain Code: Words in the World: How Language Meets Social Context
column8: Vygotsky (1978): "The zone of proximal development is the distance between the actual developmental level as determined by independent problem solving and the level of potential development as determined through problem solving under adult guidance or in collaboration with more capable peers." The ZPD defines the range between what a child can do alone and what they can achieve with support.
column9: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development is defined by the child's independent performance and the child's performance with assistance.
column13: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development (ZPD) is the distance between a child's independent problem-solving level and the higher level achievable with adult guidance or collaboration with more capable peers.

Domain Code: The Relational Foundation: Attachment, Aggression, and the Social World of Childhood
column8: Bowlby (1958): Attachment is a biologically based behavioral system shaped by natural selection, rooted in ethological theory. Infants are biologically predisposed to form attachments to caregivers because proximity to a protective adult enhances survival.
column9: Bowlby's theory of attachment was most influenced by ethological theory.
column10: Socioemotional Development - Attachment, Emotions, and Social Relationships
column13: Bowlby's attachment theory was most influenced by ethological theory, proposing that infants are biologically predisposed to seek proximity to caregivers because it enhances survival.

Domain Code: The Relational Foundation: Attachment, Aggression, and the Social World of Childhood
column8: Harlow (1958) / Berk (2018): "Contact comfort (soft physical contact) is more critical for attachment formation than feeding, as demonstrated by Harlow's experiments showing infant monkeys preferred a soft cloth surrogate over a wire surrogate that provided milk."
column9: According to Harlow and Zimmerman's research, contact comfort is most important for the development of attachment in young rhesus monkeys.
column10: Socioemotional Development - Attachment, Emotions, and Social Relationships
column13: Harlow's experiments demonstrated that contact comfort (soft physical touch) is more critical than feeding for attachment formation, as infant monkeys preferred a soft cloth surrogate over a wire surrogate that provided milk.

Domain Code: The Relational Foundation: Attachment, Aggression, and the Social World of Childhood
column8: Ainsworth et al. (1978): "The Strange Situation procedure assesses attachment patterns in infants aged 12–24 months through a series of separations and reunions with the caregiver and a stranger."
column9: Ainsworth and her colleagues used the "strange situation" to study attachment in babies one to two years of age.
column10: Socioemotional Development - Attachment, Emotions, and Social Relationships
column13: Ainsworth's Strange Situation procedure assesses attachment patterns in infants aged 12–24 months through a standardized series of separations and reunions with a caregiver and stranger.

Domain Code: The Relational Foundation: Attachment, Aggression, and the Social World of Childhood
column8: Ainsworth et al. (1978) / Berk (2018): "Insecure-avoidant attachment: infants show little distress at separation and avoid the caregiver upon return. Associated with rejecting, unresponsive, or overstimulating caregiving."
column9: Ainsworth and her colleagues distinguished between two types of insecure attachment patterns: avoidant and ambivalent, and parents of children with the avoidant pattern are often either rejecting and unresponsive or intrusive and overstimulating.
column10: Socioemotional Development - Attachment, Emotions, and Social Relationships
column13: Insecure-avoidant attachment is characterized by little distress at separation and avoidance of the caregiver upon reunion, associated with rejecting, unresponsive, or overstimulating caregiving.

Domain Code: The Relational Foundation: Attachment, Aggression, and the Social World of Childhood
column8: Bowlby (1958): Internal working models are mental representations of the self, the attachment figure, and the relationship between them. These templates guide expectations about relationships throughout life.
column9: According to Bowlby (1980), an infant's early attachment relationships lead to the development of internal working models that consist of beliefs about the self, others, and the self in relationship to others, which affect future relationships.
column10: Socioemotional Development - Attachment, Emotions, and Social Relationships
column13: Bowlby's internal working models are mental representations of the self, attachment figures, and their relationship that form through early attachment and serve as templates guiding relationship expectations throughout life.

Domain Code: The Relational Foundation: Attachment, Aggression, and the Social World of Childhood
column8: Feinman (1982) / Berk (2018): Social referencing is using another person's emotional reaction to guide one's own response in ambiguous situations. It is often studied by placing infants in situations involving a stranger, a novel object, or the visual cliff, in which the infant looks to a parent's facial expression to determine how to respond.
column9: Social referencing refers to the use of the emotional reactions of a parent or other person to determine how to respond in ambiguous situations, often studied by placing infants in situations involving a stranger, a novel object, or the visual cliff.
column10: Socioemotional Development - Attachment, Emotions, and Social Relationships
column13: Social referencing is using another person's emotional reaction to guide one's own response in ambiguous situations, commonly studied using strangers, novel objects, or the visual cliff.

Domain Code: The Relational Foundation: Attachment, Aggression, and the Social World of Childhood
column8: Crick & Dodge (1994): "High aggression is attributed to hostile attribution bias — interpreting ambiguous social cues as intentionally hostile."
column9: Crick and Dodge's social information-processing model attributes high levels of aggression in children to a hostile attribution bias.
column10: Socioemotional Development - Attachment, Emotions, and Social Relationships
column13: Crick and Dodge's social information-processing model attributes high aggression in children to a hostile attribution bias — interpreting ambiguous social cues as intentionally hostile.

Domain Code: The Relational Foundation: Attachment, Aggression, and the Social World of Childhood
column8: / [23] Patterson (1982): "High childhood aggression is linked to coercive parent-child cycles: parent makes a demand, child responds aversively, parent backs down — negatively reinforcing coercion. Intervention targets parent behavior."
column9: The Oregon model of parent management training developed by Gerald Patterson and his colleagues (1982) was based on their research that found a link between high levels of aggressiveness in children and coercive family interactions.
column10: Socioemotional Development - Attachment, Emotions, and Social Relationships
column13: Patterson's Oregon model of parent management training is based on research linking childhood aggression to coercive parent-child cycles in which parental capitulation negatively reinforces the child's aversive behavior.

Domain Code: The Relational Foundation: Attachment, Aggression, and the Social World of Childhood
column8: Damon (1977): "Three friendship stages: handy playmate (early childhood), mutual trust (middle childhood), intimacy and loyalty (adolescence)."
column9: Damon's three stages of friendship development are handy playmate, mutual trust and assistance, and intimacy and loyalty.

column13: Damon's three friendship stages progress from handy playmate (early childhood) to mutual trust (middle childhood) to intimacy and loyalty (adolescence).

column8: Rowe & Kahn (1997): Successful aging requires three components: (1) reducing disease risk and disease-related disability, (2) maintaining high cognitive and physical functioning, and (3) active engagement with life. Notably, acceptance of the normal effects of aging is not included as a component of this model.
column9: Rowe and Kahn's model of successful aging includes reducing the risk for disease and disease-related disability, maintaining high cognitive and physical functioning, and staying actively engaged in life, but not acceptance of the normal effects of aging.
