column13: Rowe and Kahn's model of successful aging includes reducing disease risk, maintaining high cognitive and physical functioning, and active engagement with life, but does not include acceptance of normal aging effects.

Domain Code: Thinking in Symbols: Preoperational Cognition, Play, and the Growing Brain
column8: Piaget (1964): "In a second stage, we have pre-operational representation — the beginnings of language, of the symbolic function, and therefore of thought, or representation." Animistic thinking is a preoperational characteristic in which children attribute life to inanimate objects.
column9: When a child says the moon is following them because it wants to help them see where they're going, this is an example of animistic thinking.
column13: Animistic thinking, a characteristic of Piaget's preoperational stage, is the tendency to attribute life and intentions to inanimate objects.

Domain Code: Thinking in Symbols: Preoperational Cognition, Play, and the Growing Brain
column8: Wimmer & Perner (1983) / Berk (2018): "Theory of mind is commonly assessed using the false belief task: a character places an object, leaves, and the object is moved. Children who pass (~age 4) predict the character will look in the original location."
column9: The change-of-location task is most often used to assess theory of mind.
column13: Theory of mind is commonly assessed using the false belief (change-of-location) task; children who pass at approximately age 4 correctly predict a character will search where an object was originally placed.

Domain Code: Thinking in Symbols: Preoperational Cognition, Play, and the Growing Brain
column8: Wood, Bruner, & Ross (1976): "This scaffolding consists essentially of the adult 'controlling' those elements of the task that are initially beyond the learner's capacity, thus permitting him to concentrate upon and complete only those elements that are within his range of competence." Scaffolding adjusts support level and gradually withdraws assistance as competence increases, within the ZPD.
column9: According to Vygotsky, assistance from adults and more experienced peers (scaffolding) helps a learner advance within his/her zone of proximal development.
column13: Scaffolding, as described by Wood, Bruner, and Ross (1976), involves an adult controlling task elements beyond the learner's current capacity and gradually withdrawing support as competence increases within the ZPD.

Domain Code: Thinking in Symbols: Preoperational Cognition, Play, and the Growing Brain
column8: Lillard, Lerner, Hopkins, Dore, Smith, & Palmquist (2013): "For Vygotsky (1978), pretense has a crucial developmental role, because it is the activity by which children learn to separate referent from object... children also develop inhibitory control through pretend play (Bodrova & Leong, 1996)." Make-believe play provides a context for practicing self-regulation and skills beyond current independent ability.
column9: According to Vygotsky, children's make-believe play provides them with a zone of proximal development.
column13: Vygotsky argued that children's make-believe play functions as a zone of proximal development, providing a context for practicing self-regulation and skills beyond their current independent ability.

Domain Code: Thinking in Symbols: Preoperational Cognition, Play, and the Growing Brain
column8: Chomsky (1959/1965): Syntax specifies how words combine to form grammatically correct sentences, including word order and relationships between elements. Two sentences can have the same meaning (semantics) but differ in syntax -- for example, "The cat chased the mouse" and "The mouse was chased by the cat" convey the same meaning but have different syntactic structures (active vs. passive voice).
column9: The sentences "The mouse was chased by the cat" and "The cat chased the mouse" have the same meaning but differ in terms of syntax.
column13: Syntax governs how words combine into grammatically correct sentences; two sentences can share the same semantic meaning but differ syntactically, as in the active "The cat chased the mouse" versus the passive "The mouse was chased by the cat."

Domain Code: Thinking in Symbols: Preoperational Cognition, Play, and the Growing Brain
column8: Casey, Getz, & Galvan (2008): "The prefrontal cortex is the last brain region to fully mature, continuing development into the early-to-mid 20s. Responsible for executive functions including planning, impulse control, and decision-making."
column9: The prefrontal cortex is the last area of the brain to become fully functional and continues to develop into the early or mid-20s.
column13: The prefrontal cortex, responsible for executive functions including planning, impulse control, and decision-making, is the last brain region to fully mature, continuing development into the early-to-mid 20s.

Domain Code: Thinking in Symbols: Preoperational Cognition, Play, and the Growing Brain
column8: Yoshinaga-Itano (2006): "Early sign language exposure does not hinder spoken language development but rather facilitates it by providing a foundation for linguistic concepts and communication."
column9: The research suggests that learning sign language benefits the acquisition of spoken language for deaf and hard-of-hearing children.
column13: Early sign language exposure facilitates rather than hinders spoken language development in deaf and hard-of-hearing children by providing a foundation for linguistic concepts and communication.

Domain Code: Thinking in Symbols: Preoperational Cognition, Play, and the Growing Brain
column8: Oller (2000) / Berk (2018): "Canonical babbling onset ranges from 5–10 months. Absence at 5 months is within normal range and not a red flag for referral."
column9: No canonical babbling at 5 months of age is not a "red flag" suggesting a young child should be referred for a speech/language evaluation.
column13: Canonical babbling onset ranges from 5–10 months, so absence at 5 months is within normal range and not a red flag requiring referral for speech/language evaluation.

Domain Code: Thinking in Symbols: Preoperational Cognition, Play, and the Growing Brain
column8: Gottman (1994): "Contempt is the single strongest predictor of divorce."
column9: Gottman and Levenson found that, of the four behaviors listed in the answers to this question, contempt (which is characterized by hostility, disrespect, and disgust) is the most damaging to a couple's relationship and is the single best predictor of divorce.
column13: Gottman identified contempt — characterized by hostility, disrespect, and disgust — as the single strongest predictor of divorce among couples.

Domain Code: Logic Takes Hold: Conservation, Moral Reasoning, and the Competent Child
column8: Piaget (1968): "Conservation of substance is simply a logical necessity. The child now understands that when there is a transformation something must be conserved because by reversing the transformation you can come back to the point of departure." Conservation develops through reversibility, decentration, and transformational thinking.
column9: Piaget proposed that the ability to conserve emerges during the concrete operational stage as the result of the emergence of reversibility of thought, decentration, and transformational thinking.
column13: Piaget proposed that conservation emerges in the concrete operational stage through reversibility, decentration, and transformational thinking, enabling children to understand that quantity remains constant despite perceptual changes.

Domain Code: Logic Takes Hold: Conservation, Moral Reasoning, and the Competent Child
column8: Piaget (1968): "The notion of substance is attained before either weight or volume... conservation of substance is simply a logical necessity." Horizontal decalage is the gradual, uneven acquisition of abilities within a single Piagetian stage (e.g., conservation of number before conservation of weight).
column9: Piaget used the term horizontal decalage to describe the gradual acquisition of abilities within a stage (e.g., the gradual development of conservation skills within the concrete operational stage).
column13: Piaget's horizontal decalage refers to the gradual, uneven acquisition of abilities within a single stage, such as children mastering conservation of number before conservation of weight in the concrete operational stage.

Domain Code: Logic Takes Hold: Conservation, Moral Reasoning, and the Competent Child
column8: Piaget (1968): "At the level of operatory conservation, children judge two collections to be equal or unequal by looking for a one-to-one correspondence between their elements." In the heteronomous stage, children judge behavior based on consequences rather than intentions.
column9: As described by Piaget, children in the heteronomous stage of moral reasoning base their judgments about a person's behavior on the consequences of the behavior.
column13: In Piaget's heteronomous stage of moral development, children judge behavior based on the magnitude of consequences rather than the actor's intentions.

Domain Code: Logic Takes Hold: Conservation, Moral Reasoning, and the Competent Child
column8: Colby, Kohlberg, Gibbs, & Lieberman (1983): "Moral judgment was found to be positively correlated with age, socioeconomic status, IQ, and education." Both Piaget and Kohlberg viewed the influence of peers as more important than the influence of parents for children's moral development. Peer interaction through negotiation and egalitarian relationships promotes autonomous moral reasoning beyond what parental authority relationships can provide.
column9: Piaget and Kohlberg both viewed the influence of peers as more important than the influence of parents for the moral development of children.
column13: Both Piaget and Kohlberg viewed peer influence as more important than parental influence for children's moral development, because egalitarian peer relationships promote autonomous moral reasoning.

Domain Code: Logic Takes Hold: Conservation, Moral Reasoning, and the Competent Child
column8: Colby, Kohlberg, Gibbs, & Lieberman (1983): "Level 1: Preconventional: Stage 1. Heteronomous morality — What Is Right: Following rules only as backed by punishment; obedience for its own sake; and avoiding physical damage to persons and property. Reasons for Doing Right: Avoidance of punishment, and the superior power of authorities." Stage 1 moral judgments are based on avoiding punishment.
column9: Individuals in the first stage of Kohlberg's preconventional level of moral development base their judgments on the consequences of the act, and a person in this stage would say that Heinz should not steal the drug because of the negative consequences of doing so.
column13: In Kohlberg's Stage 1 (Heteronomous Morality) of the Preconventional level, moral judgments are based on avoiding punishment and obedience to authority, not on the intrinsic nature of the act.

Domain Code: Logic Takes Hold: Conservation, Moral Reasoning, and the Competent Child
column8: Kohlberg (1976): Stage 4 of moral development, the "law and order" orientation, is part of the conventional level. At this stage, "right behavior consists of doing one's duty, showing respect for authority, and maintaining the given social order for its own sake." A child who refrains from stealing because it is against the law is reasoning at the law and order stage of the conventional level.
column9: The child who doesn't steal because it's against the law is in the law and order orientation stage of Kohlberg's conventional level of moral development.
column13: In Kohlberg's Stage 4 law-and-order orientation (conventional level), moral reasoning is based on doing one's duty, respecting authority, and maintaining social order, exemplified by avoiding theft because it is illegal.

Domain Code: Logic Takes Hold: Conservation, Moral Reasoning, and the Competent Child
column8: Colby, Kohlberg, Gibbs, & Lieberman (1983): "Stage 6. Universal ethical principles — What Is Right: Following self-chosen ethical principles. Particular laws or social agreements are usually valid because they rest on such principles. When laws violate these principles, one acts in accordance with the principle." Stage 6 involves self-chosen ethical principles transcending specific laws.
column9: Stage 6 of Kohlberg's model of moral development is the universal ethical principles stage.
column13: Kohlberg's Stage 6 (universal ethical principles) involves acting according to self-chosen ethical principles that supersede specific laws when those laws violate the principles.

Domain Code: Logic Takes Hold: Conservation, Moral Reasoning, and the Competent Child
column8: Colby, Kohlberg, Gibbs, & Lieberman (1983): "Moral judgment was found to be positively correlated with age, socioeconomic status, IQ, and education. Stage scores in childhood were significantly correlated with adulthood scores." The longitudinal data show moral development continuing through adulthood, contradicting Piaget's claim it concludes in late childhood.
column9: Kohlberg's theory of moral development has been criticized for claiming that moral development ends in late childhood, but this claim was actually made by Piaget, not Kohlberg, and has been challenged by research on moral development during adolescence and adulthood.
column13: Kohlberg's longitudinal research showed moral development continues through adulthood and is positively correlated with age, IQ, education, and socioeconomic status, contradicting Piaget's claim that it ends in late childhood.

Domain Code: Logic Takes Hold: Conservation, Moral Reasoning, and the Competent Child
column8: Baumrind (1966): "Three models of parental control — permissive, authoritarian, and authoritative — are described and contrasted... the position defended that authoritative control may effectively generate in the child, behavior which while well socialized is also wilful and independent." Authoritative parenting combines high expectations with warmth, open communication, and age-appropriate autonomy.
column9: Authoritative parenting style is characterized by high demandingness and high responsiveness, which leads to the best outcomes for children and adolescents, as found by research by Baumrind (1971) and others.
column13: Authoritative parenting (Baumrind) combines high demandingness with high responsiveness — warmth, open communication, and age-appropriate autonomy — producing the best developmental outcomes.

Domain Code: The Storm and the Search: Puberty, Identity, and Adolescent Cognition
column8: Elkind (1967): The personal fable is the adolescent belief in one's uniqueness and invulnerability -- that rules and consequences applying to others do not apply to oneself. For example, an adolescent who believes there is no way she could get pregnant from unprotected sex with her boyfriend is demonstrating the personal fable.
column9: Elkind's concept of the personal fable refers to the adolescent belief that one is unique and not subject to the rules or consequences that apply to other people, as exemplified by Samantha's belief that there is no way she could get pregnant from unprotected sex with her boyfriend.
column13: Elkind's personal fable is the adolescent belief in one's uniqueness and invulnerability—that rules and consequences applying to others do not apply to oneself.

Domain Code: The Storm and the Search: Puberty, Identity, and Adolescent Cognition
column8: Kling et al. (1999): "Males show higher self-esteem than females." This gender difference in self-esteem emerges in late childhood and persists into late adulthood, with the largest difference appearing in late adolescence.
column9: Males have higher levels of self-esteem than females do beginning in late childhood and persisting into late adulthood.
column13: Males show higher self-esteem than females beginning in late childhood and persisting into late adulthood, with the largest difference emerging in late adolescence.

Domain Code: The Storm and the Search: Puberty, Identity, and Adolescent Cognition
column8: Marcia (1966) / Berk (2018): "Four identity statuses based on exploration and commitment: diffusion (no exploration/no commitment), foreclosure (commitment/no exploration), moratorium (exploration/no commitment), achievement (commitment after exploration)."
column9: Marcia's (1966) identity development model identifies four identity statuses that differ with regard to crisis and choice.
column13: Marcia's four identity statuses — diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium, and achievement — are defined by the presence or absence of exploration and commitment.

Domain Code: The Storm and the Search: Puberty, Identity, and Adolescent Cognition
column8: Marcia (1966): "Moratorium status: actively exploring identity options but not yet committed."
column9: Marcia's moratorium status is characterized by the adolescent currently experiencing an identity crisis and a lack of commitment to a particular identity in terms of college major, career, or marriage.
column13: Marcia's moratorium identity status is characterized by active exploration of identity options without yet having made a commitment.

Domain Code: The Storm and the Search: Puberty, Identity, and Adolescent Cognition
column8: Sneed, Whitbourne, & Culang (2006): Erikson's industry vs. inferiority stage spans ages 6-11, during which children turn energy toward mastering culturally valued knowledge and skills. This stage co-occurs with Freud's latency stage, which also covers approximately ages 6-11, during which sexual impulses are dormant and the child focuses on developing social and intellectual skills.
column9: Freud's latency stage and Erikson's industry versus inferiority stage both occur when children are between the ages of six and 11.
column13: Freud's latency stage and Erikson's industry vs. inferiority stage both span approximately ages 6–11, with Freud emphasizing dormant sexual impulses and Erikson emphasizing mastery of culturally valued knowledge and skills.

Domain Code: The Storm and the Search: Puberty, Identity, and Adolescent Cognition
column8: Sneed, Whitbourne, & Culang (2006): "Erikson's (1963) theory of personality development characterizes individual development as occurring through a series of eight bipolar stages across the lifespan." The virtue of the autonomy vs. shame and doubt stage (toddlerhood) is will — the determination to exercise free choice and self-restraint.
column9: The positive outcome ("virtue") of Erikson's autonomy vs. shame and doubt stage of psychosocial development is will (initiative and self-determination), not purpose.
column13: The virtue of Erikson's autonomy vs. shame and doubt stage (toddlerhood) is will — the determination to exercise free choice and self-restraint.

Domain Code: The Storm and the Search: Puberty, Identity, and Adolescent Cognition
column8: Ge, Conger, & Elder (2001): "Early physical/sexual maturation is associated with increased depressive symptoms and psychological distress for both boys and girls, with effects especially pronounced for early-maturing girls who face greater risk of depression, earlier sexual activity, and negative body image."
column9: Early physical and sexual maturation during adolescence is associated with better outcomes for adolescent boys than for adolescent girls.
column13: Early physical and sexual maturation is associated with increased depression, earlier sexual activity, and negative body image, with effects especially pronounced for early-maturing girls.

Domain Code: The Storm and the Search: Puberty, Identity, and Adolescent Cognition
column8: Carskadon (2011): "The 'perfect storm' model: biological circadian phase delay + early school start times + psychosocial factors converge to produce chronic adolescent sleep deprivation."
column9: Carskadon's (2011) "perfect storm" model of adolescent sleep deprivation includes biological factors like circadian phase delay, societal factors like early school start times, and psychosocial factors like greater autonomy over bedtimes, increased academic pressures, and excessive screen time, but not bedtime snacking.
column13: Carskadon's perfect storm model explains chronic adolescent sleep deprivation as the convergence of biological circadian phase delay, early school start times, and psychosocial factors such as greater autonomy and academic pressures.

Domain Code: The Storm and the Search: Puberty, Identity, and Adolescent Cognition
column8: Ellis & Garber (2000): The relationship between maternal mood disorder and early-onset puberty in girls was mediated by biological father absence with stepfather presence and stressful family relationships. That is, maternal mood disorder predicted these family stressors, which in turn predicted earlier pubertal timing in daughters.
column9: The research by Ellis and Garber (2000) found that the relationship between maternal mood disorder and early onset puberty in girls was mediated by biological father absence with stepfather presence and stressful family relationships.
column13: Ellis and Garber (2000) found that the link between maternal mood disorder and early-onset puberty in girls was mediated by biological father absence with stepfather presence and stressful family relationships.

Domain Code: Becoming Ourselves: Gender, Temperament, and Identity Across the Lifespan
column8: Bem (1981): "Bem's gender schema theory combines cognitive developmental and social learning approaches. Children develop gender schemas from culturally transmitted information, which become cognitive lenses for processing information."
column9: Bem's gender schema theory combines elements of cognitive developmental theory and social learning theory to explain how children learn about gender roles and acquire a gender identity.
column13: Bem's gender schema theory combines cognitive developmental and social learning approaches, positing that children develop gender schemas from culturally transmitted information that become cognitive lenses for processing information.

Domain Code: Becoming Ourselves: Gender, Temperament, and Identity Across the Lifespan
column8: Ruble, Martin, & Berenbaum (2006): "As proposed by Kohlberg (1966), children's developing sense of the permanence of categorical sex ('I am a girl and will always be a girl') is a critical organizer... Slaby and Frey (1975) demonstrated that children move through a series of stages: first learning to identify their own and others' sex (basic gender identity or labeling), next learning that gender remains stable over time (gender stability), and finally learning that gender is a fixed and immutable characteristic (gender consistency)." Gender constancy parallels Piagetian conservation.
column9: Kohlberg's three stages of gender-role development are gender identity, gender stability, and gender constancy.
column13: Kohlberg's three stages of gender-role development are gender identity (labeling), gender stability (gender persists over time), and gender constancy (gender is fixed regardless of appearance or situation).

Domain Code: Becoming Ourselves: Gender, Temperament, and Identity Across the Lifespan
column8: Rothbart & Derryberry (1981): "Temperament is constitutionally based individual differences in reactivity and self-regulation, influenced by heredity, maturation, and experience."
column9: Rothbart and Derryberry (1981) describe temperament as constitutional differences in reactivity and self-regulation, influenced by heredity, maturation, and experience.
column13: Rothbart and Derryberry (1981) define temperament as constitutionally based individual differences in reactivity and self-regulation, influenced by heredity, maturation, and experience.

Domain Code: Becoming Ourselves: Gender, Temperament, and Identity Across the Lifespan
column8: Thomas, Chess, & Birch (1970): "If the two sets of demands are severely conflicting, the child may be unable to make an adaptation that reconciles the double standard." Developmental outcomes depend on the match between a child's temperament and environmental demands; no temperament is inherently problematic.
column9: The goodness-of-fit model developed by Thomas and Chess (1977) focuses on the match between a child's temperament and the demands of the social environment.
column13: Thomas and Chess's goodness-of-fit model holds that developmental outcomes depend on the match between a child's temperament and environmental demands, with no temperament being inherently problematic.

Domain Code: Becoming Ourselves: Gender, Temperament, and Identity Across the Lifespan
column8: Colby, Kohlberg, Gibbs, & Lieberman (1983): At the conventional level of Kohlberg's moral development, moral reasoning is based on conforming to social expectations, maintaining relationships, and upholding laws and social order (Stages 3 and 4). A response in the Heinz dilemma that emphasizes social expectations, relationships, or maintaining the social order would indicate reasoning at the conventional level.
column9: Morgan's response in the Heinz dilemma suggests that he is at the conventional level of Kohlberg's moral development.
column13: At Kohlberg's conventional level of moral development, reasoning is based on conforming to social expectations, maintaining relationships, and upholding laws and social order (Stages 3 and 4).

Domain Code: Becoming Ourselves: Gender, Temperament, and Identity Across the Lifespan
column8: Sneed, Whitbourne, & Culang (2006): "Ego Integrity versus Despair crisis in later adulthood when older adults reflect on the meaning of life and how they have lived it... Ego integrity involves a sense of wholeness, integration, and a deep sense of acceptance of the life as it has been lived." The virtue of ego integrity vs. despair is wisdom — a detached yet active concern with life in the face of death.
column9: According to Erikson's theory of psychosocial development, the positive outcome ("virtue") of the ego integrity versus despair stage is wisdom.
column13: The virtue of Erikson's ego integrity vs. despair stage is wisdom — a detached yet active concern with life in the face of death.

Domain Code: Becoming Ourselves: Gender, Temperament, and Identity Across the Lifespan
column8: Rubin, Provenzano, & Luria (1974): "Parents perceive and treat infants differently by sex from birth — describing boys as 'strong' and girls as 'delicate' despite no objective differences."
column9: Mothers and fathers tend to perceive and treat boys and girls differently on the basis of sex as soon as their children are born, often describing newborn boys as "strong" and "big" and handling them more firmly, and describing newborn girls as "delicate" and "little" and handling them more gently.
column13: Parents perceive and treat infants differently by sex from birth, describing boys as strong and girls as delicate despite no objective physical differences (Rubin, Provenzano, & Luria, 1974).

Domain Code: Becoming Ourselves: Gender, Temperament, and Identity Across the Lifespan
column8: Hess, Auman, Colcombe, & Rahhal (2003): Late middle-aged adults who had an "older identity" showed significantly poorer word recall when told their performance would be compared to that of older adults, compared to those told their performance would be compared to younger adults or given no comparison information. Those with an older identity were more susceptible to stereotype threat effects on memory performance.
column9: Late middle-aged adults who had an older identity had significantly poorer word recall when they were told their performance would be compared to that of older adults than did those who were told their performance would be compared to that of younger adults or were not given any comparison information.
column13: Hess et al. (2003) found that late middle-aged adults with an older identity showed significantly poorer word recall under stereotype threat when told their performance would be compared to older adults.

Domain Code: The Maturing Mind: Adult Cognition, Memory, and the Reshaping of Relationships
column8: Craik (1977): "Secondary (long-term) memory shows the greatest age-related decline among memory systems."
column9: In adulthood, secondary memory is most negatively affected by increasing age.
column13: Secondary (long-term) memory shows the greatest age-related decline among memory systems in adulthood.

Domain Code: The Maturing Mind: Adult Cognition, Memory, and the Reshaping of Relationships
column8: Hasher, Zacks, & May (1999): "The synchrony effect refers to the finding that cognitive performance is optimal when testing occurs at one's circadian peak: older adults perform best in the morning, younger adults in the late afternoon/evening." This age-related difference in optimal time of day for cognitive performance reflects shifts in circadian arousal patterns across the lifespan.
column9: The synchrony effect, where older adults perform better on certain cognitive tasks in the morning while younger adults perform better in the afternoon or evening, is due to age-related differences in circadian rhythms and peak times of arousal.
column13: The synchrony effect refers to the finding that older adults perform best on cognitive tasks in the morning while younger adults perform best in the late afternoon or evening, reflecting age-related shifts in circadian arousal patterns.

Domain Code: The Maturing Mind: Adult Cognition, Memory, and the Reshaping of Relationships
column8: Rubin, Rahhal, & Poon (1998): "The distribution of autobiographical memories across the lifespan shows a recency effect (most memories from recent past), childhood amnesia (few memories before age 5), and a reminiscence bump — a disproportionate number of memories from approximately ages 10-30." The bump is attributed to identity formation, novelty of experiences, and emotional significance during this period.
column9: When older adults are asked to recall events from their past, the largest number of recalled events are from the recent past, with a "reminiscence bump" which is a spike in memory for events that occurred in mid-adolescence to early adulthood (from about ages 15 to 25).
column13: Autobiographical memory across the lifespan shows three patterns: a recency effect, childhood amnesia for events before age 5, and a reminiscence bump of disproportionate recall for events from approximately ages 10–30.

Domain Code: The Maturing Mind: Adult Cognition, Memory, and the Reshaping of Relationships
column8: Rubin, Rahhal, & Poon (1998): "The reminiscence bump — increased autobiographical recall for events from approximately ages 10–30 — is linked to identity formation."
column9: The "reminiscence bump" in older adults' recall of past events is related to personal identity formation during adolescence and early adulthood when memories of autobiographical events receive preferential encoding and retention.
column13: The reminiscence bump refers to older adults' disproportionate autobiographical recall of events from approximately ages 10–30, attributed to identity formation during adolescence and early adulthood.

Domain Code: The Maturing Mind: Adult Cognition, Memory, and the Reshaping of Relationships
column8: Glasser & Campbell (1998): Presbyopia (farsightedness) is the age-related inability to focus on near objects, caused by a gradual loss of flexibility in the crystalline lens. It typically becomes noticeable around age 40.
column9: Presbyopia (farsightedness) is the inability to focus on near objects and, for many adults, is first evident at about 40 years of age.
column13: Presbyopia, the age-related inability to focus on near objects caused by loss of flexibility in the crystalline lens, typically becomes noticeable around age 40.

Domain Code: The Maturing Mind: Adult Cognition, Memory, and the Reshaping of Relationships
column8: Diamond (2008): "Sexual fluidity occurs in both men and women, with somewhat higher rates in women."
column9: Sexual fluidity, which refers to changes in a person's sexual attractions and/or behaviors that are inconsistent with their self-described sexual orientation, is reported by both heterosexual and homosexual men and women, with somewhat greater frequencies reported by women.
column13: Sexual fluidity — changes in attraction or behavior inconsistent with self-described orientation — occurs in both men and women, with somewhat higher rates reported by women.

Domain Code: The Maturing Mind: Adult Cognition, Memory, and the Reshaping of Relationships
column8: Carstensen, Isaacowitz, & Charles (1999): "As people age, emotionally meaningful goals gain priority while knowledge-seeking goals decline. When time is perceived as limited, people prioritize emotionally meaningful goals and close relationships."
column9: Carstensen's socioemotional selectivity theory proposes that, as we get older, emotionally meaningful goals become more important and knowledge-related goals become less important.
column13: Carstensen's socioemotional selectivity theory holds that when time is perceived as limited, emotionally meaningful goals and close relationships are prioritized over knowledge-seeking goals.

Domain Code: The Maturing Mind: Adult Cognition, Memory, and the Reshaping of Relationships
column8: Trager (1958): "Paralanguage includes vocal features that accompany speech — tone, pitch, loudness, speech rate, pauses, and inflection — that convey emotion and modify verbal meaning."
column9: Paralanguage refers to variations in tone, rhythm, volume, and stress used to express emotions and modify or clarify the meaning of verbal communication.
column13: Paralanguage refers to vocal features accompanying speech — including tone, pitch, loudness, rate, and inflection — that convey emotion and modify verbal meaning.

Domain Code: The Lifespan in Full: Memory, Perception, and the Long View of Development
column8: Singer & Salovey (1993): "Self-defining memories are vivid, affectively intense, repetitively recalled, linked to other similar memories, and focused on enduring concerns or unresolved conflicts." These autobiographical memories serve identity construction and maintenance as a subtype of episodic memory. Resistance to change is not among their defining characteristics.
column9: Self-defining memory (SDM) is a component of episodic memory and consists of memories that contribute to the construction and maintenance of one's personal identity, which have five characteristics: emotional intensity, vividness, high levels of repetition, linkage to similar memories, and connections to enduring concerns or unresolved conflicts, except for resistance to change.
column13: Self-defining memories, per Singer & Salovey, are characterized by emotional intensity, vividness, repetitive recall, linkage to similar memories, and connections to enduring concerns — resistance to change is not a defining feature.

Domain Code: The Lifespan in Full: Memory, Perception, and the Long View of Development
column8: Krull et al. (2013): "Chemotherapy and cranial irradiation for childhood ALL are both associated with neurocognitive deficits."
column9: Chemotherapy and cranial irradiation are both associated with deficits in neurocognitive functioning when used to treat childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL).
column13: Both chemotherapy and cranial irradiation used to treat childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) are associated with neurocognitive deficits.

Domain Code: The Lifespan in Full: Memory, Perception, and the Long View of Development
column8: Kellman & Arterberry (2006): Depth perception develops sequentially: kinematic/kinetic cues (motion-based depth information) are perceived first, from approximately 1 to 3 months of age; binocular depth cues (stereoscopic vision) emerge around 3-5 months; and pictorial (monocular) cues develop last, around 5-7 months of age.
column9: The development of depth perception in infancy involves becoming sensitive to kinetic cues at one to three months of age, binocular cues at three to five months, and pictorial cues at five to seven months.
column13: Depth perception develops sequentially: kinematic/kinetic cues emerge at 1–3 months, binocular/stereoscopic cues at 3–5 months, and pictorial/monocular cues last at 5–7 months.

Domain Code: The Lifespan in Full: Memory, Perception, and the Long View of Development
column8: Morrongiello (1988) / Berk (2018): Auditory localization is present at birth, disappears at approximately 2-3 months (reflecting a transition from subcortical to cortical processing), then re-emerges in voluntary form at 3-4 months. This ability improves steadily and reaches nearly adult levels by approximately 12 months of age.
column9: Infants exhibit some degree of auditory localization soon after birth, but this ability disappears between two and four months of age and then reappears and improves to nearly adult levels by about 12 months of age.
column13: Auditory localization is present at birth, disappears at 2–3 months as processing shifts from subcortical to cortical, re-emerges voluntarily at 3–4 months, and reaches near-adult levels by 12 months.

Domain Code: The Lifespan in Full: Memory, Perception, and the Long View of Development
column8: Norcia & Tyler (1985): "This visual acuity estimate increased from a mean of 4.5 c/deg during the first month to about 20 c/deg at 8-13 months of age." Vision is the least developed sense at birth; newborn visual acuity is approximately 20/400 to 20/600.
column9: Of the five senses, sight is least well-developed at birth.
column13: Vision is the least developed sense at birth, with newborn visual acuity approximately 20/400 to 20/600.

Domain Code: Wired Differently from the Start: ADHD, Autism, and Neurodevelopmental Conditions
column8: The DSM-5 diagnosis of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) requires the onset of some symptoms before 12 years of age.
column13: DSM-5 requires that some symptoms of ADHD be present before age 12 for diagnosis.

Domain Code: Wired Differently from the Start: ADHD, Autism, and Neurodevelopmental Conditions
column8: APA (2013), DSM-5: "Six (or more) symptoms of inattention [or hyperactivity-impulsivity] have persisted for at least 6 months," and "several inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms were present prior to age 12 years." The 6-month duration requirement ensures symptoms are persistent rather than transient responses to situational stressors.
column9: The DSM-5 diagnosis of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) requires an onset of symptoms before 12 years of age and a duration of symptoms for at least 6 months.
column13: DSM-5 ADHD requires symptoms to be present before age 12 and to persist for at least 6 months across multiple settings.

Domain Code: Wired Differently from the Start: ADHD, Autism, and Neurodevelopmental Conditions
column8: APA (2013): "ADHD diagnostic criteria specify symptoms present prior to age 12, present in two or more settings, and persisting for at least 6 months."
column9: The DSM-5 diagnosis of ADHD requires the presence of characteristic symptoms in at least two settings (e.g., at home and at school) with an onset before 12 years of age and a duration of at least six months.
column13: DSM-5 ADHD diagnosis requires symptoms present before age 12, in two or more settings, and persisting for at least 6 months.

Domain Code: Wired Differently from the Start: ADHD, Autism, and Neurodevelopmental Conditions
column8: APA (2013): "For adults age 17+, the DSM-5 requires at least 5 symptoms in either the inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity domain, reduced from 6 for children."
column9: To assign a diagnosis of ADHD to Adam, a 19-year-old college sophomore, he must have at least five symptoms of inattention and/or five symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity.
column13: DSM-5 requires at least 5 symptoms of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity for an ADHD diagnosis in individuals age 17 and older, compared to 6 symptoms required for younger children.

Domain Code: Wired Differently from the Start: ADHD, Autism, and Neurodevelopmental Conditions
column8: Hoogman et al. (2017), *The Lancet Psychiatry*, 4(4), 310-319: "In the largest neuroimaging study of ADHD to date (N = 3,242), individuals with ADHD showed significantly smaller volumes in the caudate nucleus, putamen, nucleus accumbens, amygdala, and hippocampus compared to controls. Effect sizes were largest in children and diminished with age."
column9: Individuals with ADHD tend to have a smaller volume in five brain structures: caudate nucleus, putamen, nucleus accumbens, amygdala, and hippocampus.
column13: Individuals with ADHD show significantly smaller volumes in the caudate nucleus, putamen, nucleus accumbens, amygdala, and hippocampus, with effects largest in children and diminishing with age.

Domain Code: Wired Differently from the Start: ADHD, Autism, and Neurodevelopmental Conditions
column8: APA (2013): "ASD symptoms must be present in the early developmental period. Symptoms are typically recognized during the second year of life (12-24 months) but may appear earlier or later depending on severity."
column9: For the diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder, the DSM-5 requires symptoms to be present during the early developmental period, with symptoms usually recognized by the time the child is between 12 and 24 months of age but may occur earlier or later, depending on the severity of the symptoms.
column13: DSM-5 requires ASD symptoms to be present in the early developmental period, typically recognized between 12 and 24 months, though onset may vary based on symptom severity.

Domain Code: Wired Differently from the Start: ADHD, Autism, and Neurodevelopmental Conditions
column8: APA (2013): "Specific learning disorder requires difficulties learning and using academic skills that persist for at least 6 months despite provision of interventions, with skills substantially below expected for age and causing significant interference."
column9: A child with dyslexia whose reading problems significantly interfere with their academic performance and have not substantially improved with appropriate intervention would receive a DSM-5 diagnosis of specific learning disorder.
column13: DSM-5 specific learning disorder requires academic skill difficulties persisting at least 6 months despite intervention, with skills substantially below age expectations and causing significant functional interference.

Domain Code: Wired Differently from the Start: ADHD, Autism, and Neurodevelopmental Conditions
column8: APA (2013): "Provisional tic disorder: motor and/or vocal tics present for less than 1 year since first tic onset."
column9: The correct DSM-5 diagnosis for a 12-year-old boy who has two motor tics that began nine months ago is provisional tic disorder.
column13: Provisional tic disorder is the DSM-5 diagnosis when motor and/or vocal tics have been present for less than 1 year since first onset.

Domain Code: Wired Differently from the Start: ADHD, Autism, and Neurodevelopmental Conditions
column8: APA (2013): "Tourette's disorder requires both multiple motor and one or more vocal tics, persisting for more than 1 year since first tic onset."
column9: The most likely DSM-5 diagnosis for a 15-year-old boy who has three motor tics and one vocal tic that started 14 months ago is Tourette's disorder.
column13: Tourette's disorder requires both multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic, persisting for more than 1 year since first tic onset.

Domain Code: The Architecture of Fear: Anxiety Disorders, Phobias, and Worry Gone Wrong
column8: APA (2013): "Separation anxiety disorder may develop after a life stress such as the death of a pet, a school change, or a move."
column9: Jessie's fear of being separated from her parents is characteristic of separation anxiety disorder which may be triggered by a life stress, such as the death of a pet.
column13: Separation anxiety disorder may be triggered by life stressors such as the death of a pet, a school change, or a move.

Domain Code: The Architecture of Fear: Anxiety Disorders, Phobias, and Worry Gone Wrong
column8: APA (2013): "Separation anxiety disorder involves excessive fear or anxiety about separation from attachment figures. Symptoms may include school refusal, nightmares involving separation themes, and physical complaints."
column9: School refusal due to separation anxiety disorder is characterized by excessive fear or anxiety about being separated from an attachment figure, accompanied by symptoms such as repeated nightmares related to separation and physical symptoms.
column13: Separation anxiety disorder involves excessive fear of separation from attachment figures and may include school refusal, separation-themed nightmares, and physical complaints.

Domain Code: The Architecture of Fear: Anxiety Disorders, Phobias, and Worry Gone Wrong
column8: APA (2013): "Specific phobias typically develop in early childhood, with a median age at onset between 7 and 11 years."
column9: The median age of onset of specific phobia is between 7 and 11 years of age according to the DSM-5.
column13: Specific phobias typically develop in early childhood, with a median age of onset between 7 and 11 years.

Domain Code: The Architecture of Fear: Anxiety Disorders, Phobias, and Worry Gone Wrong
column8: APA (2013): "Emetophobia (fear of vomiting) is classified as specific phobia, other type."
column9: Anna's symptoms are characteristic of emetophobia, a fear of vomiting, which is categorized in the DSM as a specific phobia, other type.
column13: Emetophobia, the fear of vomiting, is classified in the DSM-5 as specific phobia, other type.

Domain Code: The Architecture of Fear: Anxiety Disorders, Phobias, and Worry Gone Wrong
column8: Page (1994): "Blood-injection-injury phobia uniquely involves a vasovagal fainting response (parasympathetic drop in heart rate and blood pressure) rather than the sustained sympathetic arousal typical of other phobias."
column9: People with the blood-injection-injury type of specific phobia are more likely to experience vasovagal fainting instead of increased sympathetic nervous system arousal when confronted with the feared object or event.
column13: Blood-injection-injury phobia uniquely triggers a vasovagal fainting response (parasympathetic drop in heart rate and blood pressure) rather than the sustained sympathetic arousal characteristic of other specific phobias.

Domain Code: The Architecture of Fear: Anxiety Disorders, Phobias, and Worry Gone Wrong
column8: APA (2013): "Social anxiety disorder involves marked fear about social situations in which the individual may be scrutinized, with fear of being humiliated or embarrassed."
column9: For a DSM-5 diagnosis of social anxiety disorder, the client must exhibit a fear of being embarrassed or humiliated in social situations.
column13: Social anxiety disorder involves marked fear of social situations where one may be scrutinized, with fear of embarrassment or humiliation.

Domain Code: The Architecture of Fear: Anxiety Disorders, Phobias, and Worry Gone Wrong
column8: APA (2013): Agoraphobia requires marked fear or anxiety about two or more of five situations: using public transportation, being in open spaces, being in enclosed places, standing in line or being in a crowd, and being outside the home alone. Learning that a client has anxiety attacks not only when using public transportation but also when going outside the house alone would help confirm this diagnosis, as it establishes fear in at least two of the five required situations.
column9: The DSM-5 diagnosis of agoraphobia requires the presence of marked anxiety related to at least two of five situations - using public transportation, being in open spaces, being in enclosed spaces, standing in line or being in a crowd, and being outside of the home alone, and learning that Sonia has anxiety attacks not only when she uses public transportation but also when she goes outside her house alone would help confirm this diagnosis.
column13: DSM-5 agoraphobia requires marked fear or anxiety in at least two of five situations: public transportation, open spaces, enclosed places, crowds/lines, and being outside the home alone.

Domain Code: The Architecture of Fear: Anxiety Disorders, Phobias, and Worry Gone Wrong
column8: APA (2013): "Panic attack symptoms include depersonalization, fear of losing control, and paresthesias, among 13 total symptoms. Increased sensitivity to environmental stimuli is NOT a DSM-5 panic attack symptom."
column9: Increased sensitivity to environmental stimuli is not included in the DSM-5 as a symptom of a panic attack, whereas depersonalization, fear of losing control or "going crazy," and paresthesias (numbness or tingling sensations) are included.
column13: Increased sensitivity to environmental stimuli is not a DSM-5 panic attack symptom, whereas depersonalization, fear of losing control, and paresthesias are among the 13 recognized symptoms.

Domain Code: The Architecture of Fear: Anxiety Disorders, Phobias, and Worry Gone Wrong
column8: Weems, Silverman, & La Greca (2000): "The most common worry themes for children with GAD include academic/athletic performance and natural disasters."
column9: Children with generalized anxiety disorder are most likely to worry about academic and athletic performance and about natural disasters.
column13: Children with GAD most commonly worry about academic and athletic performance and natural disasters.

Domain Code: The Architecture of Fear: Anxiety Disorders, Phobias, and Worry Gone Wrong
column8: APA (2013): "GAD is distinguished from normal anxiety by excessive worry that is difficult to control, accompanied by physical symptoms, and the individual's perceived uncontrollability of the worry."
column9: According to DSM-5, in contrast to people with nonpathological anxiety, those with generalized anxiety disorder are more likely to experience physical symptoms in conjunction with worrying and to experience worrying as uncontrollable.
column13: GAD is distinguished from normal anxiety by excessive, uncontrollable worry accompanied by physical symptoms.

Domain Code: When the Light Goes Out: Depression, Its Models, and Who It Strikes
column8: APA (2013): "A major depressive episode requires five or more symptoms during a 2-week period. At least one must be depressed mood or loss of interest/pleasure (anhedonia)."
column9: The DSM-5 diagnosis of major depressive disorder requires the presence of at least five characteristic symptoms with at least one symptom being a depressed mood or a loss of interest or pleasure in usual activities.
column13: A DSM-5 diagnosis of major depressive disorder requires five or more symptoms over 2 weeks, with at least one being depressed mood or anhedonia.

Domain Code: When the Light Goes Out: Depression, Its Models, and Who It Strikes

column8: APA (2013): Borderline personality disorder (BPD) features include identity disturbance, affective instability, intense anger, recurrent suicidality, and frantic efforts to avoid abandonment. An individual presenting with several of these symptoms -- such as identity disturbance, affective instability, inappropriate intense anger, recurrent suicidal behavior, and frantic efforts to avoid abandonment -- would most likely meet criteria for a DSM-5 diagnosis of borderline personality disorder.
column9: Elena has several of the symptoms of borderline personality disorder identified in the DSM-5 - i.e., an identity disturbance; affective instability; inappropriate, intense anger; recurrent suicidal behavior; and frantic efforts to avoid abandonment.
column13: Borderline personality disorder is characterized by identity disturbance, affective instability, inappropriate intense anger, recurrent suicidal behavior, and frantic efforts to avoid abandonment.

Domain Code: The Patterns That Persist: Personality Disorders, Mood Variants, and Cultural Context
column8: APA (2013), DSM-5: "Schizotypal personality disorder is characterized by social and interpersonal deficits marked by acute discomfort with, and reduced capacity for, close relationships, as well as cognitive or perceptual distortions and eccentricities of behavior." Individuals may express a desire for relationships but exhibit pervasive social anxiety that does not diminish with familiarity, driven by paranoid fears rather than negative self-judgments. This distinguishes schizotypal PD from avoidant PD, where the desire for relationships is genuine and anxiety stems from fear of rejection.
column9: The most likely diagnosis for a client who says he'd like to have friends but is very uncomfortable around people and seems uninterested in taking steps to develop friendships is schizotypal personality disorder.
column13: Schizotypal personality disorder is distinguished from avoidant PD by social anxiety driven by paranoid fears rather than fear of rejection, and by reduced capacity for close relationships despite a stated desire for them.

Domain Code: The Patterns That Persist: Personality Disorders, Mood Variants, and Cultural Context
column8: APA (2013), DSM-5: "Schizotypal personality disorder is characterized by a pervasive pattern of social and interpersonal deficits marked by acute discomfort with, and reduced capacity for, close relationships as well as by cognitive or perceptual distortions and eccentricities of behavior." Features include suspiciousness or paranoid ideation, social anxiety that does not diminish with familiarity, and a preference for solitary activities. These features overlap with but are distinct from paranoid PD (which lacks the cognitive/perceptual distortions) and schizoid PD (which lacks the suspiciousness and anxiety).
column9: The personality disorder characterized by symptoms such as being suspicious of others' motives, feeling anxious around people, and preferring to be alone is schizotypal personality disorder.
column13: Schizotypal personality disorder is distinguished by cognitive/perceptual distortions and eccentricities alongside social discomfort, separating it from paranoid PD (no distortions) and schizoid PD (no suspiciousness or anxiety).

column13: DMDD requires severe temper outbursts occurring 3 or more times per week with persistently irritable or angry mood between outbursts, lasting at least 12 months.

column13: DSM-5 gender dysphoria requires marked incongruence between experienced/expressed gender and assigned gender for at least 6 months, with clinically significant distress or functional impairment.

The DSM-5 shifted from the DSM-IV term "gender identity disorder" to "gender dysphoria" to emphasize the distress rather than pathologizing the identity itself.
column9: The DSM-5 diagnosis of gender dysphoria requires a discordance between one's experienced and assigned gender.

Domain Code: Through the Unconscious and the Relationship: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Foundations
column8: Baumeister, Dale, & Sommer (1998): "The concept of reaction formation involves converting a socially unacceptable impulse into its opposite." People respond to the implication of an unacceptable trait "by behaving in a way that would show them to have the opposite trait."
column9: Gerald, age 39, converted his undesirable impulses of jealousy and resentment towards his younger sister's recent business success into the opposite behavior of praising her accomplishments and encouraging her continued success, illustrating the defense mechanism of reaction formation.
column13: Reaction formation is the defense mechanism of converting a socially unacceptable impulse into its opposite behavior, such as expressing praise toward someone one actually resents.

Domain Code: Through the Unconscious and the Relationship: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Foundations
column8: Cramer (2015): "Denial is the failure to see, recognize, or understand the existence or meaning of an internal or external stimulus." Defense mechanisms are defined as "a mental operation that occurs outside of awareness" whose "function is to protect the person from experiencing excessive anxiety."
column9: A college undergraduate who usually gets A's and B's on exams received a C on a recent midterm exam, and he immediately assumed that the low grade was a mistake, which is best explained by the defense mechanism of denial.
column13: Denial is the defense mechanism involving failure to recognize the existence or meaning of an internal or external stimulus, operating outside awareness to protect against excessive anxiety.

Domain Code: Through the Unconscious and the Relationship: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Foundations
column8: Dillon (2021): "Jung (1928/1971c) refers to the process of psychological and spiritual growth as 'individuation.'" The primary goal of Jung's analytical psychotherapy is to bring unconscious material into consciousness to facilitate individuation -- achieving individual "wholeness" by becoming conscious of and harmonizing the various parts of the psyche. This involves "a living cooperation with the collective aspects of our nature" and a "productive marriage" between the personal ego and the collective unconscious.
column9: The primary goal of Jung's analytical psychotherapy is to bring unconscious material into consciousness to facilitate the process of individuation, which involves achieving individual "wholeness" (being a unique unified person) by becoming conscious of and harmonizing the various parts of the psyche.
column13: The primary goal of Jung's analytical psychotherapy is individuation — achieving psychological wholeness by bringing unconscious material into consciousness and harmonizing the personal ego with the collective unconscious.

Domain Code: Through the Unconscious and the Relationship: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Foundations
column8: Rogers (1959): "When the individual has no awareness of [incongruence], he is merely vulnerable to the possibility of anxiety and disorganization." When incongruence is "dimly perceived," the individual responds with denial or distortion of the experience to preserve the self-concept. Denial prevents the experience from entering awareness, while distortion reshapes it to be consistent with the self-structure.
column9: According to Carl Rogers, people often respond to incongruence with denial or distortion.
column13: According to Rogers, when individuals dimly perceive incongruence between self-concept and experience, they respond defensively through denial, which blocks experience from awareness, or distortion, which reshapes experience to fit the self-structure.

Domain Code: Through the Unconscious and the Relationship: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Foundations
column8: Rogers (1959): When a discrepancy exists between the self-concept and organismic experience (incongruence), the individual experiences vulnerability and anxiety. To protect the self-structure, the person reacts defensively by either distorting the experience to make it congruent with the self-concept or denying the experience entirely. Persistent reliance on these defensive processes leads to psychological maladjustment.
column9: According to Carl Rogers, people often react defensively to incongruence by distorting or denying their experiences, which leads to psychological maladjustment.
column13: According to Rogers, when incongruence exists between self-concept and organismic experience, individuals defensively distort or deny threatening experiences to protect the self-structure, and persistent use of these defenses leads to psychological maladjustment.

Domain Code: Through the Unconscious and the Relationship: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Foundations
column8: Rogers (1957/1959): In Rogers's personality theory, conditions of worth -- the conditions under which a person feels worthy of love and acceptance -- contribute to incongruence between the self-concept and actual experience. When individuals internalize others' evaluative standards, they deny or distort experiences that conflict with those conditions, creating a state of incongruence. Rogers identified six conditions for therapeutic personality change, including that "the therapist experiences unconditional positive regard for the client."
column9: Conditions of worth contribute to incongruence according to Carl Rogers's personality theory.
column13: In Rogers's theory, conditions of worth cause individuals to deny or distort experiences conflicting with internalized evaluative standards, creating incongruence between self-concept and actual experience.

column8: Robey (2011): Wubbolding describes Glasser's framework: "Choice Theory explains human behavior and motivation (Glasser, 1998)." The theory identifies five genetically determined needs: love and belonging, power, fun, freedom, and survival. Intimacy is not listed as a separate need.
column9: Reality therapy, based on choice theory, proposes that people have five genetically encoded needs, including love and belonging, power, fun, freedom, and survival, but not intimacy.
column13: Glasser's choice theory, the basis of reality therapy, identifies five genetically determined needs: love and belonging, power, fun, freedom, and survival — with intimacy not listed as a separate need.

column8: Robey (2011): "Choice Theory explains human behavior and motivation (Glasser, 1998)." According to choice theory, all behavior is purposeful and directed toward satisfying five genetically encoded needs: love and belonging (the need for connection with others), power (the need for competence and achievement), fun (the need for enjoyment and learning), freedom (the need for autonomy), and survival (the need for physical safety and sustenance).
column9: According to choice theory, all people are motivated to satisfy five genetically encoded needs: love/belonging, power, fun, freedom, and survival.
column13: Choice theory holds that all behavior is purposeful and directed toward satisfying five genetically encoded needs: love/belonging, power, fun, freedom, and survival.

column8: Rachman & Teasdale (1969): "In aversive counterconditioning for fetishistic disorder, the fetish object serves as the conditioned stimulus that is paired with an aversive unconditioned stimulus."
column9: When using aversive counterconditioning to treat a client's fetishistic disorder, the fetish object is the conditioned stimulus.
column13: In aversive counterconditioning for fetishistic disorder, the fetish object serves as the conditioned stimulus that is paired with an aversive unconditioned stimulus.

Domain Code: Rewiring Fear: How Classical Conditioning Principles Treat Anxiety
column8: Wolpe (1968): "Reciprocal inhibition is a process of relearning whereby in the presence of a stimulus a non-anxiety-producing response is continually repeated until it extinguishes the old, undesirable response." A competing (incompatible) response "must therefore be elicited in the presence of the stimuli that would evoke the undesired response, and must be 'stronger' than the latter."
column9: Wolpe attributed the effects of systematic desensitization to reciprocal inhibition, which involves pairing presentation of a stimulus that produces anxiety with presentation of a stimulus that produces relaxation or other response that's incompatible with anxiety.
column13: Wolpe attributed systematic desensitization's effects to reciprocal inhibition, requiring a competing response incompatible with anxiety to be elicited in the presence of anxiety-producing stimuli and be stronger than the anxiety response.

Domain Code: Rewiring Fear: How Classical Conditioning Principles Treat Anxiety
column8: Wolpe (1961): Systematic desensitization involves "presenting to the imagination of the deeply relaxed patient the feeblest item in a list of anxiety-evoking stimuli -- repeatedly, until no more anxiety is evoked." Systematic desensitization operates through counterconditioning -- replacing the anxiety response with an incompatible relaxation response -- while exposure therapy operates through extinction, in which repeated presentation of the feared stimulus without the aversive outcome weakens the conditioned fear response.
column9: Systematic desensitization is counterconditioning, while exposure therapy is extinction.
column13: Systematic desensitization operates through counterconditioning — replacing anxiety with an incompatible relaxation response — whereas exposure therapy operates through extinction of the conditioned fear response.

Domain Code: Rewiring Fear: How Classical Conditioning Principles Treat Anxiety
column8: Kazdin & Wilcoxon (1976): "Dismantling research demonstrated that the effects of systematic desensitization are attributable to extinction via repeated CS presentation, and that counterconditioning through relaxation pairing is unnecessary."
column9: The effects of systematic desensitization for eliminating an anxiety response to a particular stimulus are actually due to extinction, as studies using the dismantling strategy found that it was repeated exposure to the feared (conditioned) stimulus that eliminated the anxiety response, and that pairing the feared stimulus with a stimulus that produced relaxation (counterconditioning) was unnecessary.
column13: Dismantling research showed systematic desensitization works through extinction via repeated CS exposure, not counterconditioning, as pairing the feared stimulus with relaxation was found unnecessary.

Domain Code: Rewiring Fear: How Classical Conditioning Principles Treat Anxiety
column8: Rescorla (1969): "A conditioned inhibitor is a stimulus that signals the absence of the unconditioned stimulus and thereby suppresses the conditioned response. A trusted companion may function as a conditioned inhibitor for panic responses."
column9: In terms of classical conditioning, a trusted friend is a conditioned inhibitor for a woman with panic disorder who believes she can avoid having a panic attack by having the friend with her in situations that have elicited an attack in the past.
column13: A trusted companion who prevents panic attacks functions as a conditioned inhibitor — a stimulus signaling absence of the unconditioned stimulus that suppresses the conditioned fear response.

Domain Code: Rewiring Fear: How Classical Conditioning Principles Treat Anxiety
column8: Cautela (1967): "Covert sensitization pairs imagined engagement in the unwanted behavior with an imagined aversive consequence to reduce or eliminate that behavior."
column9: Covert sensitization uses aversive counterconditioning to eliminate an undesirable behavior.
column13: Covert sensitization is a form of aversive counterconditioning that pairs imagined engagement in an unwanted behavior with an imagined aversive consequence to reduce that behavior.

Domain Code: Rewiring Fear: How Classical Conditioning Principles Treat Anxiety
column8: Stampfl & Levis (1967): "Implosive therapy eliminates fear responses through classical extinction by prolonged imaginal exposure to the feared stimulus at maximum intensity."
column9: Implosive therapy uses classical extinction to eliminate a fear response to an object or situation.
column13: Implosive therapy eliminates fear responses through classical extinction via prolonged imaginal exposure to the feared stimulus presented at maximum intensity.

column8: Stampfl & Levis (1967): "Implosive therapy uniquely integrates imaginal exposure with psychodynamic content — the therapist incorporates themes of aggression, guilt, or sexuality into the imagined feared scenario."
column9: Implosive therapy combines exposure in imagination and psychodynamic techniques, where the client imagines the feared object or situation and the therapist embellishes the imagined scene with psychodynamic themes such as aggression, guilt, or sexuality.
column13: Implosive therapy (Stampfl & Levis, 1967) combines imaginal exposure with psychodynamic content, as the therapist embellishes the feared scene with themes of aggression, guilt, or sexuality.

Domain Code: Building Behavior from the Ground Up: Operant Interventions in Clinical Practice
column8: Vollmer, Peters, Kronfli, Lloveras, & Ibanez (2020): "We propose the following definition of DRA: Providing greater reinforcement, along at least one dimension, contingent on the occurrence of one form or type of behavior, while minimizing reinforcement for another form or type of behavior." The over-arching suggestion "is to maximize reinforcement for alternative behavior and minimize or eliminate reinforcement for problem behavior."
column9: Differential reinforcement combines positive reinforcement and operant extinction.
column13: Differential reinforcement combines positive reinforcement for a target alternative behavior with extinction (minimizing or eliminating reinforcement) for the problem behavior.

Domain Code: Building Behavior from the Ground Up: Operant Interventions in Clinical Practice
column8: Athens & Vollmer (2010): Differential reinforcement of alternative behavior (DRA) is used to decrease an undesirable behavior and increase one or more specific alternative desirable behaviors. A key prerequisite is that the alternative behavior must already occur at least occasionally in the learner's repertoire. DRA involves withholding reinforcers following problem behavior (extinction) while providing reinforcement contingent on the occurrence of the specified alternative appropriate behavior.
column9: Differential reinforcement for alternative or appropriate behavior (DRA) is used to decrease an undesirable behavior and increase one or more specific alternative desirable behaviors that already occur at least occasionally.
column13: Differential reinforcement of alternative behavior (DRA) combines extinction of problem behavior with reinforcement of a specified alternative behavior that must already occur at least occasionally in the learner's repertoire.

Domain Code: Building Behavior from the Ground Up: Operant Interventions in Clinical Practice
column8: Peterson (2004): Skinner wrote that "elaborate and peculiar forms of response may be generated from undifferentiated operant behavior through successive approximation to a final form." The method involves reinforcing "upon the following steps in succession: approach to the site of the lever, lifting the nose into the air toward the lever, lifting the fore-part of the body into the air, touching the lever with the feet, and pressing the lever downward."
column9: Shaping is also known as successive approximation conditioning, a behavioral technique that involves reinforcing successive approximations to the desired behavior.
column13: Shaping, also called successive approximation conditioning, involves reinforcing progressively closer approximations to a desired final behavior until that behavior is established.

Domain Code: Building Behavior from the Ground Up: Operant Interventions in Clinical Practice
column8: Premack (1959): The Premack principle states that a high-probability (preferred) behavior can be used as a reinforcer for a low-probability (less preferred) behavior. For a student who dislikes homework but enjoys other activities, making access to the preferred activity contingent on homework completion increases the rate of the low-frequency behavior.
column9: The Premack principle, a type of positive reinforcement in which a high-frequency behavior (a highly desirable activity) is used as a reinforcer for a low-frequency behavior (an undesirable activity) to increase the low-frequency behavior, is useful for helping a middle school student who rarely finishes his homework just because he doesn't like doing it.
column13: The Premack principle states that a high-probability preferred behavior can reinforce a low-probability less-preferred behavior, increasing its frequency when access to the preferred activity is made contingent on performing the less preferred one.

Domain Code: Building Behavior from the Ground Up: Operant Interventions in Clinical Practice
column8: Kazdin (1972): "Response cost (RC), a punishment procedure in which conditioned reinforcers (points, tokens, or money) are withdrawn to suppress a response, has been used as a behavior therapy technique on its own and in conjunction with reinforcement in token economies." "RC is a punishment procedure, i.e., the contingent presentation of a noxious stimulus which reduces the future probability of a response."
column9: Response cost is an application of negative punishment, which reduces or eliminates a behavior by removing a positive reinforcer whenever the behavior occurs.
column13: Response cost is a negative punishment procedure in which conditioned reinforcers such as points, tokens, or money are withdrawn contingent on an undesired behavior to reduce its future probability.

Domain Code: Building Behavior from the Ground Up: Operant Interventions in Clinical Practice
column8: Cooper, Heron, & Heward (2020): "Overcorrection is classified as positive punishment because it involves applying an effortful consequence contingent upon the undesired behavior."
column9: Overcorrection is ordinarily classified as a type of positive punishment.
column13: Overcorrection is classified as positive punishment because it involves applying an effortful aversive consequence contingent upon occurrence of the undesired behavior.

Domain Code: Building Behavior from the Ground Up: Operant Interventions in Clinical Practice
column8: Azrin & Holz (1966): "Habituation to the punishing stimulus is one mechanism by which punishment loses effectiveness over time, as repeated exposure reduces the aversive quality of the consequence."
column9: Habituation is one of the reasons why punishment tends to become less effective over time.
column13: Habituation to a punishing stimulus — whereby repeated exposure reduces its aversive quality — is one mechanism by which punishment loses effectiveness over time.

Domain Code: Building Behavior from the Ground Up: Operant Interventions in Clinical Practice
column8: Lerman & Iwata (1996): "Operant extinction is generally contraindicated when the target behavior poses a risk of harm, because extinction typically produces an initial increase in frequency and intensity (extinction burst) before the behavior decreases."
column9: Of the interventions listed, operant extinction is the least likely to be the optimal intervention when a child's target behavior is harmful to him/herself or others because it often causes an increase in the behavior before it begins to decrease.
column13: Operant extinction is contraindicated when a target behavior is harmful because it typically produces an extinction burst — an initial increase in frequency and intensity — before the behavior decreases.

Domain Code: Thinking About Thinking: Beck's Cognitive Model and the Architecture of Depression
column8: Beck (1963/1967): Beck's cognitive model of depression describes a negative cognitive triad consisting of negative views of (1) oneself ("I am worthless"), (2) the world ("everything is against me"), and (3) the future ("things will never get better"). "The typical ideational content of the depressed patients was characterized by themes of low self-esteem, self-blame, overwhelming responsibilities, and desires to escape."
column9: Beck's cognitive model of depression describes it as involving a negative cognitive triad that consists of negative views of oneself, the world, and the future.
column13: Beck's cognitive model of depression centers on a negative cognitive triad consisting of negative views of oneself, the world, and the future.

Domain Code: Thinking About Thinking: Beck's Cognitive Model and the Architecture of Depression
column8: Beck (1963): Automatic thoughts are spontaneous cognitions that "intercede between an event or stimulus and the individual's emotional and behavioral reactions." They were "generally experienced by the patients as arising as though they were automatic responses, ie, without any apparent antecedent reflection or reasoning" and appeared to have "an involuntary quality. The patients frequently reported that these thoughts would occur even when they had resolved 'not to have them.'"
column9: Automatic thoughts are spontaneous thoughts that "intercede between an event or stimulus and the individual's emotional and behavioral reactions".
column13: Automatic thoughts, identified by Beck, are spontaneous, involuntary cognitions that intercede between a stimulus and an individual's emotional and behavioral reactions, occurring without prior reflection or reasoning.

Domain Code: Thinking About Thinking: Beck's Cognitive Model and the Architecture of Depression
column8: Beck (1963): "Arbitrary interpretation is defined as the process of forming an interpretation of a situation, event, or experience when there is no factual evidence to support the conclusion or when the conclusion is contrary to the evidence."
column9: Anna's conclusion that students in her classes already think she's stupid is an example of arbitrary inference, a cognitive distortion identified by Beck.
column13: Arbitrary inference, a cognitive distortion identified by Beck, involves forming a conclusion about a situation when there is no factual evidence to support it or when the conclusion contradicts available evidence.

Domain Code: Thinking About Thinking: Beck's Cognitive Model and the Architecture of Depression
column8: Beck (1963): "Arbitrary interpretation is defined as the process of forming an interpretation of a situation, event, or experience when there is no factual evidence to support the conclusion or when the conclusion is contrary to the evidence." The instructor's conclusion that she is "incredibly boring and incompetent" based on two students leaving a class of 65 exemplifies arbitrary inference, as the conclusion is drawn without sufficient evidence and ignores alternative explanations.
column9: A new psychology instructor's conclusion that she must be "an incredibly boring and incompetent teacher" because two of the 65 students in the class walked out of the lecture hall before the period was over illustrates the cognitive distortion of arbitrary inference, as described by Aaron Beck.
column13: Arbitrary inference, identified by Beck, is illustrated when a person draws a conclusion unsupported by evidence, such as an instructor concluding she is incompetent because two of 65 students left class early.

Domain Code: Thinking About Thinking: Beck's Cognitive Model and the Architecture of Depression
column8: Beck (1963): "Selective abstraction refers to the process of focusing on a detail taken out of context, ignoring other more salient features of the situation, and conceptualizing the whole experience on the basis of this element."
column9: The employee's conclusion that he is worthless and will never get promoted out of his entry-level job based on a single minor criticism in an otherwise positive performance review is an example of selective abstraction.
column13: Beck's selective abstraction is the cognitive distortion of focusing on a single detail out of context and using it to characterize an entire experience, ignoring more salient information.

Domain Code: Thinking About Thinking: Beck's Cognitive Model and the Architecture of Depression
column8: Braun, Strunk, Sasso, & Cooper (2015): "Socratic questioning is intended to foster active engagement and critical thinking." "In using Socratic questioning, therapists avoid a didactic style and instead use questions to help patients develop new perspectives."
