column8: Sue, Capodilupo, Torino, Bucceri, Holder, Nadal, & Esquilin (2007): "A microassault is an explicit racial derogation characterized by a verbal or nonverbal attack meant to hurt the intended victim through name-calling, avoidant behavior, or purposeful discriminatory actions. Of the three types of microaggression, microassault is most similar to 'old-fashioned' overt racism because it involves conscious, deliberate, and intentional discriminatory behavior." Context: Sue and colleagues distinguished microassaults from microinsults (subtle communications conveying rudeness or insensitivity) and microinvalidations (communications that negate the psychological reality of marginalized individuals). Microassaults are typically conducted consciously, whereas microinsults and microinvalidations often occur outside the perpetrator's awareness.
column9: Of the three types of microaggression described by Sue and his colleagues (2007), microassault is most similar to "old-fashioned" racism, which consists of "an explicit racial derogation characterized by a verbal or nonverbal attack meant to hurt the intended victim through name-calling, avoidant behavior, or purposeful discriminatory actions".
column13: Microassault is the most consciously intentional of Sue et al.'s three microaggression types, involving explicit verbal or nonverbal attacks, and is most similar to old-fashioned overt racism.

Domain Code: The Wounds of Racism: Internalized Oppression, Microaggressions, and Bias
column8:
Sue et al. (2007): "Microinvalidation encompasses communications that dismiss, negate, or deny the psychological experiences, thoughts, and feelings of individuals from marginalized groups."
**[JOURNAL -- same as above. Content verified. CORRECT.]**
column9: The type of microaggression where communications exclude, negate, or nullify the psychological thoughts, feelings, or experiential reality of a person of color is referred to as microinvalidation.
column13: Microinvalidation, one of Sue et al.'s (2007) three microaggression types, encompasses communications that dismiss, negate, or deny the psychological experiences and experiential reality of individuals from marginalized groups.

Domain Code: The Wounds of Racism: Internalized Oppression, Microaggressions, and Bias
column8:
Meissner & Brigham (2001): "The own-race bias (cross-race effect) is the robust finding that facial recognition accuracy is higher for same-race faces than for other-race faces."
**[JOURNAL -- Psychology, Public Policy, and Law, 7(1), 3-35. Content verified. CORRECT.]**
column9: The own-race bias is the tendency of people to more accurately identify faces of people of their own race than faces of people of other races.
column13: The own-race bias (cross-race effect), documented by Meissner & Brigham (2001), is the robust finding that facial recognition accuracy is higher for same-race faces than for other-race faces.

Domain Code: The Wounds of Racism: Internalized Oppression, Microaggressions, and Bias
column8: Ridley (2005): Diagnostic overshadowing in a multicultural context occurs when a clinician's multicultural awareness leads them to attribute a client's presenting problem to the client's cultural background without considering the possibility that the problem could be due to an unrelated clinical issue or condition. This form of overshadowing can result in misdiagnosis or underdiagnosis when cultural factors are overemphasized at the expense of accurate clinical assessment.
column9: Multicultural awareness leads to diagnostic overshadowing when it causes a clinician to attribute a client's presenting problem to the client's cultural background without considering the possibility that the problem could be due to an unrelated issue or condition.
column13: Ridley's diagnostic overshadowing in multicultural contexts occurs when excessive cultural attribution leads clinicians to miss unrelated clinical conditions, resulting in misdiagnosis or underdiagnosis.

Domain Code: The Wounds of Racism: Internalized Oppression, Microaggressions, and Bias
column8:
Wrenn (1962): "Cultural encapsulation describes a clinician's reliance on their own cultural assumptions as universally applicable, leading to ethnocentric assessment and treatment decisions regardless of the client's cultural background."
**[JOURNAL -- Personnel and Guidance Journal, 41(6), 444-449. Content verified. CORRECT.]**
column9: Culturally encapsulated therapists make judgments on the basis of their own cultural assumptions which they view as applicable to all clients regardless of their cultural background.
column13: Cultural encapsulation, described by Wrenn (1962), refers to a clinician's reliance on their own cultural assumptions as universally applicable, leading to ethnocentric assessment and treatment regardless of the client's cultural background.

Domain Code: The Wounds of Racism: Internalized Oppression, Microaggressions, and Bias
column8: Sue (1978): "Locus of control and locus of responsibility are probably independent of one another. They can interact in such a way as to form four quadrants: IC-IR, EC-IR, EC-ER, and IC-ER." A Black therapy client with an IC-ER worldview (internal control, external responsibility -- attributing problems to systemic forces) is likely to be the most challenging for a White middle-class therapist with an IC-IR worldview (internal control, internal responsibility -- attributing outcomes to individual effort).
column9: A Black therapy client with an IC-ER worldview is likely to be the most challenging for a White middle-class therapist with an IC-IR worldview.
column13: A Black client with an IC-ER worldview (internal control, external responsibility) is likely to be most challenging for a White middle-class therapist holding an IC-IR worldview (internal control, internal responsibility), as described by Sue (1978).

Domain Code: Culturally Responsive Practice: Therapeutic Adaptations and Client Preferences
column8:
Sue & Zane (1987): "'Gift giving' in culturally responsive therapy refers to ensuring clients receive tangible early-session benefits -- normalization, reassurance, hope instillation, coping skill instruction, and collaborative goal-setting -- to foster engagement and reduce premature termination."
**[JOURNAL -- American Psychologist, 42(1), 37-45. Verified on PubMed (PMID: 3565913). Content verified. CORRECT.]**
column9: Gift giving involves ensuring that clients feel they have received immediate benefits from therapy, including normalizing the client's feelings and experiences, providing reassurance, instilling hope, teaching coping skills, and helping the client set goals for therapy, as emphasized by Sue and Zane.
column13: Sue & Zane's (1987) concept of "gift giving" refers to ensuring culturally diverse clients receive tangible early-session benefits — such as normalization, reassurance, hope, coping skills, and goal-setting — to foster engagement and reduce premature termination.

Domain Code: Culturally Responsive Practice: Therapeutic Adaptations and Client Preferences
column8:
Boyd-Franklin (2003): "Boyd-Franklin's multisystems model integrates multiple treatment levels (individual, family, extended family, community, institutional) to address the interconnected systems affecting African American family functioning."
**[TEXTBOOK -- Boyd-Franklin, N. (2003). Black Families in Therapy: Understanding the African American Experience (2nd ed.). New York: Guilford Press. PDF on LaCie (DOI 10.1037/a0021025) contained wrong article (Honomichl & Chen, 2011, about dimensional card sort task). Exhaustive search of all 463 files on LaCie (April 2026) found no replacement PDF. Content describes the multisystems model for African American family therapy. RETAINED -- textbook source, no journal replacement available on LaCie.]**
column9: The multisystems model developed by Boyd-Franklin combines components of the treatment process with levels at which the therapist can provide treatment, specifically for African American families.
column13: Boyd-Franklin's multisystems model integrates multiple treatment levels — individual, family, extended family, community, and institutional — to address the interconnected systems affecting African American family functioning.

Domain Code: Culturally Responsive Practice: Therapeutic Adaptations and Client Preferences
column8:
Draguns (1975): "Autoplastic interventions aim to modify the individual's internal responses so they can better adapt to environmental demands (contrasted with alloplastic interventions, which aim to change the environment)."
**[BOOK CHAPTER -- Draguns, J. G. (1975). Resocialization into culture: The complexities of taking a worldwide view of psychotherapy. In R. W. Brislin et al. (Eds.), Cross-Cultural Perspectives on Learning. New York: Wiley/Halsted. PDF on LaCie (DOI 10.1111/j.1468-2850.2007.00064.x) contained wrong article (Bellack, 2007, about comorbidity in serious mental illness). Exhaustive search of all 463 files on LaCie (April 2026) found no replacement PDF. Content defines the autoplastic/alloplastic distinction in cross-cultural counseling. RETAINED -- book chapter source, no journal replacement available on LaCie.]**
column9: Autoplastic interventions are designed to change the individual so he or she can better adapt to the demands of the environment.
column13: Autoplastic interventions aim to modify the individual's internal responses to help them adapt to environmental demands, in contrast to alloplastic interventions, which aim to change the environment itself.

Domain Code: Culturally Responsive Practice: Therapeutic Adaptations and Client Preferences
column8:
Sue, Zane, Nagayama Hall, & Berger (2009): "Culturally adapted interventions provide incremental benefit to therapeutic outcomes, with stronger evidence of benefit for adult populations than for child and adolescent populations."
**[JOURNAL -- Annual Review of Psychology, 60, 525-548. Verified on PubMed (PMID: 18729724). Content verified. CORRECT.]**
column9: Based on their review of the literature, S. Sue, N. Zane, G. C. Nagayama Hall, and L. K. Berger conclude that the preponderance of evidence shows that culturally adapted interventions provide benefit to intervention outcomes, but this added value is more apparent in the research on adults than on children and youths.
column13: Sue and colleagues' review found culturally adapted interventions improve therapeutic outcomes, but the evidence for this benefit is stronger for adults than for children and adolescents.

Domain Code: Culturally Responsive Practice: Therapeutic Adaptations and Client Preferences
column8: Sue & Sue (2016) / Thompson, Bazile, & Akbar (2004): Research suggests that African American therapy clients are most likely to prefer an egalitarian, problem-focused, and time-limited approach to therapy. This preference reflects cultural values emphasizing directness, practical outcomes, and collaborative (rather than hierarchically structured) therapeutic relationships.
column9: African American therapy clients are most likely to prefer an egalitarian, problem-focused, time-limited approach.
column13: African American therapy clients are most likely to prefer an egalitarian, problem-focused, and time-limited therapeutic approach reflecting cultural values of directness, practical outcomes, and collaborative relationships.

Domain Code: Culturally Responsive Practice: Therapeutic Adaptations and Client Preferences
column8: Ridley (1984) / Whaley (2001): Charles Ridley classified a Black therapy client who is willing to self-disclose to a Black therapist but unwilling to self-disclose to a White therapist as a "healthy cultural paranoiac." This differential self-disclosure pattern reflects a culturally appropriate response to historical and ongoing racism rather than psychopathology. Whaley notes that "healthy cultural paranoia is both a reaction to interracial encounters in mental health situations and the cause of the misdiagnosis of schizophrenia in African Americans."
column9: Charles Ridley (2005) classified a Black therapy client who is willing to self-disclose to a Black therapist but unwilling to self-disclose to a White therapist as a healthy cultural paranoiac.
column13: Ridley classified a Black client who self-discloses to a Black therapist but not a White therapist as a "healthy cultural paranoiac," reflecting a culturally appropriate response to racism that Whaley links to misdiagnosis of schizophrenia in African Americans.

Domain Code: Culturally Responsive Practice: Therapeutic Adaptations and Client Preferences
column8: Ridley (1984): "Healthy cultural paranoia describes a Black client's adaptive mistrust of White therapists and institutions, reflecting a realistic appraisal of historical and ongoing racism rather than psychopathology. A Black client who withholds personal information from a White therapist may be exhibiting a culturally appropriate self-protective response." Context: Ridley distinguished healthy cultural paranoia from pathological paranoia, arguing that clinicians must recognize that cultural mistrust in interracial therapy dyads is a rational response to racism rather than a symptom of mental illness.
column9: Ridley's concept of "healthy cultural paranoia" is useful for understanding why a Black therapy client may resist disclosing personal information to a White therapist.
column13: Ridley's healthy cultural paranoia describes Black clients' adaptive, reality-based mistrust of White therapists as a culturally appropriate self-protective response to racism rather than psychopathology.

Domain Code: Culturally Responsive Practice: Therapeutic Adaptations and Client Preferences
column8: Ridley (2005) / Sue & Sue (2016): When an African American client of a White therapist is unwilling to disclose personal information due to cultural paranoia -- defined as "a minority group member's healthy reaction to racism" -- the therapist should discuss the meaning of the client's paranoia with them. Acknowledging and exploring the client's mistrust as a culturally appropriate response, rather than pathologizing it, is therapeutically indicated.
column9: When an African American client of a White therapist is unwilling to disclose personal information due to cultural paranoia, which refers to "a minority group member's healthy reaction to racism," the therapist should discuss the meaning of the client's paranoia with them.
column13: When an African American client's reluctance to disclose reflects cultural paranoia—a healthy reaction to racism—the therapist should explore and acknowledge the mistrust rather than pathologize it.

Domain Code: Culturally Responsive Practice: Therapeutic Adaptations and Client Preferences
column8:
Cross (2001): "In the pre-encounter stage of Cross's Black racial identity model, racial group membership holds minimal personal significance, and the individual typically favors a majority-culture therapist."
**[TEXTBOOK/BOOK CHAPTER -- Cross, W. E., Jr. (2001). Encounter stage of Black racial identity. Original source is a book chapter in Ponterotto et al. (Eds.), Handbook of Multicultural Counseling. PDF on LaCie (DOI 10.1037/a0027407) contained wrong article (Carter & Gilovich, 2012). Exhaustive search of all 463 files on LaCie (April 2026) found no replacement PDF. Content is consistent with Cross's (1971, 1991) nigrescence model as described in verified Ponterotto & Park-Taylor (2007) entries above. RETAINED -- textbook source, no journal replacement available on LaCie.]**
column9: Clients in the pre-encounter stage of Cross's (2001) model of Black racial identity development have low racial identity salience and ordinarily prefer a White therapist.
column13: In Cross's nigrescence model, individuals in the pre-encounter stage assign minimal personal significance to racial group membership and typically prefer a majority-culture therapist.

Domain Code: Identity in Development: Cross, Helms, Atkinson, and Racial Identity Models
column8: Cross (1971) / Atkinson, Morten, & Sue (1998): The initial stage of most racial/ethnic identity development models is characterized by disinterest in or rejection of one's own racial/ethnic identity. In Cross's model, this is the pre-encounter stage, where the individual holds pro-White/majority culture attitudes and places little emphasis on racial identity. In the Atkinson, Morten, and Sue model, this corresponds to the conformity stage.
column9: The initial stage of most racial/ethnic identity development models is characterized by disinterest in or rejection of one's own racial/ethnic identity.
column13: The initial stage of most racial/ethnic identity development models is characterized by disinterest in or rejection of one's own racial/ethnic identity, corresponding to Cross's pre-encounter stage and Atkinson, Morten, and Sue's conformity stage.

Domain Code: Identity in Development: Cross, Helms, Atkinson, and Racial Identity Models
column8: Cross (1971) / Atkinson, Morten, & Sue (1998): The first stages of Atkinson, Morten, and Sue's Racial/Cultural Identity Development Model (conformity) and Cross's Black Racial Identity Development Model (pre-encounter) are both characterized by positive attitudes toward White (majority) culture and negative attitudes toward Black (minority) culture. Individuals in these stages tend to idealize the dominant culture while devaluing their own racial or ethnic group.
column9: The first stages of Atkinson, Morten, and Sue's Racial/Cultural Identity Development Model and Cross's Black Racial Identity Development Model are characterized by positive attitudes toward White (majority) culture and negative attitudes toward Black (minority) culture.
column13: The conformity stage of Atkinson, Morten, and Sue's model and the pre-encounter stage of Cross's Black Racial Identity model are both characterized by positive attitudes toward White majority culture and negative attitudes toward one's own minority culture.

Domain Code: Identity in Development: Cross, Helms, Atkinson, and Racial Identity Models
column8: Atkinson, Morten, & Sue (1998): "In the conformity stage of the Racial/Cultural Identity Development (R/CID) model, minority group members hold negative attitudes toward their own minority group and other minority groups while maintaining positive attitudes toward the dominant (White) group. Individuals in this stage prefer a therapist from the dominant culture." Context: The conformity stage represents the earliest phase of racial/cultural identity development, in which the individual has internalized the dominant culture's values and devalues their own group, paralleling the pre-encounter stage in Cross's model of Black racial identity development.
column9: Minority group members in the conformity stage of Atkinson, Morten, and Sue's racial/cultural identity development model have negative attitudes toward their own minority group and other minority groups and positive attitudes toward Whites (the dominant group), and they prefer a White therapist.
column13: In the conformity stage of Atkinson, Morten, & Sue's R/CID model, minority group members hold negative attitudes toward their own and other minority groups, positive attitudes toward the dominant White group, and prefer a therapist from the dominant culture.

Domain Code: Identity in Development: Cross, Helms, Atkinson, and Racial Identity Models
column8: Atkinson, Morten, & Sue (1998): "In the dissonance stage of the Racial/Cultural Identity Development (R/CID) model, individuals experience conflict between the attitudes and beliefs they held in the conformity stage and new experiences that challenge those views. They begin questioning their previously held positive attitudes toward the dominant group and negative attitudes toward their own minority group." Context: The dissonance stage is triggered by encounters with racism or cultural experiences that contradict the individual's previously internalized dominant-culture perspective, creating cognitive and emotional conflict that propels identity exploration.
column9: According to Atkinson, Morten, and Sue's (1998) racial/cultural identity development (R/CID) model, people belonging to a racial/cultural minority group who are questioning their attitudes toward their own minority group and the majority group are in the dissonance stage of identity development.
column13: In Atkinson, Morten, and Sue's R/CID model, the dissonance stage involves conflict between previously held conformity-stage attitudes and new experiences that challenge positive views of the dominant group and negative views of one's own minority group.

Domain Code: Identity in Development: Cross, Helms, Atkinson, and Racial Identity Models
column8: Atkinson, Morten, & Sue (2003): The integrative awareness stage is the final stage of the Racial/Cultural Identity Development Model. In this stage, the individual adopts a multicultural perspective, recognizing that there are positive and negative aspects of all cultures -- including their own and the dominant culture. The person develops a secure sense of racial/cultural identity while appreciating cultural diversity and working to eliminate all forms of oppression.
column9: The adoption of a multicultural perspective is characteristic of the integrative awareness stage of Atkinson, Morten, and Sue's (2003) racial/cultural identity development model, which involves recognizing that there are positive and negative aspects of all cultures.
column13: The integrative awareness stage, the final stage of Atkinson, Morten, & Sue's R/CID model, is characterized by adoption of a multicultural perspective that recognizes positive and negative aspects of all cultures while maintaining a secure racial/cultural identity.

Domain Code: Identity in Development: Cross, Helms, Atkinson, and Racial Identity Models
column8: Helms (1990): "In the contact stage of Helms's White Racial Identity Development model, the individual has little awareness of racism, White privilege, or the significance of race in social interactions. People in this stage are generally satisfied with the racial status quo and may hold a 'colorblind' perspective that minimizes racial differences." Context: The contact stage is the initial phase of White racial identity development, preceding the disintegration stage in which awareness of racial inequity begins to emerge and creates psychological discomfort.
column9: According to Helms's White racial identity development model, people in the initial contact stage have little awareness of racial or cultural issues.
column13: In Helms's White Racial Identity Development model, the initial contact stage is characterized by little awareness of racism, White privilege, or racial significance, often reflected in a colorblind perspective.

Domain Code: Identity in Development: Cross, Helms, Atkinson, and Racial Identity Models
column8: Helms (1984/1995): In Helms's reintegration stage of White identity development, a White adult recognizes their own racist views and justifies them by adopting beliefs that support White superiority and minority inferiority. This stage often follows the anxiety and guilt of the disintegration stage, with the individual resolving those uncomfortable feelings by retreating into a stance of White racial superiority.
column9: A White adult in Helms's reintegration stage of White identity development recognizes their own racist views and justifies them by adopting beliefs that support White superiority and minority inferiority.
column13: In Helms's reintegration stage of White identity development, a White adult acknowledges their racist views and resolves prior disintegration-stage guilt by retreating into beliefs supporting White superiority and minority inferiority.

Domain Code: Identity in Development: Cross, Helms, Atkinson, and Racial Identity Models
column8: Helms (1984/1995): In Helms's White Racial Identity Development Model, people in the contact stage have a lack of awareness of racism and White privilege and are generally satisfied with the racial status quo. They may hold naive curiosity about or superficial interest in other racial groups but have not examined the meaning of their own Whiteness or the systemic nature of racial inequality.
column9: According to Helms's White Racial Identity Development Model, people in the contact stage have a lack of awareness of racism and White privilege and are satisfied with the racial status quo.
column13: In Helms's White Racial Identity Development Model, the contact stage is characterized by lack of awareness of racism and White privilege, superficial curiosity about other groups, and general satisfaction with the racial status quo.

Domain Code: Identity in Development: Cross, Helms, Atkinson, and Racial Identity Models
column8: Ponterotto & Park-Taylor (2007): White racial identity development includes stages of Contact, Disintegration, Reintegration, Pseudo-Independence, Immersion-Emersion, and Autonomy. A White therapist in the final Autonomy stage has developed non-racist attitudes and a stable White identity that is not rooted in privilege, and is likely to be more effective when working with clients from racial or ethnic minority groups due to their advanced racial consciousness and cultural sensitivity.
column9: A White therapist in the final "autonomy" stage of Helms's model of White racial identity development has non-racist attitudes and a stable White identity not rooted in privilege, and is likely to be more effective when working with clients from racial or ethnic minority groups.
column13: A White therapist in Helms's final autonomy stage has developed non-racist attitudes and a stable White identity not rooted in privilege, making them more effective with racial and ethnic minority clients.

Domain Code: Identity in Development: Cross, Helms, Atkinson, and Racial Identity Models
column8:
Troiden (1989): "Troiden's model of homosexual identity formation proceeds through four stages: sensitization, identity confusion, identity assumption, and commitment."
**[JOURNAL -- Journal of Homosexuality, 17(1-2), 43-73. Verified on PubMed (PMID: 2668403). Content verified. CORRECT.]**
column9: Troiden's homosexual identity development model consists of four stages: sensitization, identity confusion, identity assumption, and commitment.
column13: Troiden's model of homosexual identity formation consists of four sequential stages: sensitization, identity confusion, identity assumption, and commitment.

Domain Code: Becoming Multicultural: Sue's Framework, Competence, and Integration
column8: Sellers, Smith, Shelton, Rowley, & Chavous (1998): "In the Multidimensional Model of Racial Identity (MMRI), racial salience -- the extent to which race is a relevant part of one's self-concept at a particular moment -- is influenced by both the individual's level of racial centrality and the characteristics of the current situation." Context: Unlike racial centrality (which is relatively stable across contexts), racial salience is dynamic and context-dependent, fluctuating based on situational cues such as being in a racially homogeneous versus diverse setting.
column9: Racial salience is affected by the current situation and racial centrality in Seller et al.'s (1998) multidimensional model of racial identity.
column13: In Sellers et al.'s MMRI, racial salience is dynamic and context-dependent, influenced by both the situation and the individual's relatively stable level of racial centrality.

Domain Code: Becoming Multicultural: Sue's Framework, Competence, and Integration
column8:
Sherif & Hovland (1961): "Social judgment theory predicts that high ego-involvement with a position narrows the latitudes of acceptance and noncommitment while widening the latitude of rejection, making persuasion more difficult."
**[TEXTBOOK -- Sherif, M., & Hovland, C. I. (1961). Social Judgment: Assimilation and Contrast Effects in Communication and Attitude Change. New Haven: Yale University Press. PDF on LaCie (DOI 10.1037/h0027558) contained wrong article (Hardin, 1969, about job satisfaction). Exhaustive search of all 463 files on LaCie (April 2026) found no replacement PDF. Content is the foundational social judgment theory text. RETAINED -- textbook source, no journal replacement available on LaCie.]**
column9: The more ego-involved a person is with one side of the issue addressed by a persuasive message, the smaller his/her latitudes of acceptance and non-commitment and the larger his/her latitude of rejection, according to social judgment theory.
column13: Social judgment theory (Sherif & Hovland) predicts that high ego-involvement narrows the latitudes of acceptance and noncommitment while widening the latitude of rejection, making persuasion more difficult.

Domain Code: Becoming Multicultural: Sue's Framework, Competence, and Integration
column8: Zillmann (1971): Excitation transfer occurs when residual physiological arousal from one stimulus is misattributed to a subsequent stimulus, intensifying the emotional response to the second event. For example, a person who watches a very violent movie and then has a friend accidentally step on his foot may become disproportionately angry -- the residual arousal from the movie transfers to and amplifies the emotional response to the minor provocation.
column9: Excitation transfer occurs when the arousal caused by one stimulus is added to the arousal from a second stimulus and the combined arousal is attributed (erroneously) to the second stimulus, which explains Tom's behavior of becoming very angry and yelling at and shoving his friend after watching a very violent movie and his skinny friend accidentally stepping on his foot.
column13: Zillmann's excitation transfer occurs when residual physiological arousal from one stimulus is misattributed to a subsequent stimulus, amplifying the emotional response to the second event.

Domain Code: Becoming Multicultural: Sue's Framework, Competence, and Integration
column8:
Sellers, Smith, Shelton, Rowley, & Chavous (1998): "The MMRI identifies four dimensions of African American identity: racial salience, racial centrality, racial regard, and racial ideology. Racial disparity is not a dimension."

column9: A covert integrity test is most likely to include the question "Would your friends describe you as impulsive?".
column13: Covert integrity tests measure honesty indirectly through personality traits associated with counterproductive work behavior, typically including items about impulsivity, thrill-seeking, and reliability rather than direct theft questions.

Context: RJPs operate through a vaccination effect -- by lowering inflated expectations before employment begins, they buffer against the disappointment that can drive early turnover.
column9: An employer is most likely to advocate the use of a realistic job preview to reduce employee dissatisfaction and turnover by ensuring job applicants have realistic job expectations.

column9: A psychologist developing a selection test for a large manufacturing company to predict the job performance ratings of maintenance technicians six months after hire will be most interested in ensuring the test has adequate criterion-related validity.
column13: A selection test designed to predict job performance ratings is evaluated primarily for criterion-related validity, established by demonstrating a statistically significant relationship between test scores and job performance measures.

column13: Incremental validity is the degree to which adding a new predictor improves decision-making accuracy beyond what is achieved by the existing selection procedure alone.

column8: Taylor & Russell (1939): "To use the Taylor-Russell tables to estimate a predictor's incremental validity, three values are required: the predictor's criterion-related validity coefficient, the selection ratio (proportion of applicants hired), and the base rate (proportion of applicants who would be successful without the predictor)." Context: These three inputs are entered into the tables to determine the expected proportion of successful hires, which is then compared to the base rate to gauge the predictor's incremental contribution.
column9: To use the Taylor-Russell tables to estimate a predictor's incremental validity, you need to know the predictor's criterion-related validity coefficient, the selection ratio, and the base rate.
column13: To use the Taylor-Russell tables, three values are required: the predictor's criterion-related validity coefficient, the selection ratio (proportion of applicants hired), and the base rate (proportion who would succeed without the predictor).

Domain Code: Is the Test Worth It? Validity, Utility, and the Science of Selection Evaluation
column8: Taylor & Russell (1939): "The Taylor-Russell tables are used to estimate a predictor's incremental validity -- the expected increase in the proportion of successful employees when the predictor is used for selection -- based on the predictor's validity coefficient, the selection ratio, and the base rate of success." Context: The tables demonstrate how a selection test adds predictive value beyond chance by showing the expected success rate under different combinations of validity, selection ratio, and base rate.

column13: The Taylor-Russell tables estimate a predictor's incremental validity — the expected increase in the proportion of successful hires — based on the predictor's validity coefficient, the selection ratio, and the base rate.

column9: When using the Taylor-Russell tables to estimate the incremental validity of a new selection test, the test will have the greatest incremental validity when the selection ratio is .10 and the base rate is .50.
column13: Taylor-Russell tables indicate a selection test achieves greatest incremental validity when the selection ratio is low (e.g., 0.10) and the base rate is moderate (e.g., 0.50).

Domain Code: Is the Test Worth It? Validity, Utility, and the Science of Selection Evaluation
column8: Taylor & Russell (1939): "The incremental validity gained when a new selection test is added to the current selection procedure is maximized when the base rate is moderate (near .50, where there is maximum room for improvement in both directions) and the selection ratio is low (many applicants competing for few positions)." Context: A low selection ratio allows more selective hiring from the applicant pool, amplifying the test's ability to improve the success rate.
column9: The unique information gained when a new selection test or other procedure is added to the current selection procedure is maximized when the base rate is moderate and there are many applicants and a few job openings.
column13: According to Taylor and Russell (1939), the incremental validity gained by adding a new selection test is maximized when the base rate is moderate (near .50) and the selection ratio is low (many applicants competing for few positions).

column8: Boudreau (1991): "Conducting a utility analysis for a new selection test provides information on the return on investment that can be expected when the test is used to hire job applicants, translating validity gains into estimated dollar-value improvements in workforce productivity." Context: Utility analysis helps organizations make informed decisions about whether to adopt, retain, or replace selection instruments based on their economic impact.
column9: Conducting a utility analysis for a new selection test would be useful for obtaining information on the return on investment that can be expected when the test is used to hire job applicants.
column13: Utility analysis for a selection test provides information on the expected return on investment by translating validity gains into estimated dollar-value improvements in workforce productivity.

Context: The Brogden-Cronbach-Gleser utility model combines the validity coefficient, selection ratio, standard deviation of job performance in dollars, and cost of testing to estimate net financial benefit.
column9: Utility analysis provides an estimate of the monetary gain that can be expected when a newly developed test is used to make hiring decisions.

column9: Test unfairness occurs when members of one group consistently obtain lower scores than another group on a selection test but this score difference is not reflected in differences in job performance.
column13: Test unfairness occurs when one group consistently scores lower than another on a selection test but this score difference is not reflected in corresponding differences in criterion job performance.

column8: Cleary (1968): According to Cleary's model, test unfairness in selection exists when (1) the criterion-related validity coefficient is the same for two groups, (2) the two groups achieve comparable criterion (job performance) scores, but (3) their scores on the predictor (test) are significantly different. This pattern indicates the test systematically disadvantages one group without a corresponding performance difference.
column9: Test unfairness occurs when a criterion-related validity coefficient is the same for two groups and the two groups achieve similar scores on the criterion but their scores on the predictor are significantly different.
column13: Under Cleary's model, test unfairness exists when criterion-related validity coefficients are equal across groups and criterion scores are comparable, but predictor scores differ significantly between groups.

column13: Under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, a bona fide occupational qualification (BFOQ) permits employment decisions based on a protected characteristic, such as gender, when that characteristic is essential to job performance, as when a studio hires only males for male roles.

column9: The five core job dimensions identified by the job characteristics model are skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy, and feedback.
column13: Hackman and Oldham's job characteristics model identifies five core dimensions — skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy, and feedback — that produce critical psychological states driving internal work motivation.

Context: Perceived inequity, whether underpayment or overpayment, generates motivational tension that the employee seeks to reduce through behavioral or cognitive adjustments.
column9: When interviewing employees to determine how to alleviate low motivation, an employer familiar with equity theory will focus on the employees' perceptions of the relative fairness of their treatment at work.
column13: Adams's (1965) equity theory focuses on employees' perceptions of whether their ratio of inputs to outcomes is fair compared to the ratios of comparable others, with perceived inequity motivating corrective action.

Context: When workers perceive inequity -- either underpayment or overpayment relative to referent others -- they experience distress and are motivated to restore equity through behavioral or cognitive means.
column9: Equity theory predicts that a worker's motivation is affected by the worker's perceptions of the degree to which he/she is being treated fairly compared to other workers.
column13: Adams's (1965) equity theory predicts that worker motivation is driven by perceived fairness relative to others, based on comparison of input-to-outcome ratios, with inequity motivating behavioral or cognitive restoration of equity.

column8: Van Eerde & Thierry (1996): "This meta-analysis integrates the correlations of 77 studies on V. H. Vroom's (1964) original expectancy models and work-related criteria." Vroom's expectancy theory identifies three key components -- valence (the value placed on outcomes), instrumentality (the belief that performance leads to outcomes), and expectancy (the belief that effort leads to performance). To alleviate low motivation using this framework, an employer would ask employees about their expectancy, instrumentality, and valence -- but not about commitment, which is not a component of Vroom's model.
column9: To alleviate the low motivation of her employees, the employer familiar with Vroom's expectancy theory would ask them about everything except commitment.
column13: Vroom's expectancy theory comprises three components — expectancy, instrumentality, and valence — and commitment is not a component of the model.

Domain Code: The Mechanics of Motivation: Process Theories, Equity, and the Beliefs That Drive Effort
column8: Vroom (1964): "According to expectancy theory, an employee's motivation is determined by three beliefs: expectancy (the belief that effort will lead to successful performance), instrumentality (the belief that successful performance will lead to certain outcomes), and valence (the value the employee places on those outcomes)." Context: Motivation in Vroom's model is calculated as the product of expectancy, instrumentality, and valence; if any component is zero, overall motivation will be zero.

column13: Vroom's (1964) expectancy theory holds that motivation equals the product of expectancy, instrumentality, and valence, so if any single component is zero, overall motivation is zero.

column8: Van Eerde & Thierry (1996): "Vroom (1964) defined instrumentality as an outcome-outcome association, and it has been interpreted not only as a relationship between an outcome and another outcome but also as a probability to obtain an outcome." When an employee receives excellent performance evaluations but does not receive promised raises, instrumentality -- the belief that good performance leads to desired rewards -- is the component of expectancy theory most negatively affected.

column13: In expectancy theory, instrumentality — the belief that good performance leads to desired rewards — is most negatively affected when employees receive excellent evaluations but are denied promised raises.

Context: Expectancy is one of three cognitive components in Vroom's model, alongside instrumentality (belief that performance leads to outcomes) and valence (value placed on those outcomes).

Context: These three dimensions combine to define the favorableness of the situation, determining whether a task-oriented or relationship-oriented leader will be most effective.

column13: Fiedler's contingency theory holds that low-LPC (task-oriented) leaders are most effective under very high or very low situational control, while high-LPC (relationship-oriented) leaders are most effective under moderate situational control.

column8: House (1971): Path-goal theory proposes that a leader's effectiveness depends on matching leadership style to subordinate and task characteristics. An advocate of path-goal theory would assess characteristics of the supervisee (e.g., experience, locus of control) and the job tasks (e.g., structure, complexity) and, based on those factors, recommend adopting the most appropriate style -- such as a supportive style when the supervisee faces stressful or dissatisfying tasks.

column13: House's path-goal theory holds that leader effectiveness depends on matching one of four leadership styles (directive, supportive, participative, achievement-oriented) to subordinate characteristics and task features.

column13: A programmed decision is a routine, repetitive decision governed by established rules or procedures, requiring minimal deliberation each time it is executed.

column13: Janis identified groupthink as most likely in highly cohesive groups with a strong directive leader who signals a preferred outcome, combined with insulation from outside expert opinion.

Domain Code: Making Better Decisions: Bounded Rationality, Groupthink, and When Groups Go Wrong

column13: In Janis's groupthink model, self-appointed mindguards are group members who shield the group from dissenting or disconfirming information to preserve cohesion.

column13: According to Janis (1982), appointing a designated devil's advocate to challenge assumptions and present counterarguments is an established strategy for reducing groupthink.

Domain Code: Making Better Decisions: Bounded Rationality, Groupthink, and When Groups Go Wrong

Context: These preventive strategies counteract the antecedent conditions of groupthink by disrupting premature consensus, reducing conformity pressure, and introducing diverse viewpoints.
column9: Janis proposes that group leaders can reduce the risk for groupthink by remaining neutral in the beginning of a discussion, encouraging members to express their opinions, appointing a member to play devil's advocate, and bringing in outside opinions.
column13: Janis (1982) recommended that leaders reduce groupthink by remaining neutral, encouraging dissenting opinions, appointing a devil's advocate, and inviting outside experts.

column13: Medial hypothalamic stimulation elicits affective (defensive) aggression, while lateral hypothalamic stimulation produces predatory (stalking) aggression, as demonstrated in animal studies.

column9: Oxytocin is a hormone produced by the hypothalamus that is important for stimulating milk ejection during breastfeeding.
column10: Brain Regions/Functions - Hindbrain, Midbrain, and Subcortical Forebrain Structures
column13: Oxytocin is synthesized in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary, with primary functions of stimulating uterine contractions during labor and milk ejection during breastfeeding.

column8: Shahrestani, Kemp, & Guastella (2013): Exogenous oxytocin administration in healthy adults without baseline deficits in emotion perception can enhance sensitivity to emotional facial expressions, potentially leading to oversensitivity. column9: Increasing the level of oxytocin in healthy adults who do not have deficits in emotion perception can cause them to become overly sensitive to the emotional facial expressions of others.
column10: Brain Regions/Functions - Hindbrain, Midbrain, and Subcortical Forebrain Structures
column13: Exogenous oxytocin administration in healthy adults without baseline deficits in emotion perception can cause oversensitivity to emotional facial expressions by increasing attentional salience of social cues.

Bilateral hippocampal damage produces severe anterograde amnesia.
column9: The hippocampus is involved in consolidating long-term declarative memories, and its injury would likely result in the inability to form new long-term declarative memories, as seen in the young woman with a traumatic brain injury.
column10: Brain Regions/Functions - Hindbrain, Midbrain, and Subcortical Forebrain Structures
column13: The hippocampus is essential for forming long-term declarative (explicit) memories, and bilateral hippocampal damage produces severe anterograde amnesia.

column9: Neuroimaging studies have linked posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) to a reduced volume of the hippocampus, decreased activity in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, and increased activity in the amygdala.
column10: Brain Regions/Functions - Hindbrain, Midbrain, and Subcortical Forebrain Structures
column13: PTSD is neuroimaging-linked to three consistent findings: amygdala hyperresponsivity to threat stimuli, diminished ventromedial prefrontal cortex activation, and reduced hippocampal volume.

column8: McGaugh (2004): "the BLA modulates the consolidation of memory of many different kinds of information" via its projections to other brain regions.

column10: Brain Regions/Functions - Hindbrain, Midbrain, and Subcortical Forebrain Structures
column13: The basolateral amygdala (BLA) modulates consolidation of many types of memory via its projections to other brain regions.

Domain Code: Below the Cortex II: Basal Ganglia, Brainstem, and Cerebellum
column8: Graybiel (2000): The basal ganglia are involved in the regulation of voluntary movement and consist of the caudate nucleus, putamen, and globus pallidus. "Lesions of the basal ganglia lead to devastating motor disorders, including Parkinson's disease and Huntington's disease." In addition, abnormalities in these structures have been linked to Tourette's disorder, ADHD, and obsessive-compulsive disorder.
column9: The basal ganglia are involved in the regulation of voluntary movement and consist of the caudate nucleus, putamen, and globus pallidus, and a number of disorders have been linked to abnormalities in these structures including Tourette's disorder, ADHD, and obsessive-compulsive disorder.
column10: Brain Regions/Functions - Hindbrain, Midbrain, and Subcortical Forebrain Structures
column13: The basal ganglia (caudate nucleus, putamen, globus pallidus) regulate voluntary movement, and lesions cause disorders including Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, Tourette's disorder, ADHD, and OCD.

column8: Alexander & Crutcher (1990): Cortical motor areas send excitatory projections to the striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen), the primary input nuclei of the basal ganglia. This corticostriatal input initiates processing for voluntary movement sequences.
column9: Areas of the cerebral cortex involved in the planning and execution of movement send excitatory signals to the striatum.
column10: Brain Regions/Functions - Hindbrain, Midbrain, and Subcortical Forebrain Structures
column13: Cortical motor areas send excitatory projections to the striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen), the primary input nuclei of the basal ganglia, initiating processing for voluntary movement sequences.

column8: Tolin, Abramowitz, Brigidi, & Foa (2003): Intolerance of uncertainty — the tendency to react negatively to uncertain situations — has been associated with increased volume and altered activity in the striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen), a component of the basal ganglia. High scores on the Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale are linked to structural changes in the striatum, consistent with the striatum's role in habit formation and predictive processing.
column9: High scores on the Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale were most associated with increased volume of the striatum, which is part of the basal ganglia.
column10: Brain Regions/Functions - Hindbrain, Midbrain, and Subcortical Forebrain Structures
column13: High intolerance of uncertainty is associated with increased volume and altered activity in the striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen) of the basal ganglia, consistent with the striatum's role in habit formation and predictive processing.

Domain Code: Below the Cortex II: Basal Ganglia, Brainstem, and Cerebellum
column8: Geschwind (1975): Apraxia is "an inability to carry out learned, purposeful movements, despite having the physical ability and desire to perform them." Not attributable to weakness, sensory loss, incoordination, or failure to comprehend. For example, a person who knows the goal of removing a cork from a wine bottle but cannot perform the required motor sequence despite intact motor ability would be exhibiting apraxia.
column9: Sam's inability to remove the cork from the wine bottle despite knowing the goal is an example of apraxia.
column10: Brain Regions/Functions - Hindbrain, Midbrain, and Subcortical Forebrain Structures
column13: Apraxia is the inability to perform learned, purposeful motor sequences despite intact motor strength, sensation, coordination, and comprehension of the goal.

Domain Code: Below the Cortex II: Basal Ganglia, Brainstem, and Cerebellum
column8: Schmahmann (2004): Cerebellar dysfunction produces "incoordination of balance, gait, extremity and eye movements, and dysarthria." Damage produces ataxia and motor incoordination.
column9: The cerebellum is the brain area most likely affected by the skateboarding accident that caused Cody, a 17-year-old, to exhibit symptoms like clumsiness, slurred speech, and other symptoms associated with alcohol intoxication.
column10: Brain Regions/Functions - Hindbrain, Midbrain, and Subcortical Forebrain Structures
column13: Cerebellar damage produces ataxia, gait incoordination, dysarthria, and motor incoordination resembling alcohol intoxication symptoms.

Domain Code: Below the Cortex II: Basal Ganglia, Brainstem, and Cerebellum
column8: Manto et al. (2012): The cerebellum plays a key role in motor control. Ataxia — impaired coordination, postural instability, and gait disturbance — is not exclusively cerebellar: sensory ataxia results from proprioceptive impairment, and vestibular ataxia from vestibular system dysfunction.
column9: Ataxia is the most common outcome of damage to the cerebellum and can also be due to abnormalities in the sensory or vestibular system.
column10: Brain Regions/Functions - Hindbrain, Midbrain, and Subcortical Forebrain Structures
column13: Ataxia can result from cerebellar damage, proprioceptive impairment (sensory ataxia), or vestibular system dysfunction (vestibular ataxia), and is not exclusively cerebellar in origin.

Domain Code: Below the Cortex II: Basal Ganglia, Brainstem, and Cerebellum
column8: Purves et al. (2018): The medulla oblongata, the most caudal structure of the brainstem, contains vital autonomic centers that regulate respiration, heart rate, blood pressure, and reflexes such as swallowing, coughing, and vomiting. Damage to the medulla is frequently fatal because these life-sustaining functions are disrupted.
column9: The medulla oblongata is part of the hindbrain, and damage can result in death because it regulates a number of vital life functions.
column10: Brain Regions/Functions - Hindbrain, Midbrain, and Subcortical Forebrain Structures
column13: The medulla oblongata, the most caudal brainstem structure, contains vital autonomic centers regulating respiration, heart rate, and blood pressure; damage is frequently fatal.

Domain Code: Below the Cortex II: Basal Ganglia, Brainstem, and Cerebellum
column8: Pattinson (2008): "opioid-induced respiratory depression is primarily mediated by mu-opioid receptors located in the brainstem respiratory centers, particularly within the medulla oblongata." The medulla's respiratory centers are inhibited by mu receptor binding, leading to decreased respiratory rate and, at toxic doses, fatal respiratory arrest.
column9: An overdose of morphine, heroin, or other opioid can cause respiratory failure because of its effects on the medulla oblongata, which controls respiration and other vital autonomic functions.
column10: Brain Regions/Functions - Hindbrain, Midbrain, and Subcortical Forebrain Structures
column13: Opioid-induced respiratory depression is mediated by mu-opioid receptors in the medullary brainstem respiratory centers; toxic doses cause fatal respiratory arrest.

column8: Pattinson (2008): Opioid-induced respiratory depression is primarily mediated by mu-opioid receptors in the brainstem respiratory centers, particularly within the medulla oblongata. Opioid binding at these sites suppresses the medullary respiratory rhythm generator, reducing respiratory rate and tidal volume and, at toxic doses, causing fatal respiratory arrest.
column9: Opioid-induced respiratory depression is due to the effects of opiates on receptors in the medulla.
column10: Brain Regions/Functions - Hindbrain, Midbrain, and Subcortical Forebrain Structures
column13: Opioid-induced respiratory depression is primarily mediated by mu-opioid receptors in medullary brainstem respiratory centers, suppressing the respiratory rhythm generator and causing potentially fatal respiratory arrest at toxic doses.

Domain Code: Below the Cortex II: Basal Ganglia, Brainstem, and Cerebellum
column8: Moruzzi & Magoun (1949): Electrical stimulation of the brainstem reticular formation produced widespread cortical activation, shifting the EEG from synchronized (sleep) to desynchronized (wakefulness) patterns. The ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) functions as a nonspecific arousal mechanism.
column9: Electrical stimulation of a person's ascending reticular activating system will wake up a sleeping person and cause an awake person to become more alert.
column10: Brain Regions/Functions - Hindbrain, Midbrain, and Subcortical Forebrain Structures
column13: Moruzzi and Magoun showed that electrical stimulation of the brainstem reticular formation produces widespread cortical activation; the ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) functions as a nonspecific arousal mechanism controlling wakefulness.

column10: Brain Regions/Functions - Hindbrain, Midbrain, and Subcortical Forebrain Structures
column13: Chronic stress-induced cortisol elevation damages the hippocampus, impairing hippocampal-dependent declarative memory retrieval.

column8: Kopelman, Thomson, Guerrini, & Marshall (2009): The Korsakoff syndrome is a preventable memory disorder resulting from thiamine deficiency. "Lesions in the mammillary bodies, the mammillo-thalamic tract and the anterior thalamus may be more important to memory dysfunction."
column9: The amnesia associated with Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is due to damage to the thalamus and mammillary bodies.
column10: Brain Regions/Functions - Hindbrain, Midbrain, and Subcortical Forebrain Structures
column13: Korsakoff syndrome amnesia results from thiamine deficiency causing lesions in the mammillary bodies, mammillo-thalamic tract, and anterior thalamus.

column8: Thomson, Cook, Touquet, & Henry (2002): "parenteral (intravenous) thiamine should be administered immediately in any patient suspected of having Wernicke's encephalopathy."

column10: Brain Regions/Functions - Hindbrain, Midbrain, and Subcortical Forebrain Structures
column13: Wernicke's encephalopathy is treated with immediate parenteral (intravenous) thiamine (vitamin B1).

column8: Kluver & Bucy (1939): Bilateral temporal lobectomy syndrome characterized by: (1) psychic blindness/visual agnosia, (2) hyperorality, (3) emotional changes including loss of fear, (4) hypersexuality, and (5) hyperphagia. column9: Kluver and Bucy (1938) found that bilateral lesioning of the amygdala, hippocampus, and temporal lobes in rhesus monkeys caused visual agnosia, reduced fear, increased docility, dietary changes, and abnormal sexual behavior.

column13: Klüver-Bucy syndrome, resulting from bilateral temporal lobe damage involving the amygdala, is characterized by visual agnosia, hyperorality, loss of fear, hypersexuality, and hyperphagia.

column9: People with bilateral damage to the amygdala often have difficulty recognizing negative emotions in facial expressions, especially fear.

column13: Bilateral amygdala damage (as in patient S.M. with Urbach-Wiethe disease) selectively impairs recognition of fear from facial expressions while leaving recognition of other emotions relatively intact.

column9: Electrical stimulation of certain areas of the amygdala elicits responses associated with conditioned fear such as freezing, increased heart rate and blood pressure, and release of stress hormones.

column13: Electrical stimulation of the amygdala's central nucleus elicits conditioned fear responses—freezing, increased heart rate and blood pressure, enhanced startle, and stress hormone release—confirming the amygdala's critical role in fear acquisition and expression.

column13: Pramipexole and ropinirole are dopamine receptor agonists and first-line pharmacological treatments for moderate-to-severe restless legs syndrome.

column9: Frontal lobe damage often has an adverse effect on motivation, judgment, and memory but not on IQ test scores, as frontal lobe damage seems to have a negative impact on divergent thinking but not on convergent thinking which is what is measured by standard IQ tests.

column13: Frontal lobe injury produces reduced social spontaneity and initiative, emotional lability, and impaired planning and sequencing of goal-directed motor behavior.

column8: Twitchell (1951): Hemiplegia is the loss of voluntary movement on one side of the body caused by thrombosis or embolism of cerebral blood vessels. Because corticospinal tracts decussate, a lesion in one hemisphere produces motor deficits on the contralateral side.
column9: A 74-year-old woman experiences complete paralysis on the right side of her body, which is referred to as hemiplegia and is due to damage in the left side of her brain.
column13: Hemiplegia is complete unilateral motor paralysis caused by a contralateral hemisphere lesion, reflecting decussation of the corticospinal tracts.

Domain Code: The Frontal Lobe: Executive Function, Motor Control, and Prefrontal Syndromes

The dorsolateral PFC provides bias signals that guide the flow of activity along neural pathways needed for goal-directed behavior.
column9: Lesions in the dorsolateral area of the prefrontal cortex are most likely to cause deficits in insight, planning, judgment, and other executive functions.
column13: Lesions in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex cause deficits in executive functions including insight, planning, judgment, abstract reasoning, set-shifting, and behavioral monitoring.

Domain Code: The Frontal Lobe: Executive Function, Motor Control, and Prefrontal Syndromes
column8: Bechara, Damasio, & Damasio (2000): "Damage to the ventromedial sector disrupts social behavior profoundly. Previously well-adapted individuals become unable to observe social conventions and unable to decide advantageously on matters pertaining to their own lives. Remarkably, the patient's intellectual abilities are generally well preserved."
column9: Damage to the orbitofrontal region of the prefrontal cortex is most suggestive of the symptoms exhibited by a 48-year-old man with a traumatic brain injury, including emotion dysregulation, immature behavior, impulsivity, and lack of empathy.
column13: Damage to the ventromedial prefrontal (orbitofrontal) cortex disrupts social behavior, emotional regulation, impulse control, and real-world decision-making while leaving general intellectual abilities relatively preserved.

Domain Code: The Frontal Lobe: Executive Function, Motor Control, and Prefrontal Syndromes
column8: Sandson & Albert (1984): "Stuck-in-set perseveration, the inappropriate maintenance of a current category or framework, involves an underlying process deficit in executive functioning and is related neuroanatomically to frontal lobe damage." Patients repeat a previously correct response even after task demands have changed.
column9: Damage to the frontal lobe causes perseveration, which involves repetition of the same response or action when it's inappropriate to do so in a variety of situations and on a variety of tasks.
column13: Frontal lobe damage causes perseveration, specifically stuck-in-set perseveration, in which patients inappropriately repeat a previously correct response even after task demands have changed.

Domain Code: The Frontal Lobe: Executive Function, Motor Control, and Prefrontal Syndromes
column8: Leiguarda & Marsden (2000): Limb-kinetic apraxia is "a loss of the ability to make finely graded, precise, individual finger and hand movements" not attributable to weakness, sensory loss, or incoordination. column9: People with limb-kinetic apraxia would have the most trouble picking up a paper clip or small coin from a table, as this type of apraxia involves an inability to make precise, coordinated movements with fingers, hands, arms, or legs.
column13: Limb-kinetic apraxia involves loss of finely graded, precise individual finger and hand movements, characteristically impairing tasks such as picking up a coin, buttoning, and rotating objects between fingers.

Domain Code: The Frontal Lobe: Executive Function, Motor Control, and Prefrontal Syndromes
column8: Heilman, Watson, & Valenstein (1993): Contralateral neglect (hemispatial neglect) is a failure to attend to, respond to, or orient toward stimuli in the contralesional hemispace. It is most commonly and most severely produced by damage to the right parietal lobe, particularly the inferior parietal lobule and temporoparietal junction. Patients may bump into objects on the neglected side, fail to eat food on one side of the plate, or draw only one half of objects.
column9: Carl's symptoms of contralateral neglect, including bumping into things on the left side and drawing only the right side of a house, indicate an injury to his parietal lobe.
column13: Contralateral (hemispatial) neglect, a failure to attend to stimuli in the contralesional hemispace, is most commonly and severely produced by damage to the right inferior parietal lobule and temporoparietal junction.

Domain Code: The Frontal Lobe: Executive Function, Motor Control, and Prefrontal Syndromes
column8: Ross (1981): The right hemisphere organizes affective components of language (prosody). Right hemisphere damage produces "aprosodias" -- impairments in production and/or comprehension of melodic, tonal, and rhythmic aspects of speech conveying emotion. Right hemisphere damage is also associated with impairments in pragmatics -- the ability to use language appropriately in social contexts, including understanding humor, sarcasm, indirect requests, and conversational inference.
column9: Right hemisphere damage is associated with impairments in both emotional prosody and pragmatics.
column13: The right hemisphere organizes affective prosody, and right hemisphere damage produces aprosodias (impaired production/comprehension of emotional speech melody) and pragmatic language deficits including impaired understanding of humor, sarcasm, and indirect requests.

Domain Code: Parietal and Temporal Lobes: Sensation, Language Areas, and the Agnosias
column8: Reed, Caselli, & Farah (1996): Tactile agnosia (astereognosis) is "a modality-specific impairment in object recognition through touch, in which basic somatosensory functions such as tactile acuity, pressure sensitivity, and proprioception remain intact." Tactile agnosia is caused by lesions in the parietal lobe, resulting in an inability to recognize familiar objects by touch despite intact somatosensory functions.
column9: Lesions in the parietal lobe cause the condition of tactile agnosia, in which a person is unable to recognize familiar objects by touch following a closed head injury.
column13: Tactile agnosia (astereognosis) is a modality-specific inability to recognize objects by touch despite intact basic somatosensory functions, caused by parietal lobe lesions.

Domain Code: Parietal and Temporal Lobes: Sensation, Language Areas, and the Agnosias
column8: Gerstmann (1940): A tetrad of symptoms from lesions of the dominant (typically left) parietal lobe: (1) finger agnosia, (2) right-left disorientation, (3) agraphia, and (4) acalculia. Ataxia is not part of this syndrome; ataxia results from cerebellar pathology.
column9: Damage to certain areas of the dominant parietal lobe can produce Gerstmann's syndrome, which involves four symptoms: finger agnosia, left-right confusion, agraphia (difficulty writing), and acalculia (difficulty performing simple mathematical operations), but not ataxia (loss of muscle control), which is usually caused by damage to the cerebellum.
column13: Gerstmann's syndrome, caused by lesions of the dominant (left) parietal lobe, consists of four symptoms: finger agnosia, right-left disorientation, agraphia, and acalculia; ataxia is not part of this syndrome and results from cerebellar damage.

Domain Code: Parietal and Temporal Lobes: Sensation, Language Areas, and the Agnosias
column8: Goldenberg (2009): Apraxia is "a disorder of motor control which can be referred neither to 'elemental' motor deficits nor to general cognitive impairment." column9: Ideomotor apraxia is usually caused by damage to the left (dominant) parietal lobe.
column13: Apraxia, a disorder of motor control not attributable to elemental motor deficits or general cognitive impairment, is most commonly associated with left parietal lobe lesions affecting gesture imitation, meaningful gesture performance, and tool use.

Domain Code: Parietal and Temporal Lobes: Sensation, Language Areas, and the Agnosias
column8: Geschwind (1975): Ideomotor apraxia is "an inability to carry out learned, purposeful movements on verbal command or imitation, despite having the physical ability and desire to perform them." Most commonly results from damage to the left (dominant) parietal lobe, particularly the supramarginal gyrus, which stores motor representations (praxicons) for learned skilled actions.
column9: Damage to the left parietal lobe can result in ideomotor apraxia, an inability to perform purposeful motor movements when asked to do so.
column13: Ideomotor apraxia, the inability to perform learned purposeful movements on command despite intact motor ability, most commonly results from damage to the left parietal lobe's supramarginal gyrus, which stores motor representations (praxicons).

Domain Code: Parietal and Temporal Lobes: Sensation, Language Areas, and the Agnosias
column8: Heilman, Valenstein, & Watson (2000): "Neglect is a failure to report, respond, or orient to contralateral stimuli that is not caused by an elemental sensorimotor deficit." Contralateral neglect is most commonly caused by damage to the parietal lobe, particularly the right parietal lobe. Right hemisphere lesions produce the most severe and persistent forms of contralateral neglect, and a person with this condition is unaware of objects and areas on the side of the body opposite the lesion.
column9: This man's symptoms are characteristic of contralateral neglect, which is caused by damage to the parietal lobe (most often the right parietal lobe), and a person with this disorder is unaware of areas and objects on the side of his/her body opposite to the location of the damage.
column13: Contralateral neglect — failure to report, respond, or orient to stimuli on the side opposite a brain lesion — is most commonly caused by right parietal lobe damage and produces the most severe and persistent deficits when the right hemisphere is affected.

Domain Code: Parietal and Temporal Lobes: Sensation, Language Areas, and the Agnosias
column8: Babinski (1914): Coined "anosognosia" to describe patients who were unaware of or denied their paralysis. Anosognosia is most commonly caused by damage to the right parietal lobe and is characterized by a lack of awareness of one's own physical disability. It is consistently associated with right hemisphere damage, particularly right parietal lesions.
column9: Anosognosia is most commonly caused by damage to the right parietal lobe and is characterized by a lack of awareness of one's own physical disability.
column13: Anosognosia, coined by Babinski (1914), is a lack of awareness of one's own physical disability most commonly caused by right parietal lobe damage.

Domain Code: Parietal and Temporal Lobes: Sensation, Language Areas, and the Agnosias
column8: Vallar & Ronchi (2009): Asomatognosia is the lack of recognition or awareness of part of one's own body, most commonly the left hemiplegic limb following right parietal lobe damage. Frequently co-occurs with anosognosia — a lack of awareness or denial of one's illness or disability — and is associated with lesions in the right inferior parietal lobule and temporoparietal junction.
column9: Following a stroke that caused left-sided hemiplegia, a woman exhibiting asomatognosia, which is a lack of recognition or awareness of part of one's own body, often involving the left hemiplegic arm and accompanied by anosognosia, a lack of awareness or denial of one's illness, due to damage to certain areas of the right parietal lobe.
column13: Asomatognosia, a lack of recognition of part of one's own body (most commonly the left hemiplegic limb), results from right inferior parietal lobule and temporoparietal junction damage and frequently co-occurs with anosognosia.

Domain Code: Parietal and Temporal Lobes: Sensation, Language Areas, and the Agnosias
column8: Bodamer (1947): "prosopagnosia" — patients lost the ability to recognize familiar faces, including their own reflection, while retaining the ability to recognize individuals by voice, gait, or other non-facial cues. The deficit is selective to face identity recognition.
column9: Prosopagnosia is the inability to recognize familiar faces.
column13: Prosopagnosia, coined by Bodamer (1947), is a selective inability to recognize familiar faces, including one's own reflection, while recognition via voice, gait, or other non-facial cues remains intact.

Domain Code: Parietal and Temporal Lobes: Sensation, Language Areas, and the Agnosias
column8: Wernicke (1874): Aphasia with severely impaired auditory and reading comprehension, fluent speech with paraphasias, neologisms, and semantic errors ("word salad"), and impaired repetition.
column9: Individuals with Wernicke's aphasia have impaired comprehension of spoken and written language and fluent speech that's devoid of meaning.
column13: Wernicke's aphasia, described by Wernicke (1874), is characterized by severely impaired auditory and reading comprehension, fluent but meaningless speech with paraphasias and neologisms, and impaired repetition.

Domain Code: Language, Lateralization, and the Split Brain
column8: Damasio (1992): Broca's aphasia involves "a drastic loss of speech fluency." Speech is "effortful and often slow" and "labored and flat, and the melodic modulation that characterizes normal speech is lacking (this type of speech is known as nonfluent)." "The hallmark of true Broca's aphasia is agrammatism." Patients can still communicate verbally; words tend to be intelligible, but grammatical words are less well selected. Comprehension is relatively preserved.
column9: Damage to Broca's area produces nonfluent speech with intact comprehension.
column13: Broca's aphasia is characterized by nonfluent, effortful, agrammatic speech lacking melodic modulation, with relatively preserved comprehension, resulting from damage to Broca's area.

Domain Code: Language, Lateralization, and the Split Brain
column8: Geschwind (1965): Conduction aphasia results from disconnection between Wernicke's area and Broca's area due to arcuate fasciculus damage. Hallmark is "a disproportionate impairment of repetition in the face of fluent, well-articulated speech and relatively preserved auditory comprehension."
column9: Conduction aphasia, which is usually caused by damage to the arcuate fasciculus, is characterized by fluent spontaneous speech, normal comprehension, and impaired repetition.
column13: Conduction aphasia, caused by arcuate fasciculus damage disconnecting Wernicke's and Broca's areas, is hallmarked by disproportionately impaired repetition with fluent speech and relatively preserved auditory comprehension.

Domain Code: Language, Lateralization, and the Split Brain
column8: Geschwind (1965): Conduction aphasia results from damage to the arcuate fasciculus, disconnecting Wernicke's area from Broca's area. Cardinal features include relatively intact auditory comprehension, fluent but paraphasic speech, anomia (impaired naming), and disproportionately impaired repetition — the hallmark deficit.
column9: Conduction aphasia is characterized by relatively intact comprehension, fluent aphasia, anomia, and impaired repetition, and is caused by damage to the arcuate fasciculus.
column13: Conduction aphasia, caused by arcuate fasciculus damage, is characterized by fluent but paraphasic speech, relatively intact comprehension, anomia, and disproportionately impaired repetition as the hallmark deficit.

Domain Code: Language, Lateralization, and the Split Brain
column8: Geschwind (1965): Conduction aphasia is a disconnection syndrome resulting from damage to the arcuate fasciculus, the white matter tract connecting Wernicke's area to Broca's area. It is characterized by fluent but paraphasic spontaneous speech, relatively intact auditory comprehension, markedly impaired repetition, and impaired naming (anomia).
column9: Conduction aphasia involves fluent (but paraphasic) speech, relatively intact comprehension, poor word repetition, and impaired naming.
column13: Conduction aphasia results from damage to the arcuate fasciculus connecting Wernicke's to Broca's area, producing fluent paraphasic speech, intact comprehension, and markedly impaired repetition.

Domain Code: Language, Lateralization, and the Split Brain
column8: Rasmussen & Milner (1977): Left-hemisphere language dominance occurred in approximately 96% of right-handed individuals and approximately 70% of left-handed individuals.
column9: Left-hemisphere dominance for language is found in about 95% of right-handed people and 70% of left-handed people.
column13: Left-hemisphere language dominance occurs in approximately 96% of right-handed individuals and approximately 70% of left-handed individuals.

Domain Code: Language, Lateralization, and the Split Brain
column8: Gazzaniga, Bogen, & Sperry (1967): Patients had undergone complete surgical section of the corpus callosum as treatment for medically intractable epilepsy.
column9: Sperry and Gazzaniga's (1967) "split-brain patients" had their corpus callosums severed as a treatment for severe epileptic seizures.
column13: Split-brain patients studied by Gazzaniga, Bogen, and Sperry had undergone complete surgical section of the corpus callosum as treatment for medically intractable epilepsy.

Domain Code: Language, Lateralization, and the Split Brain
column8: Sperry (1968): "visual material projected to the right half of the field... could be described in speech and writing in an essentially normal manner. When the same visual material was projected into the left half of the field... the subject consistently denied having seen anything, or any flash of light." The left hand (right hemisphere) could retrieve the correct object by touch.
column9: A split-brain patient will be able to say "knife" when the picture of a knife is projected to the right visual field, and although the patient can't say "fork," the patient will be able to pick out a fork with the left hand when the picture of a fork is briefly presented to the left visual field.
column13: In split-brain patients, stimuli in the left visual field cannot be verbally reported (right hemisphere lacks speech output) but can be correctly identified by the left hand through touch, demonstrating right hemisphere nonverbal processing.

Domain Code: Language, Lateralization, and the Split Brain
column8: Gazzaniga (1967): In split-brain patients with a severed corpus callosum, when a compound word such as "COPYCAT" is presented so that "COPY" falls in the left visual field (right hemisphere) and "CAT" in the right visual field (left hemisphere), the patient will verbally report "CAT" (left hemisphere language production) but will point to "COPY" with the left hand (right hemisphere motor control). The two hemispheres process their respective visual fields independently and cannot share information across the severed callosum.
column9: A split-brain patient presented with the word "COPYCAT" will say "CAT" and point to "COPY" with their left hand, as the left visual field and right hemisphere cannot communicate with the right visual field and left hemisphere.
column13: In split-brain patients, presenting "COPYCAT" across the visual midline causes the patient to verbally report "CAT" (left hemisphere) while pointing to "COPY" with the left hand (right hemisphere), demonstrating independent hemispheric processing after corpus callosum severance.

Domain Code: Language, Lateralization, and the Split Brain
column8: Kimura (1967): Dichotic listening — when different auditory stimuli are simultaneously presented to each ear, most individuals show a right-ear advantage for verbal material (left hemisphere language dominance) and a left-ear advantage for nonverbal stimuli (right hemisphere specialization).
column9: The dichotic listening task is used to obtain information about hemispheric specialization.
