column13: In dichotic listening, simultaneous presentation of different stimuli to each ear reveals a right-ear advantage for verbal material and a left-ear advantage for nonverbal stimuli, reflecting hemispheric specialization.

Domain Code: Memory Architecture: From Sensory Store to Long-Term Memory
column8: Sperling (1960): Iconic (visual) sensory memory has much larger capacity than previously believed but decays within approximately 250-500 milliseconds. Echoic (auditory) sensory memory persists approximately 3-4 seconds with similarly large capacity and rapid decay.
column9: Sensory memory has a large capacity and brief duration, storing information directly from the environment for about one-quarter second to four seconds.
column13: Sperling (1960) established that iconic sensory memory decays within ~250–500 milliseconds, while echoic sensory memory persists ~3–4 seconds; both have large capacity and rapid decay.

Domain Code: Memory Architecture: From Sensory Store to Long-Term Memory
column8: Miller (1956): "the span of immediate memory imposes severe limitations on the amount of information that we are able to receive, process, and remember," approximately seven items (plus or minus two). The capacity unit is the "chunk" — a meaningful unit that can range from a digit to a complex phrase.
column9: Miller's (1956) "magical number seven, plus or minus two" refers to the capacity of short-term memory, which Miller found to be limited to between five and nine (seven plus and minus two) chunks of information.
column13: Miller (1956) established that short-term memory capacity is approximately seven chunks (plus or minus two), where a chunk is any meaningful unit of information.

Domain Code: Memory Architecture: From Sensory Store to Long-Term Memory
column8: Peterson & Peterson (1959): When rehearsal is prevented, retention of a consonant trigram declines rapidly to near zero after approximately 18-20 seconds. Established the transient nature of short-term memory without active rehearsal.
column9: Without rehearsal, information remains in short-term memory for about 20 to 30 seconds.
column13: Peterson & Peterson (1959) established that without rehearsal, information in short-term memory decays to near zero within approximately 18–20 seconds.

Domain Code: Memory Architecture: From Sensory Store to Long-Term Memory
column8: Baddeley (2000): Working memory has four components: (1) central executive — attentional control system; (2) phonological loop — auditory-verbal information; (3) visuospatial sketchpad — visual and spatial representations; (4) episodic buffer — integrates across subsystems and long-term memory. No "semantic register" exists in the model.
column9: Baddeley's (2000) multi-component model describes working memory as consisting of a central executive and three subsystems, which do not include a semantic register.
column13: Baddeley's (2000) multi-component working memory model includes four components — central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and episodic buffer — and does not include a semantic register.

Domain Code: Memory Architecture: From Sensory Store to Long-Term Memory
column8: Baddeley (2003): "The model of the phonological loop comprises a phonological store, which can hold memory traces for a few seconds before they fade, and an articulatory rehearsal process that is analogous to subvocal speech."
column9: As described by Baddeley (2000), the phonological loop temporarily stores auditory information.
column13: Baddeley's phonological loop comprises a phonological store that holds memory traces for a few seconds and an articulatory rehearsal process analogous to subvocal speech that refreshes decaying traces.

Domain Code: Memory Architecture: From Sensory Store to Long-Term Memory
column8: Baddeley (2000): The episodic buffer is "a limited capacity system that provides temporary storage of information held in a multimodal code, which is capable of binding information from the subsidiary systems, and from long-term memory, into a unitary episodic representation."
column9: Baddeley's multi-component model of working memory identifies the episodic buffer as responsible for integrating new verbal and visual information.
column13: Baddeley's (2000) episodic buffer is a limited-capacity component of working memory that integrates information from the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and long-term memory into unified episodic representations.

Domain Code: Memory Architecture: From Sensory Store to Long-Term Memory
column8: Baddeley (2000): The episodic buffer is a limited-capacity component of working memory that "provides temporary storage of information held in a multimodal code, which is capable of binding information from the subsidiary systems, and from long-term memory, into a unitary episodic representation." It is the fourth component of the multi-component model alongside the central executive, phonological loop, and visuospatial sketchpad.
column9: The episodic buffer is a component of working memory, as described by Baddeley (2000).
column13: Baddeley's (2000) episodic buffer is a limited-capacity, multimodal working memory component that binds information from the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and long-term memory into unified episodic representations.

Domain Code: Memory Architecture: From Sensory Store to Long-Term Memory
column8: Baddeley (2000): The episodic buffer integrates information across the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and long-term memory into coherent episodic representations. It is controlled by the central executive and serves as the interface between working memory subsystems and long-term memory stores.
column9: In Baddeley's (2000) multi-component model of working memory, the episodic buffer is responsible for integrating information in working memory with information in long-term memory.
column13: In Baddeley's (2000) working memory model, the episodic buffer integrates information across the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and long-term memory into coherent episodic representations under central executive control.

Domain Code: Memory Architecture: From Sensory Store to Long-Term Memory
column8: Tulving (1972): Episodic memory — "memory for personally experienced events, situated in a particular time and place." Semantic memory — "organized knowledge about the world, including facts, concepts, and word meanings, that is independent of any specific episode of learning." Both are declarative memory accessible to conscious recollection.
column9: Episodic and semantic memory are types of declarative memory.
column13: Tulving (1972) distinguished episodic memory (personally experienced events tied to specific time and place) from semantic memory (general world knowledge independent of learning context), both being forms of declarative memory.

Domain Code: Memory Architecture: From Sensory Store to Long-Term Memory
column8: Schacter (1987): Implicit memory is "revealed when previous experiences facilitate performance on a task that does not require conscious or intentional recollection of those experiences." Priming is a key paradigm for investigating implicit memory. Types of priming include repetition priming, in which prior presentation of a word or object facilitates later identification of that same item in a different format or context. Common repetition priming tasks include word-stem completion and word-fragment completion.
column9: Priming is a method for studying implicit memory, and there are several types of priming, including repetition priming, which occurs when presentation of a word or object facilitates later identification of that word or object in a different format or context, and word-stem completion and word-fragment completion are two of the repetition priming tasks that are used to investigate implicit memory.
column13: Implicit memory (Schacter, 1987) is revealed when prior experience facilitates task performance without conscious recollection; priming—including repetition priming tasks like word-stem and word-fragment completion—is the key investigative paradigm.

Domain Code: How We Learn and Remember: Encoding, Retrieval, and Mnemonics
column8: Craik & Lockhart (1972): "Trace persistence is a function of depth of analysis, with deeper levels of analysis associated with more elaborate, longer lasting, and stronger traces." Elaborative rehearsal engaging deep semantic processing is far more effective than maintenance rehearsal (rote repetition).
column9: Elaborative rehearsal is considered the most effective way to transfer new information from short- to long-term memory.
column13: Craik & Lockhart (1972) proposed that elaborative rehearsal involving deep semantic processing produces more durable memory traces than maintenance rehearsal (rote repetition), as trace persistence is a function of depth of processing.

Domain Code: How We Learn and Remember: Encoding, Retrieval, and Mnemonics
column8: Tulving & Thomson (1973): "specific encoding operations performed on what is perceived determine what is stored, and what is stored determines what retrieval cues are effective in providing access to what is stored." Forgetting often reflects a mismatch between retrieval cues and the encoded trace rather than decay or storage failure.
column9: According to the encoding specificity hypothesis, forgetting is caused by inadequate retrieval cues, where conditions at the time of recall are not the same as the conditions at the time of encoding new information.
column13: Tulving & Thomson's (1973) encoding specificity principle states that retrieval cues are effective only when they match the conditions present during encoding, so forgetting often reflects cue-trace mismatch rather than storage failure.

Domain Code: How We Learn and Remember: Encoding, Retrieval, and Mnemonics
column8: Tulving & Thomson (1973): The encoding specificity principle states that "specific encoding operations performed on what is perceived determine what is stored, and what is stored determines what retrieval cues are effective in providing access to what is stored." Retrieval from long-term memory is maximized when conditions at recall match the conditions present during encoding.
column9: Retrieval from long-term memory is maximized when the conditions at the time of learning (encoding) new information are the same as the conditions when the information must be recalled, as described by the encoding specificity hypothesis.
column13: Tulving & Thomson's (1973) encoding specificity principle states that retrieval is maximized when conditions at recall match those present during encoding, because what is stored depends on how material was encoded.

Domain Code: How We Learn and Remember: Encoding, Retrieval, and Mnemonics
column8: Rundus (1971): The primacy effect is attributable to differential rehearsal: early list items receive more rehearsals due to less competition for rehearsal time. Strong positive correlation between number of rehearsals and recall probability, confirming greater transfer into long-term memory.
column9: The primacy effect in the serial position effect is due to the transfer of information from short- to long-term memory.
column13: Rundus (1971) demonstrated that the primacy effect occurs because early list items receive more rehearsals due to less competition for rehearsal time, enabling greater transfer into long-term memory.

Domain Code: How We Learn and Remember: Encoding, Retrieval, and Mnemonics
column8: Yates (1966): The method of loci involves selecting a well-known spatial route and mentally placing each item at successive locations. During retrieval, one mentally "walks" through the route, each location serving as a retrieval cue.
column9: The method of loci, which involves visually placing each item in a list of unrelated words in different locations in a familiar place, is most useful for remembering such a list.
column13: The method of loci involves mentally placing items at successive locations along a familiar spatial route, then mentally retracing that route at retrieval, with each location serving as a cue.

Domain Code: How We Learn and Remember: Encoding, Retrieval, and Mnemonics
column8: Yates (1966): The method of loci is a mnemonic strategy in which each item to be remembered is mentally placed at a distinct location along a well-known spatial route. During retrieval, one mentally "walks" through the route, and each location serves as a retrieval cue for the associated item. Effective for encoding and recalling lists of unrelated words.
column9: In the method of loci, each word in a list is visually linked to a familiar site or object to help encode and recall the list of unrelated words.
column13: In the method of loci, items to be remembered are mentally placed at distinct locations along a familiar spatial route, and mental "walking" of that route during retrieval uses each location as a cue for the associated item.

Domain Code: How We Learn and Remember: Encoding, Retrieval, and Mnemonics
column8: Atkinson (1975): The keyword method is a two-stage process: (1) "acoustic link" — an English word that sounds like part of the foreign word; (2) "imagery link" — a vivid mental image associating the keyword with the translation. Significantly enhanced vocabulary learning compared to rote rehearsal.
column9: The keyword method is particularly useful for foreign (second) language learning.
column13: Atkinson's (1975) keyword method enhances foreign vocabulary learning through two links: an acoustic link (an English word sounding like the foreign word) and an imagery link (a vivid image associating the keyword with its translation).

Domain Code: How We Learn and Remember: Encoding, Retrieval, and Mnemonics
column8: Bellezza (1981): An acrostic is a mnemonic device in which the first letter of each word in a sentence corresponds to the first letter of each item to be remembered. "On old Olympus' towering top, a Finn and German viewed some hops" is a classic acrostic for the twelve cranial nerves (olfactory, optic, oculomotor, trochlear, trigeminal, abducens, facial, auditory/vestibulocochlear, glossopharyngeal, vagus, spinal accessory, hypoglossal).
column9: The use of the phrase "on old Olympus towering top, a Finn and German viewed some hops" by a psychology student is an example of an acrostic technique to remember the 12 cranial nerves.
column13: An acrostic is a mnemonic device in which the first letter of each word in a sentence corresponds to the first letter of each item to be recalled, as in the cranial nerves sentence "On old Olympus' towering top, a Finn and German viewed some hops."

Domain Code: How We Learn and Remember: Encoding, Retrieval, and Mnemonics
column8: Tolman & Honzik (1930): Rats exploring a maze without reward showed sudden, dramatic improvement when food was introduced, immediately matching rewarded rats' performance. Learning had occurred but remained "latent" until motivation was introduced. Evidence of "cognitive maps" formed during unrewarded exploration.
column9: Tolman and Honzik concluded that rats allowed to explore a maze without being given a reward formed cognitive maps of the maze, confirming that latent learning occurs without reinforcement.
column13: Tolman & Honzik (1930) demonstrated latent learning: rats exploring a maze without reward formed cognitive maps, showing sudden performance improvement matching rewarded rats when food was introduced.

Domain Code: How We Learn and Remember: Encoding, Retrieval, and Mnemonics
column8: Einstein & McDaniel (1990): Prospective memory is "memory for intentions — remembering to carry out an action at some point in the future." Requires self-initiated retrieval.
column9: Prospective memory refers to memory for tasks that must be performed or events that will occur in the future, such as remembering that you have a dentist appointment next Thursday morning.
column13: Prospective memory, as defined by Einstein & McDaniel (1990), is memory for intentions — remembering to perform an action at a future point — and requires self-initiated retrieval.

Domain Code: How Memory Fails: Forgetting, Interference, and False Memory
column8: Underwood (1957): Proactive interference (PI) — impairment of new learning by previously acquired material — is a major source of forgetting.
column9: Proactive interference occurs when prior learning (e.g., Spanish) interferes with the ability to learn or recall new information (e.g., French), as illustrated by Ella's experience.
column13: Underwood (1957) identified proactive interference—where previously learned material impairs acquisition or recall of new information—as a major source of forgetting.

Domain Code: How Memory Fails: Forgetting, Interference, and False Memory
column8: McGeoch & McDonald (1931): Retroactive interference (RI) — impairment of previously learned material by subsequently learned material. Participants learning a second list showed significantly poorer recall of the first list compared to those who rested.
column9: Retroactive interference, where more recently acquired information interferes with the ability to recall previously learned information, explains why you called your co-worker's husband "Bob" after earlier meeting him as "Bill".
column13: McGeoch & McDonald (1931) demonstrated retroactive interference, in which subsequently learned material impairs recall of previously learned information, with greater similarity between lists producing greater interference.

Domain Code: How Memory Fails: Forgetting, Interference, and False Memory
column8: McGeoch & McDonald (1931): Retroactive interference occurs when newly learned material impairs recall of previously learned material. Participants who learned a second list of words showed significantly poorer recall of the original list compared to a rest-only control group, establishing that interpolated learning — not mere passage of time — is the primary cause of forgetting.
column9: Retroactive interference occurs when recently learned information interferes with the ability to recall previously learned information.
column13: McGeoch & McDonald (1931) established that retroactive interference — not mere passage of time — is the primary cause of forgetting, as interpolated learning impairs recall of previously learned material.

Domain Code: How Memory Fails: Forgetting, Interference, and False Memory
column8: Peterson & Peterson (1959): The distractor task paradigm — participants study material then perform an interpolated task (counting backward) before recall. Prevents rehearsal and introduces potentially interfering information. Standard procedure for studying retroactive interference.
column9: Subjects in a memory experiment are asked to recite the alphabet two times after memorizing a list of words in order to prevent rehearsal of the list, which can be used to assess the effects of retroactive interference.
column13: Peterson & Peterson (1959) used a distractor task paradigm (backward counting after study) to prevent rehearsal and measure retroactive interference on short-term memory retention.

Domain Code: How Memory Fails: Forgetting, Interference, and False Memory
column8: Pyc & Rawson (2010): The mediator effectiveness hypothesis — the testing effect occurs because retrieval practice prompts learners to generate and strengthen mediators (semantic links) that are more effective for later recall than those established during restudy.
column9: Research suggests that the mediator effectiveness hypothesis is most useful for understanding the "testing effect."
column13: The mediator effectiveness hypothesis (Pyc & Rawson, 2010) explains the testing effect by proposing that retrieval practice strengthens semantic mediators that are more effective for later recall than those formed during restudy.

Domain Code: How Memory Fails: Forgetting, Interference, and False Memory
column8: Jenkins & Dallenbach (1924): Participants who slept during the retention interval recalled significantly more than those who remained awake. Superior retention after sleep supports interference-based accounts of forgetting rather than trace decay.
column9: The research by Jenkins and Dallenbach (1924) found that people who slept after learning new information recalled the information better than those who stayed awake for the same length of time after learning the information and engaged in an unrelated activity, contradicting the predictions of trace decay theory.
column13: Jenkins & Dallenbach (1924) found that sleep during the retention interval produced superior recall compared to waking activity, supporting interference rather than trace decay as the primary cause of forgetting.

Domain Code: How Memory Fails: Forgetting, Interference, and False Memory
column8: Roediger & McDermott (1995): DRM paradigm — lists of semantically associated words cause frequent recall and recognition of a nonpresented critical lure with high confidence. False memories are subjectively indistinguishable from veridical memories.
column9: Subjects in a research study who read a list of semantically related words and then recalled "anger" as one of the words, even though it was not included in the list, illustrate the phenomenon of illusory memory or false memory.
column13: The Roediger & McDermott (1995) DRM paradigm demonstrates false memory: study of semantically associated word lists causes confident recall and recognition of nonpresented critical lures subjectively indistinguishable from real memories.

Domain Code: How Memory Fails: Forgetting, Interference, and False Memory
column8: Tolman & Honzik (1930): Rats that explored a maze without reinforcement showed no improvement in performance until a food reward was introduced, at which point their error rate dropped immediately to match that of consistently rewarded rats. This demonstrated that learning had occurred during unrewarded exploration but remained latent until motivation was provided — confirming that learning can occur without being apparent in behavior.
column9: Tolman's research with rats confirmed that learning can occur without being apparent in behavior.
column13: Tolman & Honzik (1930) demonstrated latent learning: rats explored a maze without reinforcement showed no performance improvement until food was introduced, whereupon error rates immediately matched those of consistently rewarded rats.

Domain Code: How Memory Fails: Forgetting, Interference, and False Memory
column8: Bandura (1977): "Fortunately, most human behavior is learned observationally through modeling: from observing others one forms an idea of how new behaviors are performed, and on later occasions this coded information serves as a guide for action."
column9: Bandura's (1986) social cognitive theory attributes the acquisition of many complex behaviors to observing the behavior of others.
column13: Bandura (1977) proposed that most complex human behavior is acquired through observational learning, in which watching others provides coded information that guides later action.

Domain Code: The Biology of Memory and Sleep
column8: Bliss & Lomo (1973): Long-term potentiation (LTP) — brief, high-frequency stimulation of hippocampal pathways produced sustained increase in synaptic transmission efficiency. Considered a primary neural mechanism underlying memory storage.
column9: Long-term potentiation (LTP), which involves an increase in synaptic efficacy as the result of repetitive stimulation, has been linked to memory storage.
column13: Bliss & Lomo (1973) demonstrated that brief, high-frequency stimulation of hippocampal pathways produces long-term potentiation (LTP), a sustained increase in synaptic transmission efficiency considered the primary neural mechanism underlying memory storage.

Domain Code: The Biology of Memory and Sleep
column8: Kandel (2001): In Aplysia, short-term memory involves covalent modification of pre-existing proteins and enhanced neurotransmitter release. Long-term memory requires new protein synthesis and growth of new synaptic connections. Learning produces structural and functional changes at the synapse.
column9: Kandel's (2001) research with the sea snail, Aplysia, provided information on neuronal changes associated with learning and memory.
column13: Kandel's research with Aplysia showed that short-term memory involves modification of pre-existing proteins, while long-term memory requires new protein synthesis and growth of new synaptic connections.

Domain Code: The Biology of Memory and Sleep
column8: Kandel (1976): The marine sea slug Aplysia californica was selected as a model organism for studying the neuronal basis of learning and memory because it possesses a simple nervous system of approximately 20,000 large, identifiable neurons. This simplicity allowed the mapping of specific synaptic changes — including enhanced neurotransmitter release and structural growth of new synaptic connections — underlying habituation, sensitization, and classical conditioning.
column9: Kandel and his associates (e.g., Kandel, 1976) used sea slugs (Aplysia) as subjects for their research on neuronal changes associated with learning and memory because sea slugs have a simple nervous system that consists of a small number of large neurons.
column13: Kandel used the sea slug Aplysia californica to study learning and memory because its simple nervous system of ~20,000 large identifiable neurons allowed mapping of specific synaptic changes underlying habituation, sensitization, and classical conditioning.

Domain Code: The Biology of Memory and Sleep
column8: Davis & Squire (1984): "inhibitors of protein synthesis, when administered around the time of training, prevent the formation of long-term memory while leaving short-term memory intact." Consolidation of short-term into long-term memory requires de novo protein synthesis.
column9: Drugs that block protein synthesis while acquiring new information interfere with the formation of long-term memories but not short-term memories.
column13: Protein synthesis inhibitors administered around the time of training prevent long-term memory formation while leaving short-term memory intact, demonstrating that consolidation into long-term memory requires de novo protein synthesis.

Domain Code: The Biology of Memory and Sleep
column8: Squire (2004): Nondeclarative (implicit) memory — procedural/skill learning, habit formation, classical conditioning, and priming — depends on structures distinct from the hippocampal system. Procedural learning depends on the basal ganglia; conditioned motor responses depend on the cerebellum. Preserved in amnesic patients.
column9: Implicit memories, including memories of learned skills and actions (procedural memory) and conditioned responses, are stored in the cerebellum and basal ganglia areas of the brain.
column13: Implicit/nondeclarative memory is preserved in amnesic patients; procedural learning depends on the basal ganglia and conditioned motor responses depend on the cerebellum, both distinct from the hippocampal system.

Domain Code: The Biology of Memory and Sleep
column8: Ribot (1882): Ribot's law of regression states that in retrograde amnesia, more recently formed memories are more vulnerable to disruption than older, well-consolidated memories. During recovery, many patients exhibit "shrinking retrograde amnesia," in which the temporal extent of the amnesia contracts progressively — with the most distant (remote) memories returning first and the most recent pre-injury memories returning last or remaining permanently lost.
column9: Following a traumatic brain injury, a middle-aged woman experiencing considerable anterograde and retrograde amnesia will most likely remember where she and her family went on vacation three years ago first, as many patients with retrograde amnesia exhibit "shrinking retrograde amnesia" over time, with the most distant memories returning first.
column13: Ribot's law states that in retrograde amnesia, recently formed memories are more vulnerable than remote memories; recovery follows a shrinking pattern with most distant memories returning first and most recent pre-injury memories last.

Domain Code: The Biology of Memory and Sleep
column8: Berry et al. (2017): NREM sleep has three stages: N1, N2, and N3. All NREM stages show progressively increasing amplitude and decreasing frequency reflecting increasing cortical synchronization.
column9: The three stages of non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep are characterized by high-amplitude, low-frequency EEG activity.
column13: NREM sleep has three stages (N1, N2, N3) showing progressively increasing amplitude and decreasing EEG frequency, reflecting increasing cortical synchronization with deeper sleep.

Domain Code: The Biology of Memory and Sleep
column8: Kryger, Roth, & Dement (2017): Delta waves are "high-amplitude (>75 microvolts), low-frequency (0.5-4 Hz) EEG oscillations that define slow-wave sleep (stage N3)."
column9: Delta waves are characteristic of deep sleep.
column13: Delta waves are high-amplitude (>75 microvolts), low-frequency (0.5–4 Hz) EEG oscillations that define slow-wave sleep (stage N3).

Domain Code: The Biology of Memory and Sleep
column8: Hobson, Pace-Schott, & Stickgold (2000): "dreaming is not confined to REM sleep; mentation reports can be obtained from NREM sleep awakenings." REM dreams are "longer, more vivid, more hallucinatory, more emotionally intense, more bizarre, and more readily recalled than NREM dream reports."
column9: Dreams occur during REM and non-REM sleep, but they occur more often during REM sleep, and are longer, more bizarre and emotional, and more likely to be recalled when they occur during REM sleep.
column13: Dreams occur in both REM and NREM sleep, but REM dreams are longer, more vivid, more hallucinatory, more emotionally intense, more bizarre, and more readily recalled than NREM dream reports.

Domain Code: The Biology of Memory and Sleep
column8: Roffwarg, Muzio, & Dement (1966): Neonates begin each sleep period with active sleep, the developmental precursor of REM sleep. Active sleep in newborns is characterized by irregular respirations, rapid eye movements, facial grimaces, and limb twitches. This is the functional equivalent of stage R (REM) sleep in adults, which adults typically enter only after progressing through NREM stages.
column9: Fred and Ethel's newborn infant will begin each sleep period with active sleep, which is most similar to stage R sleep in adults.
column13: Unlike adults who enter REM only after NREM stages, neonates begin each sleep period with active sleep (the developmental precursor of REM), characterized by irregular respirations, rapid eye movements, facial grimaces, and limb twitches.

Domain Code: Sleep Across the Lifespan and Sensation/Perception
column8: Roffwarg, Muzio, & Dement (1966): "the neonate enters sleep through an initial period of active (REM) sleep, in contrast to the NREM-onset pattern that characterizes sleep in older children and adults." This pattern persists through approximately the first three months of life.
column9: Infants less than three months of age usually begin a sleep period with REM sleep.
column13: Infants under approximately three months of age begin sleep periods with REM (active) sleep, in contrast to the NREM-onset pattern that characterizes sleep in older children and adults.

Domain Code: Sleep Across the Lifespan and Sensation/Perception
column8: Roffwarg, Muzio, & Dement (1966): "The neonate sleeps approximately 16-18 hours per day, with REM sleep comprising approximately 50% of total sleep time. REM sleep proportion declines steeply during the first years of life, reaching approximately 25-30% by age 5, and then remains relatively stable at 20-25% throughout adulthood."
column9: Infants spend about 16 to 20 hours each day sleeping, with about 50% of this time in REM sleep, and this proportion of REM sleep drops to about 25% by age five and continues at that level during the rest of childhood, adolescence, and adulthood.
column13: Neonates sleep approximately 16-18 hours per day with REM sleep comprising 50% of total sleep time; this proportion declines to 25-30% by age 5 and remains relatively stable at 20-25% throughout adulthood.

Domain Code: Sleep Across the Lifespan and Sensation/Perception
column8: Duffy & Czeisler (2002): Healthy older adults show an advance in circadian phase relative to younger adults, with earlier sleep-wake timing and a shift toward greater morningness preference. A shortening of circadian period with age cannot account for the advanced circadian phase.
column9: Advanced sleep phase, involving an earlier sleep-wake cycle, is most characteristic of older adults.
column13: Healthy older adults show an advance in circadian phase relative to younger adults, characterized by earlier sleep-wake timing and greater morningness preference.

Domain Code: Sleep Across the Lifespan and Sensation/Perception
column8: Hering (1878/1964): Color vision is mediated by three opponent neural channels: red vs. green, blue vs. yellow, black vs. white. Stimulation of one member inhibits the other. Explains negative afterimages: prolonged viewing of one color fatigues that channel, and the opponent process temporarily dominates.
column9: Opponent process theory best explains the experience of negative afterimages, proposing that there are three types of bipolar receptor cells in the visual system - red/green, yellow/blue, and white/black.
column13: Hering's opponent process theory explains negative afterimages through three opponent neural channels (red/green, blue/yellow, black/white), where prolonged stimulation fatigues one channel and allows the opposing process to temporarily dominate.

Domain Code: Sleep Across the Lifespan and Sensation/Perception
column8: Howard & Rogers (2012): Retinal (binocular) disparity is "the difference in the positions of corresponding points in the two retinal images that arises because the two eyes view the world from slightly different horizontal positions." Most effective at close distances; beyond that, monocular cues become primary.
column9: Retinal disparity refers to differences in retinal images in the left and right eyes and is responsible for depth perception of objects that are at a close distance, in contrast to motion parallax, interposition, and linear perspective which are responsible for depth perception of objects at a greater distance.
column13: Retinal (binocular) disparity — the difference between the two eyes' retinal images due to their horizontal separation — is the most effective depth cue at close distances, while monocular cues dominate at greater distances.

Domain Code: Sleep Across the Lifespan and Sensation/Perception
column8: Green & Swets (1966): In signal detection theory, d-prime (d') is a measure of sensitivity — the ability to discriminate signal from noise. It is calculated as the difference between the z-transformed hit rate and the z-transformed false alarm rate: d' = z(hit rate) - z(false alarm rate). A higher d' indicates greater discriminability between signal and noise.
column9: In signal detection theory, d-prime (d') indicates the difference between the standard scores for the hit rate and false alarm rate.
column13: In signal detection theory, d-prime (d') measures sensitivity and is calculated as the difference between the z-transformed hit rate and z-transformed false alarm rate: d' = z(hit rate) − z(false alarm rate).

Domain Code: Sleep Across the Lifespan and Sensation/Perception
column8: Farah (2004): Prosopagnosia — "patients can perceive individual facial features and determine that a stimulus is a face (intact bottom-up processing) but cannot match the perceived face to stored identity representations (impaired top-down recognition)."
column9: Prosopagnosia (face blindness) is best described as involving intact bottom-up processing with a lack of top-down processing.
column13: Prosopagnosia involves intact bottom-up perceptual processing of faces but impaired top-down matching of perceived faces to stored identity representations.

Domain Code: Emotion, Arousal, and Stress: The Feeling Brain
column8: James (1884): "the bodily changes follow directly the perception of the exciting fact, and that our feeling of the same changes as they occur IS the emotion." The emotion does not cause the physiological response; rather, the physiological response produces the emotional experience ("we feel sad because we cry").
column9: The James-Lange theory suggests that a stimulus is perceived, bodily arousal and behavior occur, and emotion is then experienced.
column13: The James-Lange theory proposes that physiological responses to stimuli produce emotional experience, not the reverse — we feel sad because we cry, rather than crying because we feel sad.

Domain Code: Emotion, Arousal, and Stress: The Feeling Brain
column8: Cannon (1927): An emotion-provoking stimulus activates the thalamus, which simultaneously sends signals to the cortex (subjective experience) and to the autonomic nervous system/skeletal muscles (physiological arousal). Experience and arousal are concurrent and independent.
column9: The Cannon-Bard theory proposes that physiological arousal and the experience of emotion occur simultaneously and independently in response to a stimulus.
column13: The Cannon-Bard theory proposes that an emotion-provoking stimulus activates the thalamus, which simultaneously and independently sends signals producing subjective emotional experience and physiological arousal.

Domain Code: Emotion, Arousal, and Stress: The Feeling Brain
column8: Schachter & Singer (1962): "An emotional state may be considered a function of a state of physiological arousal and of a cognition appropriate to this state of arousal." An important assumption of their two-factor theory is that the bodily responses (physiological arousal) associated with different emotions are essentially the same -- what differs is the cognitive interpretation of that arousal. Participants injected with epinephrine adopted the emotional tone of a confederate, labeling identical arousal as euphoria or anger depending on context.
column9: According to Schachter and Singer's (1962) two-factor theory, emotions are the consequence of physiological arousal plus the cognitive interpretation of that arousal. An important assumption of their theory is that the bodily responses associated with different emotions are essentially the same and what differs is the cognitive interpretation of those responses.
column13: Schachter & Singer's two-factor theory holds that emotions result from physiological arousal plus cognitive interpretation, and that physiological arousal is essentially identical across different emotions — only the cognitive label differs.

Domain Code: Emotion, Arousal, and Stress: The Feeling Brain
column8: Schachter & Singer (1962): The two-factor (cognitive arousal) theory proposes that emotional experience results from two components: (1) physiological arousal in response to an external event, and (2) a cognitive label or attribution for that arousal based on environmental cues. Physiological arousal is assumed to be similar across emotions; the subjective experience of different emotions depends on the cognitive interpretation of the arousal.
column9: Schachter and Singer's cognitive arousal theory proposes that emotions are due to a combination of physiological arousal in response to an external event and cognitive attributions for that arousal, and that physiological arousal is similar for all emotions with differences in the experience of emotions due to differences in the attributions.
column13: Schachter & Singer's (1962) two-factor theory holds that emotional experience requires both physiological arousal and a cognitive label attributing that arousal to an environmental cause, with arousal being nonspecific across emotions.

Domain Code: Emotion, Arousal, and Stress: The Feeling Brain
column8: Strack, Martin, & Stepper (1988): "We investigated the hypothesis that people's facial activity influences their affective responses." Subjects reported more intense humor responses to cartoons under facilitating conditions (pen in teeth, activating smile muscles) than under inhibiting conditions (pen in lips). Consistent with James-Lange peripheral-first model.
column9: The facial feedback hypothesis, which proposes that facial expressions can produce the corresponding emotions, is consistent with the James-Lange theory of emotion.
column13: Strack, Martin, & Stepper's facial feedback research demonstrated that facial muscle activity influences emotional experience, consistent with the James-Lange theory's peripheral-first model of emotion.

Domain Code: Emotion, Arousal, and Stress: The Feeling Brain
column8: Lazarus (1991/1993): According to Lazarus's cognitive appraisal theory, primary appraisal involves evaluating whether an external event is (1) irrelevant, (2) benign-positive, or (3) stressful. When appraised as stressful, the event is further classified as involving harm (damage already done), threat (anticipated harm), or challenge (difficult demands one feels confident about overcoming). "Appraisal is a universal process in which people constantly evaluate the significance of what is happening for their personal well-being."
column9: According to Lazarus's (1991) cognitive appraisal theory, primary appraisal involves considering whether an external event is relevant or irrelevant and, if relevant, whether it's positive/benign or stressful.
column13: In Lazarus's cognitive appraisal theory, primary appraisal categorizes events as irrelevant, benign-positive, or stressful; stressful appraisals are further classified as harm, threat, or challenge based on anticipated impact and coping confidence.

Domain Code: Emotion, Arousal, and Stress: The Feeling Brain
column8: Lazarus (1991): Cognitive appraisal theory distinguishes three types of appraisal. Primary appraisal evaluates whether an event is irrelevant, benign-positive, or stressful. Secondary appraisal involves evaluating one's available coping resources and options — what personal and environmental resources a person has to manage a stressful event. Reappraisal is the ongoing reassessment of both the event and one's coping capacity.
column9: Cognitive appraisal theory distinguishes between three types of appraisal, where secondary appraisal involves determining what personal and environmental resources a person has to cope with a stressful event.
column13: In Lazarus's (1991) cognitive appraisal theory, secondary appraisal involves evaluating one's available personal and environmental resources for coping with a stressful event.

Domain Code: Emotion, Arousal, and Stress: The Feeling Brain
column8: Papez (1937): A circuit of hippocampus, cingulate gyrus, mammillary bodies, and anterior thalamic nuclei as the neural substrate of emotional experience, emotional expression, and encoding of emotionally significant memories.
column9: The Papez circuit plays a fundamental role in emotions and memory, as it is involved in the experience and expression of emotions, as well as the storage of emotional memories.
column13: The Papez circuit — comprising the hippocampus, cingulate gyrus, mammillary bodies, and anterior thalamic nuclei — serves as the neural substrate for emotional experience, emotional expression, and encoding of emotionally significant memories.

Domain Code: Emotion, Arousal, and Stress: The Feeling Brain
column8: Gainotti (1972): Patients with damage to the right (nondominant) hemisphere frequently exhibit an "indifference reaction" — characterized by anosognosia, emotional blunting, inappropriate unconcern, or euphoria. Patients with left (dominant) hemisphere damage are more likely to display a "catastrophic reaction" — marked by anxiety, tearfulness, depression, and emotional volatility.
column9: People with damage to the certain areas of the right (non-dominant) hemisphere are likely to exhibit an indifference reaction, while people with damage to the left (dominant) hemisphere are more likely to exhibit a catastrophic reaction.
column13: Gainotti (1972) found that right hemisphere damage produces an indifference reaction (anosognosia, euphoria, emotional blunting), while left hemisphere damage produces a catastrophic reaction (anxiety, tearfulness, depression).

Domain Code: Emotion, Arousal, and Stress: The Feeling Brain
column8: Sterling & Eyer (1988): Allostasis refers to the process of achieving stability through physiological change. Unlike homeostasis, which implies a fixed set point, allostasis emphasizes that the body actively adjusts cardiovascular, neuroendocrine, and immune parameters to meet anticipated demands. McEwen (1998) extended this concept with "allostatic load" — the cumulative wear and tear resulting from chronic stress or inefficient allostatic responses.
column9: Allostasis refers to the body's ability to adapt to stress and achieve a state of stability through a process of change.
column13: Allostasis describes achieving stability through physiological change by actively adjusting parameters to meet anticipated demands, while allostatic load (McEwen, 1998) refers to cumulative wear and tear from chronic stress or inefficient allostatic responses.

Domain Code: When the Brain Breaks: Neurocognitive and Neurological Disorders
column8: Braak & Braak (1991): The neuropathology of Alzheimer's disease involves progressive accumulation of neuritic (amyloid) plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. The earliest changes (Braak stages I-II) appear in the transentorhinal and entorhinal cortex, then spread to the hippocampus (stages III-IV) and amygdala, and eventually to widespread neocortical areas (stages V-VI).
column9: Neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer's disease is associated with an accumulation of neuritic plaques and neurofibrillary tangles in the entorhinal cortex, hippocampus, and amygdala.
column13: Alzheimer's disease neuropathology involves progressive accumulation of neuritic plaques and neurofibrillary tangles beginning in the transentorhinal/entorhinal cortex (Braak I-II), spreading to hippocampus and amygdala, and eventually to widespread neocortical areas.

Domain Code: When the Brain Breaks: Neurocognitive and Neurological Disorders
column8: Francis, Palmer, Snape, & Wilcock (1999): "the cholinergic hypothesis proposes that the deficit of acetylcholine in the hippocampus and neocortex is a major contributor to the cognitive and memory dysfunction characteristic of Alzheimer's disease."
column9: Memory loss associated with neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer's disease has been most consistently linked to abnormal levels of acetylcholine in the hippocampus and cerebral cortex.
column13: The cholinergic hypothesis proposes that deficits of acetylcholine in the hippocampus and neocortex are a major contributor to the cognitive and memory dysfunction characteristic of Alzheimer's disease.

Domain Code: When the Brain Breaks: Neurocognitive and Neurological Disorders
column8: Terracciano et al. (2014): "high neuroticism and low conscientiousness were significantly and independently associated with increased risk of developing Alzheimer's disease."
column9: The research has most consistently linked a low score on conscientiousness and a high score on neuroticism to an increased risk for a diagnosis of neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer's disease.
column13: High neuroticism and low conscientiousness are independently and significantly associated with increased risk of developing Alzheimer's disease.

Domain Code: When the Brain Breaks: Neurocognitive and Neurological Disorders
column8: McKeith et al. (2017): DLB motor symptoms (rigidity, bradykinesia, gait disturbance) appear early and cause greater functional disability than early-stage Alzheimer's, where cognitive deficits predominate.
column9: Motor disturbances are a more important cause of disability in the early stages of neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies than in the early stages of Alzheimer's disease.
column13: Motor symptoms (rigidity, bradykinesia, gait disturbance) cause greater functional disability in early-stage neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies than in early-stage Alzheimer's disease, where cognitive deficits predominate.

Domain Code: When the Brain Breaks: Neurocognitive and Neurological Disorders
column8: DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association, 2013): The diagnosis of probable major or mild neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies requires at least two of the following core features, or one core feature plus one or more suggestive features. Core features: (1) fluctuating cognition with pronounced variations in attention and alertness, (2) recurrent visual hallucinations that are typically well formed and detailed, (3) spontaneous features of parkinsonism with onset subsequent to the development of cognitive decline. Suggestive features include REM sleep behavior disorder, severe neuroleptic sensitivity, and low dopamine transporter uptake in the basal ganglia.
column9: The DSM-5 diagnosis of probable major or mild neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies requires that the patient's symptoms include at least two core features or one core feature and one suggestive feature, with visual hallucinations being a core feature and concurrent REM sleep behavior disorder being a suggestive feature.
column13: DSM-5 diagnosis of probable neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies requires at least two core features (fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism) or one core feature plus a suggestive feature such as REM sleep behavior disorder or severe neuroleptic sensitivity.

Domain Code: When the Brain Breaks: Neurocognitive and Neurological Disorders
column8: McKeith et al. (2017): The core clinical features of neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies include fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, and parkinsonism. Perseverative or compulsive behavior is not a characteristic feature of Lewy body dementia; rather, it is a diagnostic criterion for behavioral variant frontotemporal neurocognitive disorder (Rascovsky et al., 2011).
column9: Neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies is not characterized by perseverative behavior, which is a diagnostic criterion for frontotemporal neurocognitive disorder.
column13: Perseverative or compulsive behavior is a diagnostic criterion for behavioral variant frontotemporal neurocognitive disorder, not for neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies, whose core features include fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, and parkinsonism.

Domain Code: When the Brain Breaks: Neurocognitive and Neurological Disorders
column8: Johnson (2005): Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a degenerative disorder of the nervous system caused by misfolded prion proteins. Its exceptionally rapid course distinguishes CJD from all other neurocognitive disorders.
column9: Neurocognitive disorder due to Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, categorized in DSM-5 as neurocognitive disorder due to prion disease, typically progresses very rapidly compared to other types of neurocognitive disorders.
column13: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, classified in DSM-5 as neurocognitive disorder due to prion disease, is distinguished from all other neurocognitive disorders by its exceptionally rapid and invariably fatal course.

Domain Code: When the Brain Breaks: Neurocognitive and Neurological Disorders
column8: Vonsattel & DiFiglia (1998): Huntington's disease neuropathology is "characterized by progressive degeneration of the striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen), with selective loss of GABAergic neurons." Disrupts basal ganglia pathways. Glutamate excitotoxicity contributes to selective neuronal vulnerability.
column9: The motor symptoms of Huntington's disease have been linked to GABA and glutamate abnormalities in the basal ganglia, especially the caudate nucleus and putamen.
column13: Huntington's disease involves progressive degeneration of striatal GABAergic neurons in the caudate nucleus and putamen, with glutamate excitotoxicity contributing to selective neuronal vulnerability.

Domain Code: When the Brain Breaks: Neurocognitive and Neurological Disorders
column8: Kalia & Lang (2015): Parkinson's disease is a neurological disorder characterized by the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta.
column9: A progressive loss of dopamine-producing cells in the substantia nigra has been linked to Parkinson's disease.
column13: Parkinson's disease is characterized by progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta.

Domain Code: When the Brain Breaks: Neurocognitive and Neurological Disorders
column8: Gainotti (1972): Left brain-damaged patients show a significantly higher incidence of catastrophic reactions (anxiety, tears, aggressive behavior, swearing, depressive symptoms). Right hemisphere-damaged patients show significantly more indifference reactions (anosognosia, minimization of deficits, joking in a "fatuous, euphoric or ironical way").
column9: Damage to the left hemisphere of the cerebral cortex is most likely to produce depression or emotional volatility, while damage to the right hemisphere can produce inappropriate indifference or euphoria.
column13: Left hemisphere damage produces catastrophic reactions (anxiety, depression, aggression), while right hemisphere damage produces indifference reactions (anosognosia, minimization of deficits, inappropriate euphoria or joking).

Domain Code: Guarding the Gate: Ethical Foundations of Assessment Under Standard 9
column8: APA (2017), Standard 3.10: Treatment of a minor requires written parental consent and the child's verbal assent, obtained as early as feasible.
column9: To be consistent with ethical requirements, a psychologist must obtain written consent from a child's parents and verbal assent from the child as soon as possible when seeing the child in individual therapy.
column13: APA Standard 3.10 requires that treatment of a minor include written parental consent and the child's verbal assent, obtained as early as feasible in the therapeutic process.

Domain Code: Guarding the Gate: Ethical Foundations of Assessment Under Standard 9
column8: APA (2017), Standard 9.03: When assessment data collected for clinical purposes will also be used in research, separate informed consent must be obtained for the research use.
column9: An ethical psychologist must obtain the patients' consent to use their test information in a research study, in addition to the consent obtained for the initial assessment.
column13: APA Standard 9.03 requires psychologists to obtain separate informed consent for research use of assessment data originally collected for clinical purposes.

Domain Code: Guarding the Gate: Ethical Foundations of Assessment Under Standard 9
column8: APA (2017), Standard 9.03: Psychologists may use assessment results for both clinical and research purposes provided informed consent is obtained for each distinct use.
column9: As long as Dr. Shadid obtains informed consent from the clients for use of the assessment results for both therapy and research, it is acceptable for him to use the test results in his research study.
column13: APA Ethics Code Standard 9.03 permits psychologists to use assessment results for both clinical and research purposes provided informed consent is obtained for each distinct use.

Domain Code: Guarding the Gate: Ethical Foundations of Assessment Under Standard 9
column8: APA (2017), Standard 9.02(b): Psychologists must use assessment instruments whose validity and reliability have been established for the purpose for which they are being used; using a personality test that has not been validated as a predictor of job performance for a specific occupation would violate this standard.
column9: As an ethical psychologist, you cannot comply with a request to use a personality test that has not been validated as a predictor of job performance for salespeople.
column13: APA Ethics Code Standard 9.02(b) requires psychologists to use assessment instruments whose validity and reliability have been established for the specific purpose for which they are being used.

Domain Code: Guarding the Gate: Ethical Foundations of Assessment Under Standard 9
column8: APA (2017), Standard 9.06: When the validity and reliability of a test have not been established for a particular racial or ethnic group, a psychologist may still administer the test if no appropriate alternative is available, provided the psychologist describes the strengths and limitations of the results and their interpretation.
column9: It may be acceptable to administer a psychological test to members of a particular racial/ethnic group when the reliability and validity of the test have not been established for that group but have been established for other populations, if alternative measures are unavailable and the possible limitations of the test's results are specified, according to the ethics codes of the American and Canadian Psychological Associations.
column13: APA Standard 9.06 permits administering a test to a racial or ethnic group for whom reliability and validity have not been established when no appropriate alternative exists, provided the psychologist describes the strengths and limitations of the results.

Domain Code: Guarding the Gate: Ethical Foundations of Assessment Under Standard 9
column8: APA (2017), Standard 9.06: When evaluating examinees with limited English proficiency, a psychologist may use a qualified interpreter and must document possible limitations of the results.
column9: To be consistent with ethical requirements when evaluating students with limited English skills, Dr. Bernstein may use an interpreter who is fluent in both Spanish and English and has appropriate training, and must indicate the possible limitations of the test results in his report.
column13: Per APA Ethics Code Standard 9.06, psychologists evaluating examinees with limited English proficiency may use a qualified interpreter but must document the possible limitations of the results in their report.

Domain Code: Guarding the Gate: Ethical Foundations of Assessment Under Standard 9
column8: APA (2017), Standard 9.06: When a test lacks normative data for a specific population and no validated alternative exists, a psychologist may administer the measure provided the possible limitations of the results are clearly documented.
column9: The psychologist can administer the measure to older clients if alternative measures are unavailable and he explains the possible limitations of its results to the clients.
column13: APA Standard 9.06 permits administering a test lacking normative data for a specific population when no validated alternative exists, provided the psychologist clearly documents the limitations of the results.

Domain Code: Guarding the Gate: Ethical Foundations of Assessment Under Standard 9
column8: APA (2017), Standard 9.11: Providing a client's attorney with actual test items and item-level responses may violate ethical obligations to maintain test security, even when the client authorizes release.
column9: A psychologist would likely violate ethical requirements for maintaining test security by providing a client's attorney with a copy of test items and the client's answers, even with the client's permission.
column13: APA Ethics Code Standard 9.11 prohibits providing a client's attorney with actual test items and item-level responses because doing so violates test security obligations, even when the client authorizes release.

Domain Code: Guarding the Gate: Ethical Foundations of Assessment Under Standard 9
column8: AERA, APA, & NCME (2014): Test modifications alter the construct being measured by the original test, whereas test accommodations change administration conditions without affecting the measured construct.
column9: As described in the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing, test modifications (but not accommodations) alter the construct measured by the original test.
column13: Per Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing, test modifications alter the construct being measured by the original test, whereas test accommodations change administration conditions without affecting the measured construct.

Domain Code: Beyond the Clinician's Hands: Automated Scoring, Delegation, and the Boundaries of Test Use
column8: APA (2017), Standard 9.09: Psychologists may utilize automated test scoring and interpretation services but remain responsible for the appropriate application, interpretation, and use of the results.
column9: Psychologists may use automated and other professional test scoring and interpretation services, but the psychologists are responsible for the appropriate application, interpretation, and use of tests.
column13: Per APA Ethics Code Standard 9.09, psychologists may use automated test scoring and interpretation services but retain responsibility for the appropriate application, interpretation, and use of the results.

Domain Code: Beyond the Clinician's Hands: Automated Scoring, Delegation, and the Boundaries of Test Use
column8: APA (2017), Standard 9.09: Psychologists who employ automated test scoring and interpretation services retain professional responsibility for the validity and appropriateness of the conclusions derived from those services.
column9: Psychologists who use automated scoring and interpretation services are responsible for the validity of the conclusions they derive from them.
column13: APA Standard 9.09 holds that psychologists who use automated test scoring and interpretation services retain full professional responsibility for the validity and appropriateness of conclusions derived from those services.

Domain Code: Beyond the Clinician's Hands: Automated Scoring, Delegation, and the Boundaries of Test Use
column8: APA (2017), Standard 9.07: A psychologist may delegate administration of objective personality measures to a trained graduate student, provided the student receives adequate supervision.
column9: Hiring a graduate student to administer the MMPI-2 and similar tests may be acceptable as long as the student has had adequate training and will be supervised by the psychologist.
column13: APA Standard 9.07 permits a psychologist to delegate administration of objective personality measures such as the MMPI-2 to a trained graduate student, provided adequate supervision is given.

Domain Code: Beyond the Clinician's Hands: Automated Scoring, Delegation, and the Boundaries of Test Use
column8: APA (2017), Standard 4.01: When a supervisor holds legal responsibility for a psychology intern's actions, the intern must disclose the supervisory arrangement to clients and provide the supervisor's name.
column9: When the supervisor has legal responsibility for the actions of a psychology intern, the intern must inform clients that he/she is being supervised and give them the supervisor's name.
column13: APA Ethics Code Standard 4.01 requires that when a supervisor holds legal responsibility for a psychology intern's actions, the intern must disclose the supervisory arrangement and provide the supervisor's name to clients.

Domain Code: Beyond the Clinician's Hands: Automated Scoring, Delegation, and the Boundaries of Test Use
column8: APA (2017), Standard 9.08: Psychologists must decline requests to base professional decisions primarily on obsolete or outdated test results and should recommend current, validated assessment procedures.
column9: As an ethical psychologist, you will explain to the director why you cannot comply with the request to base your decisions primarily on outdated test results and recommend an alternative procedure for evaluating the employees.
column13: APA Ethics Code Standard 9.08 requires psychologists to decline requests to base professional decisions primarily on obsolete or outdated test results and to recommend current, validated assessment procedures instead.

Domain Code: Beyond the Clinician's Hands: Automated Scoring, Delegation, and the Boundaries of Test Use
column8: APA (2017), Standard 9.08: Psychologists may use obsolete tests or outdated test data under certain limited circumstances as specified by ethical guidelines.
column9: Psychologists may use obsolete tests and test results in certain circumstances according to the ethical guidelines.
column13: APA Ethics Code Standard 9.08 specifies limited circumstances under which psychologists may use obsolete tests or outdated test data.

Domain Code: Beyond the Clinician's Hands: Automated Scoring, Delegation, and the Boundaries of Test Use
column8: APA (2017), Standard 9.04(a): Psychologists may withhold test data from clients or their designees when releasing the data would cause substantial harm to the client or others, or when there is a risk of misuse or misrepresentation of the data or test.
column9: Psychologists may refrain from releasing test data to protect a client/patient or others from substantial harm or misuse or misrepresentation of the data or the test, as per the requirements of the APA's Ethics Code and Canadian Code of Ethics.
column13: APA Standard 9.04(a) permits psychologists to withhold test data from clients or their designees when release would cause substantial harm or risk misuse or misrepresentation of the data or test.

Domain Code: Beyond the Clinician's Hands: Automated Scoring, Delegation, and the Boundaries of Test Use
column8: APA (2017), Standard 9.04: Psychologists may withhold test results from the adult client when releasing those results poses a risk of imminent serious physical harm.
column9: Psychologists may refuse to release a client's test results to the adult client when they believe that doing so may cause imminent serious physical harm to the client.
column13: APA Standard 9.04 permits psychologists to withhold test results from an adult client when releasing those results poses a risk of imminent serious physical harm.

Domain Code: Beyond the Clinician's Hands: Automated Scoring, Delegation, and the Boundaries of Test Use
column8: Melton, Petrila, Poythress, & Slobogin (2018): When testifying as a fact witness, a psychologist may only testify about directly observed facts and may not offer professional opinions about a defendant's mental state; opinion testimony is restricted to expert witnesses.
column9: When acting as a fact witness in a legal proceeding, psychologists cannot offer their opinions about a defendant's mental state, as fact witnesses testify about the facts (what they have observed), while expert witnesses offer opinions.
column13: A psychologist serving as a fact witness may not offer professional opinions about a defendant's mental state, as opinion testimony is restricted to expert witnesses who have been qualified by the court.

Domain Code: The Therapeutic Perimeter: Standard 10 and the Ethics of Clinical Relationships
column8: APA (2017), Standard 10.10: When a psychologist's preferred treatment modality requires participation from family members who are unwilling to attend, the psychologist should refer the client to a provider whose approach can accommodate the available participants.
column9: Since Dr. Stein believes therapy is most effective when all members of the immediate family attend all therapy sessions, the best course of action when Mrs. Miller says her husband is unwilling to attend additional sessions is for Dr. Stein to refer Mrs. Miller to another family therapist who is willing to see only some members of the family.
column13: Under APA Ethics Code Standard 10.10, when a psychologist's preferred treatment modality requires unwilling participants, the psychologist must refer the client to a provider whose approach accommodates available participants.

Domain Code: The Therapeutic Perimeter: Standard 10 and the Ethics of Clinical Relationships
column8: APA (2017), Standard 10.03: In group therapy, psychologists are obligated to discuss the importance of maintaining confidentiality with group members during the initial session and at appropriate points thereafter.
column9: When conducting group therapy, psychologists should discuss the importance of maintaining confidentiality with group members in the initial and subsequent sessions, as stated in the APA Ethics Code and the Canadian Code of Ethics.
column13: APA Ethics Code Standard 10.03 requires psychologists conducting group therapy to discuss the importance of maintaining confidentiality during the initial session and at appropriate points thereafter.

Domain Code: The Therapeutic Perimeter: Standard 10 and the Ethics of Clinical Relationships
column8: APA (2017), Standard 10.04: When a client discloses concurrent treatment with another mental health professional, the psychologist should discuss the situation with the client to understand the rationale and determine the most appropriate course of action.
column9: At the beginning of his fourth therapy session, Antonio tells Dr. Wickham that he's also seeing another therapist who was referred to him by a co-worker, and to be consistent with ethical guidelines, Dr. Wickham should discuss the situation with Antonio to find out why he's seeing two therapists at the same time and determine the best course of action.
column13: APA Ethics Code Standard 10.04 requires that when a client discloses concurrent treatment with another mental health professional, the psychologist should discuss the situation with the client to understand the rationale and determine the appropriate course of action.

Domain Code: The Therapeutic Perimeter: Standard 10 and the Ethics of Clinical Relationships
column8: APA (2017), Standard 3.05: A psychologist may maintain a social relationship with the relative of a former client provided it does not compromise professional objectivity or risk exploitation.
column9: Dr. Browne will continue dating Susie, who is the sister of one of his former clients, as an ethical psychologist, in accordance with the APA's Ethics Code and the Canadian Code of Ethics.
column13: Per APA Ethics Code Standard 3.05, a psychologist may maintain a social relationship with a former client's relative provided it does not compromise professional objectivity or risk exploitation.

Domain Code: The Therapeutic Perimeter: Standard 10 and the Ethics of Clinical Relationships
column8: APA (2017), Standard 10.05: Psychologists do not engage in sexual intimacies with current therapy clients. Standard 10.08(a): Sexual intimacies with former therapy clients are prohibited for at least two years after cessation of therapy, and even after two years, the psychologist must demonstrate that no exploitation has occurred. When a therapeutic relationship involves deep emotional involvement, the prohibition may effectively be permanent.
column9: Agreeing to date Ms. Kazinsky, a client Dr. Moore has been seeing in therapy for three months, would be unethical regardless of how much time passes between the last therapy session and their first date, as this would violate the APA's and Canadian Code of Ethics' standards regarding therapist-client relationships.
column13: APA Standards 10.05 and 10.08 prohibit sexual intimacies with current clients absolutely, and with former clients for at least two years post-termination; when deep emotional involvement existed, the prohibition may be effectively permanent.

Domain Code: The Therapeutic Perimeter: Standard 10 and the Ethics of Clinical Relationships
column8: APA (2017), Standard 10.08: Sexual relationships with former clients are prohibited unless at least two years have elapsed since the last professional contact, and even then the psychologist bears the burden of demonstrating that no exploitation occurred.
column9: Ethical guidelines prohibit psychologists from becoming sexually involved with former clients unless certain conditions are met.
column13: APA Standard 10.08 prohibits sexual relationships with former clients unless at least two years have elapsed since last professional contact, and even then the psychologist must demonstrate no exploitation occurred.

Domain Code: The Therapeutic Perimeter: Standard 10 and the Ethics of Clinical Relationships
column8: APA (2017), Standard 10.07: Psychologists do not accept as therapy clients persons with whom they have engaged in sexual intimacies. This prohibition is absolute and applies regardless of the time elapsed since the sexual relationship.
column9: Providing therapy to former sexual partners is unacceptable under any circumstances, as stated in the APA's Ethics Code and the Canadian Code of Ethics.
column13: APA Standard 10.07 absolutely prohibits providing therapy to former sexual partners regardless of how much time has elapsed since the sexual relationship ended.

Domain Code: The Therapeutic Perimeter: Standard 10 and the Ethics of Clinical Relationships
column8: APA (2017), Standard 10.10(b): A psychologist may terminate therapy when threatened or otherwise endangered by the client or another person with whom the client has a relationship, and is not required to provide pretermination counseling under such circumstances.
column9: Based on the ethical requirements, the psychologist may terminate therapy with Bonnie with or without providing her with pretermination counseling and referrals, due to the threat from Bonnie's boyfriend Bruno.
column13: Per APA Ethics Code Standard 10.10(b), a psychologist may terminate therapy when threatened by the client or a person associated with the client without being required to provide pretermination counseling.

Domain Code: Closing the Loop: Termination Ethics, Crisis Boundaries, and the Bridge to Assessment
column8: APA (2017), Standard 10.07: Psychologists are prohibited from providing therapy to individuals with whom they previously had a sexual relationship; this prohibition applies regardless of time elapsed.

column13: APA Ethics Code Standard 10.07 prohibits psychologists from providing therapy to individuals with whom they previously had a sexual relationship, regardless of time elapsed.

Domain Code: Closing the Loop: Termination Ethics, Crisis Boundaries, and the Bridge to Assessment
column8: APA (2017), Standard 10.10: When a psychologist determines that a client is no longer benefiting from treatment and no new therapeutic goals can be identified, the psychologist should not continue providing services. This requirement is consistent with both the APA Ethics Code and the Canadian Code of Ethics, which similarly direct psychologists to discontinue therapy when the client is not benefiting.
column9: Unless a reason for continuing therapy (e.g., new therapy goals) can be identified, a therapist should not continue seeing a client when they believe the client is no longer benefitting from therapy, which is consistent with the requirements of the APA Ethics Code and the Canadian Code of Ethics.
column13: APA Standard 10.10 requires psychologists to discontinue therapy and not continue providing services when a client is no longer benefiting and no new therapeutic goals can be identified, consistent with both APA and Canadian Ethics Codes.

Domain Code: Closing the Loop: Termination Ethics, Crisis Boundaries, and the Bridge to Assessment
column8: APA (2017), Standard 10.10: When a client or third party associated with the client threatens the therapist with physical harm, the therapist may terminate treatment with or without providing pretermination counseling.
column9: According to the Ethics Code and the Canadian Code of Ethics, if a client's spouse threatens to harm the therapist, the therapist may terminate therapy with the client with or without providing pretermination counseling.
column13: APA Ethics Code Standard 10.10 permits a therapist to terminate treatment with or without pretermination counseling when a client or associated third party threatens the therapist with physical harm.

Domain Code: Closing the Loop: Termination Ethics, Crisis Boundaries, and the Bridge to Assessment
column8: APA (2017), Standard 10.10: When a third-party payer discontinues payment and the client cannot afford the full fee, the psychologist should provide pretermination counseling and referrals to alternative services.
column9: When a parent, insurance company, or other third party is no longer willing to pay a client's fee for therapy and the client is unable to pay the full fee him/herself, a psychologist should provide pretermination counseling and referrals to alternative services.
column13: APA Standard 10.10 requires that when a third-party payer discontinues payment and the client cannot afford the full fee, the psychologist must provide pretermination counseling and referrals to alternative services.

Domain Code: Closing the Loop: Termination Ethics, Crisis Boundaries, and the Bridge to Assessment
column8: APA (2017), Standard 10.04: When a psychologist learns that a client is also receiving mental health services from another professional, the psychologist should discuss the situation with the client to minimize confusion and potential conflict, and determine the most appropriate course of action.

column13: APA Standard 10.04 requires a psychologist who learns a client is receiving concurrent mental health services from another provider to discuss the situation with the client to minimize confusion and determine the best course of action.

Domain Code: Closing the Loop: Termination Ethics, Crisis Boundaries, and the Bridge to Assessment
column8: APA (2017), Standard 10.04: When a client reports receiving concurrent therapy from another provider, the psychologist should discuss the implications with the client and collaboratively determine the best course of action to avoid confusion and conflict among providers.

column13: APA Standard 10.04 requires that when a client discloses concurrent therapy with another provider, the psychologist discuss the implications with the client and collaboratively determine the best course of action to avoid provider conflict.

Domain Code: Closing the Loop: Termination Ethics, Crisis Boundaries, and the Bridge to Assessment
column8: APA (2017), Standard 2.01: When providing crisis intervention and long-term therapy is outside one's competence area, the appropriate course of action is to provide short-term crisis services and then refer the client for ongoing treatment.

column13: Under APA Ethics Code Standard 2.01, when ongoing therapy exceeds a psychologist's competence, the appropriate response is to provide short-term crisis services and then refer the client for continuing treatment.
